BOISE, Idaho — Joshua and Ashley Durham run a family medicine practice, and for the first time in their lives, they have no health insurance.
When the Durhams began their practice at the end of 2023 — he as a primary care physician and she as a pharmacist who handles the billing — the couple bought coverage for themselves and their two kids on the Affordable Care Act marketplace. But they said their monthly premiums for a similar health plan for this year rose several hundred dollars to nearly $1,600.
They decided to pay out-of-pocket for their medical expenses instead, leaning on $50,000 they had set aside in a health savings account over several years.
“It’s nerve-racking,” said Joshua Durham, 47. “It just takes, you know, one little accident, and then you got a big fat bill.”
The healthcare industry traditionally has more of its workforce on medical insurance than many other fields. Nationwide, 7% of all healthcare workers were uninsured in 2024, compared with 11% of all adults under 65, according to a KFF analysis of the most recent American Community Survey data. And doctors were especially unlikely to forgo health insurance, with just 2% uninsured.
But even healthcare workers are feeling the pinch as health insurance costs rise each year, with employers expecting that costs will jump an additional 8.2% for 2027.
The Republican-led Congress also opted last year not to renew Affordable Care Act marketplace credits enacted during the covid pandemic. While subsidies remain in place for people with low incomes, the pandemic-era credits helped reduce many consumers’ premium payments, especially those working in small businesses such as independent medical practices. Nearly half of marketplace enrollees worked for small businesses or were self-employed in 2024; some of the most common occupations included chiropractic care and dentistry.
Jack Dillon, executive director of the Association for Independent Medicine, which represents 4,000 physician-led practices, said premium increases have become untenable for small businesses, whether employers seek coverage through the marketplace or directly from insurers.
“The cost has become so astronomical,” Dillon said. “You’re looking at it and saying, ‘What’s the value?’”
As health insurance continues to become less affordable, Dillon said, more healthcare employers may seek alternatives to their standard coverage, such as providing higher hourly wages or providing only minimal plans.
The number of people without insurance in the U.S. is expected to increase by roughly 15 million over 10 years because of the expiration of the expanded ACA subsidies and $1.1 trillion in estimated cuts resulting from President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
Healthier people are the most likely to opt out of insurance. That leaves insurance covering a smaller pool of people who tend to be sicker and need more expensive care. So insurers raise prices to cover the remaining enrollees, which fuels even higher premium costs.
‘Healthcare Is a Business’
Samantha LeGault, a nurse practitioner at a health clinic in Boise, said her employer-offered plan’s premium payment rose from $700 to $1,500 a month this year to insure herself, her husband, and four of their kids. LeGault has Crohn’s disease and two of their daughters also have medical conditions, so she said her family has no choice but to continue to pay for that health coverage.
But she decided to skip dental insurance to save money, and she prioritizes dental visits for her children over herself.
She had already struggled to set aside retirement savings and had switched her children from a private school they liked to public school to cut down on costs. Then the new health insurance costs tightened her budget even more. She estimated that about one-fifth of her income now goes toward her monthly premium payments.
“I know how the clinics work, that I am an expensive patient,” LeGault said. “At the end of the day, healthcare is a business in the United States.”
The Durhams have three other employees in their practice. Two of them receive health insurance through their spouses, Ashley Durham said. The Durhams said they pay $420 monthly toward their physician assistant’s premiums.
As a primary care physician, Joshua Durham said he doesn’t need regular doctor visits, because he can diagnose and treat himself — and, if needed, the rest of his family, though he acknowledged that’s frowned upon. The American Medical Association’s code of ethics generally discourages doctors from treating themselves or relatives but makes exceptions for emergency situations or short-term, minor problems. Ashley Durham said she’s filled prescriptions for her family.
Arthur Caplan, a bioethicist and professor emeritus at New York University’s Grossman School of Medicine, said that as more people are “turning toward relatives because they can’t access or easily see a regular doctor,” it may make sense to revisit that aspect of the code of ethics.
Out-of-Pocket Expenses
Healthcare workers with less advanced medical certifications than the Durhams often don’t have the option of treating themselves or family members — or don’t have savings to fall back on for healthcare expenses. And many healthcare professionals, such as Jill Kordick, a 64-year-old retired healthcare executive in Norwalk, Iowa, aren’t willing to go without the safety net of insurance.
In her work, Kordick saw hospitalizations become financially devastating for patients, so she said she would never opt out of health insurance — even for just the 16 months before she’d become eligible for Medicare at age 65.
Last year, she qualified for the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits, allowing her to pay $75 a month for health coverage. Her premiums rose to $800 a month this year when those subsidies expired.

Almost nobody wants a data center for a neighbor. Residents fear noise and air pollution, excessive energy and water use and the loss of open land. In Pennsylvania, a hot spot for new data centers, researchers see an opportunity to solve some of these issues by taking advantage of a much older environmental hazard: abandoned coal mines.
Pennsylvania has the most abandoned coal mines in the country, totaling around 5,586 sites across the state. The state reports it would take roughly $5 billion to reclaim these polluted and sometimes dangerous areas, which have contaminated thousands of miles of waterways and are linked to underground fires, subsidence and sinkholes. At the same time, local opposition to data centers is growing.
Building data centers on abandoned mine lands would provide an alternative to destroying farmlands or local forests, instead making use of already unwanted acreage. Underground mine pools could cool data centers without relying on outside water sources. And companies could help shoulder cleanup costs of existing contamination. The idea is appealing enough that federal researchers investigated it in 2023, concluding that abandoned mine lands offer “land, power infrastructure, and mine water cooling” to data center developers, particularly in a place like Pennsylvania.
“If the data centers can demonstrate that they can clean up, treat the acid water and help restore their local environment, the local people are more likely to accept such development proposals,” says Zhongyang He, a researcher in Penn State’s Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering who’s been examining possible data center development on abandoned mine lands in the state. His research suggests that it’s a proposition worth pursuing—at least compared to building data centers in people’s non-polluted backyards. But could it actually work at scale? Or would Pennsylvania end up replacing one intractable environmental problem with another?
An Opportunity for Reuse
There’s already some proof of concept in western Pennsylvania, where a former mine has housed a data center since 2013. The site of an old limestone mine, Iron Mountain’s West Pennsylvania data center in Boyers sits 220 feet below ground, a 330,000-square-foot facility on a 315-acre campus that doesn’t bring in any outside water. Instead, the data center cools through a closed-loop system that relies on the 53-degree water in a 100-acre, underground lake (not a mine pool, but a comparable concept).
“We are using what the miners had left behind,” said Iron Mountain’s senior director of energy and sustainability, Chris Pennington. Boreholes, dug in mines to reach deep water or minerals, provide infrastructure for internet access, and data center clients appreciate the security of storing their information deep underground. Though the facility regularly recycles its lake water, Iron Mountain brings in some refrigeration to supplement the system.
Former coal mine sites in Western Pennsylvania slated to become data centers include the former Robena Mine in Greene County, which members of the county’s Planning Commission voted in favor of late last year and would use water from a nearby river that it would convert into steam. Another proposed data center at the former Consol coal mine in Washington County, owned by natural gas company CNX Resources, would use nearby natural gas reserves and “remediated mine gas,” per the Pittsburgh Business Times.
There’s precedent outside of Pennsylvania, too. In West Virginia, Energy DELTA Lab’s 450-acre Data Center Ridge boasts access to almost “10 billion gallons of underground water” for cooling at a former mine site. In Italy, an active dolomite mine is home to a data center located 328 feet underground, cooled by the surrounding rock and chilly air.
Typically in the 40s or low 50s degrees Fahrenheit, mine pool temperatures are theoretically low enough to cool data centers. Mechanical cooling accounts for around 40 percent of an average data center’s energy consumption, and medium-sized data centers can consume around 100 million gallons of water per year. Penn State researcher He and his colleagues found that of the 5,586 abandoned mine sites they analyzed in Pennsylvania, 160 had mine pools large enough to accommodate data centers (there are currently at least 100 data centers proposed in Pennsylvania).
He’s research team landed on other advantages in addition to natural cooling, like “legacy infrastructure,” he said. That could include proximity to roads and the electricity grid, which can be repurposed for data centers. Transmission lines powered large equipment at former mines, and some of that infrastructure remains. “That does not mean that…the line transmission capacity is enough for data centers,” He said, but it does mean relevant permits could be in place.
Both Penn State and the Eastern Pennsylvania Coalition for Abandoned Mine Reclamation have assessed a former mine in northeastern Pennsylvania called Morea as a possible data center site. It harbors an estimated 7 billion gallons of underground water via a nearby creek that was routed underground when the mine was active. It still has an electric transmission line, “sufficient for utility-scale solar or a large industrial facility, and expensive and slow to replicate,” per the coalition’s report.
That report also acknowledges the ongoing economic burdens carried by communities that once produced coal. In Mahanoy Township, home to the Morea site, the coalition notes a 20.3 percent poverty rate (compared to 11.6 percent statewide)—a commonality across former Pennsylvania mining regions. A study published in Nature in 2024 notes that people living in areas of Pennsylvania exposed to mine drainage had incomes 30 percent lower than people in unaffected areas.

On 4 June 2020, as a deadly wave of Covid-19 swept through India, celebrity manager Disha Salian asked her father Satish Salian to call a police helpline to check if it was safe for her to travel.
She was excited about an advertising campaign she was going to shoot and showed her parents a photo of the cheque she had received as advance remuneration.
As she walked out of the door, she told her parents that she would be back in two days.
It was the last time the Salians saw their 28-year-old daughter alive.
On the intervening night of 8 and 9 June, Satish Salian was called by the police to a hospital where he learnt that his only child was dead.
Police said she had fallen from the 12th floor of a building in the western city of Mumbai.
Disha's friends at the hospital said she had been drinking alcohol and fell accidentally.
Police later said their investigation had shown that her death was a suicide.
But earlier this month, the Bombay High Court ordered the federal police - the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) - to reopen the case and reinvestigate Disha's death.
The court order came after a petition filed last year by Satish Salian, who had insisted from the start that his daughter's death was not a suicide or an accident and alleged that she was gang-raped and murdered.
His allegations that some senior police officers had destroyed evidence and created a false story of suicide to protect some ministers and influential politicians who had a role in the alleged crime has made it one of India's most discussed deaths in recent years.
In the order, external on 2 September, Judges Sarang V Kotwal and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale criticised the police and said there were "too many glaring discrepancies" in their investigation, which was carried out in two phases over more than six years.
The judges insisted that they were not holding "a mini trial" but said "the investigation carried out by the police raises more questions than it answers".
They pointed out the unexplained delay in police paperwork, that no blood had been found at the spot where the body had fallen and said that the injuries mentioned in the post-mortem report did not seem consistent with a fall.
"We find this difficult to accept," they wrote.
One of the biggest criticisms from the court was that the police had only investigated it as a case of suspicious or unnatural death and not registered an FIR (First Information Report) - a document police have to prepare when they receive information about a crime.
Satish Salian's accusations are only allegations so far, but they have formed the basis of a new investigation by the CBI, which last week registered an FIR based on a written complaint from him.
The BBC has reviewed this FIR and read through the court order in the case.
Summarising Satish Salian's allegations, the court order said that at the time of her death, Disha was working with Kwan Entertainment - a celebrity management company - and represented Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput.
"She got to know about some objectionable activities of the powerful people. She gave that information to Rajput, who innocently divulged that to others. Ultimately that information reached back those people and she was murdered to silence her," it added.
Rajput mourned her death in an Instagram story. "It's such devastating news. My deepest condolences to Disha's family and friends. May your soul rest in peace," he wrote.
In the initial days, Disha's death went largely unnoticed until less than a week later, Rajput himself was found dead in his home.
Police also ruled his death to be a case of suicide, saying he had mental health issues for which he was under treatment.
But weeks later, his actress girlfriend Rhea Chakraborty was arrested following accusations from Rajput's father that she had contributed to his suicide. He also denied that his son had any mental health issues.
Following outrage, Sushant's case was also handed over to the CBI which, last year, closed the case, saying he had indeed died by suicide and that neither Chakraborty nor her family had a role in his death.
In the FIR Satish Salian has registered with the CBI, he has alleged that the deaths of Disha and Rajput are linked.
Disha, he says, shared with the actor "incriminating and objectionable information concerning alleged drug trafficking, child abuse and other unlawful activities" involving a former minister and some others and the two intended to hold a press conference to bring it into the public domain.
"In order to prevent that and protect the persons involved, a well-orchestrated criminal conspiracy was hatched. The victim was gang raped and murdered, and thereafter evidence was suppressed /fabricated and a false story of suicide was created to cover up the crimes and shield the accused."
In its order, the court said that registration of the FIR "does not imply any finding of guilt against anyone" and that no-one shall be treated as an accused unless the investigating officer finds "sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against them".
But as the FIR names some of the state's top politicians, police officers and Bollywood actors, the case has dominated headlines in India amid allegations of misuse of political power, denials and claims of political vendetta.
Satish Salian, who's been fighting for six years to get justice for his daughter, says he's felt "some peace" after the court ordered the fresh investigation into her death.
Disha, he told the BBC, was "very bright, she did well in her studies and read a lot. She had a heart of gold and was very helpful. She was our only child and she loved us very much".
His wife, he says, has been unable to come to terms with her tragic death and has gone into depression.
"I want the death penalty for those who hurt my daughter. Those who inflicted pain on her must die a painful death too. That is what justice for Disha would look like to me," he says.

A rare first edition of the novel To Kill A Mockingbird has been found among items donated to Oxfam, according to the charity.
The copy of Harper Lee's seminal 1960 work was discovered in a box of American books given to the charity's bookshop in Portobello Road, west London.
It has since been acquired by the British Library and will join its national collection.
Shop manager Olivia Haysman-Walker, who identified the copy as being a first US edition, said the book could easily have been missed. "There were lots of books to work through in the donation, but we recognised To Kill A Mockingbird and thought it was worth taking a closer look."
She added: "We realised quite quickly that we had something really special.
"The dust jacket showed its age, and although it was worn around the edges, the pages inside were in beautiful condition.
"It's amazing to think that this book has passed through our Oxfam bookshop and into the national collection at the British Library.
"It really has been quite a journey, and it's a lovely reminder, during Second Hand September, of the kind of treasures that can be hiding among the shelves and donations in our shops."
Second Hand September is Oxfam's annual campaign encouraging people to buy second-hand.
Lee's Pulitzer Prize-winning book tells the story of lawyer Atticus Finch as he defends Tom Robinson, a black man wrongly accused of raping a white woman.
Her story of racial injustice and childhood innocence, set in Alabama in 1934, has sold more than 40 million copies around the world and has been translated into 40 languages.
The US novelist, who was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, died in 2016 at the age of 89.

The man was attempting to rescue two people - a father and son - who were in distress in the water near the San Siro municipality on the lake's western shore on Monday afternoon, Italian media report.
The man and the family he was friends with had reportedly been on a boating trip at the time. The father and son were later rescued by another passing boat, but the man has not been seen again.
The UK Foreign Office said: "We are supporting the family of a British national missing in Italy and are in contact with the local authorities."
Emergency services including a helicopter, divers and boat units have responded at the scene, where the lake's depth can reach more than 200m, according to Italian news agency Ansa.

The curtain might have fallen on London Fashion Week (LFW) - but bosses hope the runway of the future will start to look a bit different.
Fashion Britain is the British Fashion Council's initiative to open up access to talent outside of London - so how do you shift the focus away from the traditional centre of that world?
The council told BBC Newsbeat it has been working with LFW on a series of pop-up events in England, Wales and Scotland to show this year's event was "bigger than London".
Northern Ireland wasn't included as a location for this year's initiative - but will be included next year, the council said.
A recent House of Commons report, external found that more than half (51%) of the creative industries' economic output was generated in London in 2022.
However, it did report that there are "clusters of creative industries" across the country, which included cities like Manchester and Leeds.
"A lot of people think in order to make it big, you have come to this big city because it has the schools here," says Charles Jeffrey, founder and creative director of international fashion label Loverboy.
"But actually, there is so much amazing education that happens in different places," the Scottish designer tells Newsbeat.
"I first started [in] a tiny studio in Dalston [in east London] and we were having to use fabrics from these cheap fabric shops that you would probably only really get in London because of the rag trade," he recalls.
"Now a lot of them have gone and what made London a capital city for fashion has been taken away, so you're probably better getting your fabrics from a little fabric shop in Manchester - it's probably ten times cheaper."
Jeffrey supported Fashion Britain this year, with the aim of opening doors in the industry for creatives outside of London, but how feasible will that be?
Birmingham City University graduate Imarnie Bennett knows a bit about the struggle.
She travelled to the capital to showcase her project with fellow BCU fashion graduates to an audience at Somerset House.
"London is such a big city, it's really well known and there are lots of opportunities," says the 22-year-old.
"You hear Birmingham and it's a bit like, 'will they get us the same opportunities as London?', but I feel like Birmingham is becoming more noticed for what we do."
Bennett says you can harness the power of being different.
"Even colours, some cities are brighter and warmer than others, so it changes people's perspectives on things," she says.
Yet fellow designer Sean Pajarillo says he is hopeful about job opportunities because of how the technology and fashion industry is moving.
"The merging of industries is what's going to create new opportunities for someone in the future," says the 25-year-old.
Natalie Potter is network director at the British Fashion Council, and says the Fashion Britain initiative is "about recognising that British fashion is bigger than London".
Potter says that in the run up to LFW there were events in London, Bristol, Manchester, Liverpool, Newcastle, Edinburgh, Dundee and Cardiff.
But what happens after the catwalk leaves town?
Potter says the aim of Fashion Britain is that it will connect talent to "the infrastructure and opportunities that they need to grow".
"So working with the big global businesses that we do across the country to make sure that they've got routes to retail, to give them active mentorship," she explains.
Potter says this will happen "locally and regionally".
This is something that British designer Priya Ahluwalia believes is vital.
"I do think there is a genuine issue with London being seen as the centre of the universe in terms of fashion," she says.
"There is incredible talent from all over the UK, some of the best designers have come from the north, come from Wales, Scotland".
Ahluwalia spoke to Newsbeat after showcasing her archive at Westfield Stratford City shopping centre as part of Fashion Week.
The designer explained how practical help is important in helping talent access the industry.
"Whether we decentralise or not, London is still going to be the centre of UK fashion.
"There needs to also be support for people to be able to travel to London, show up in London", Ahluwalia says.
For Jeffrey, formal training isn't the only way into the fashion world.
"Sometimes having a university degree does kind of put your foot in the door - but honestly, I really think it's just about the work and work ethic."

A video showing a teenaged girl being sexually assaulted and her male friend beaten by a group of men in India's Bihar state has sparked widespread outrage.
The school students, both minors, were stopped in Jamui district on 19 September. Footage shared widely online shows them surrounded and repeatedly pleading to be allowed to leave.
The boy is seen being slapped and pulled by his collar, while the girl is touched inappropriately and, in another clip, carried away by a man as the boy tries to intervene.
Three accused, also minors, have been arrested in connection with the assault. A special investigation team has been set up to catch the other suspects.
The disturbing footage has prompted anger over the harassment of the two teenagers and renewed a wider debate about the safety of women and girls in Bihar, as well as questions over the response of state authorities.
The outrage intensified after Bihar minister Shravan Kumar said that "sporadic incidents keep happening" and that the government was keeping a watch on them.
"The world is not entirely free of crime," he said, adding that those responsible would not be allowed to escape and would face strict action.
Umesh Kushwaha, of the governing Janata Dal (United), also faced criticism after referring to such cases as "isolated incidents" and contrasting the government's record with that of the previous RJD administration.
Kushwaha later said his remarks had been "distorted and misrepresented" and promised action against those responsible.
Police said the incident took place around 19:00 local time [13:30 GMT] on Saturday, but it came to light on Monday after the video of the assault went viral.
The teenagers, both students of 10th standard, attended the same coaching institute and had gone to the area to take photographs after their classes, according to police.
Jamui police chief Bishwajeet Dayal said neither of them had initially reported the incident - officers began investigating after the video circulated widely online and traced the pair using the registration number of a vehicle visible in the footage.
Their statements were subsequently recorded and a case was registered following a written complaint from the girl.
A case has been registered under India's stringent Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, or Pocso.
Police have also invoked sections of India's criminal code covering assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, assault or criminal force with intent to disrobe, and acts carried out with a common intention.
Senior police officer KS Anupam said three minors had been arrested and that investigators had established the involvement of two other people.
Police have also begun action against 32 social media accounts accused of circulating footage in which the teenagers could be identified, she added.
The shocking nature of the assault has provoked outrage online, with many social media users expressing horror and questioning why a group of men believed they had the right to confront two teenagers for being together.
Some characterised the incident as an extreme form of "moral policing", while others tagged Bihar police and demanded strict action against the harassers.
Shreyasi Singh, a Bihar minister and legislator from Jamui, told NDTV news channel, external the incident had brought "shame to society".
Singh, a former international-level sport shooter, said women in Bihar were advancing in many areas but concerns about their safety persisted.
She called for the remaining suspects to be arrested quickly and for strict action against those responsible.
Opposition leaders, meanwhile, have seized on the case to question the state government's record on women's safety.
Rahul Gandhi, MP and senior leader of India's main opposition Congress party, described the footage as "deeply disturbing" and said the incident reflected a patriarchal "belief that men could police a girl's body, movements and choices".
"This is not culture. It is patriarchy," Gandhi wrote on X (formerly Twitter).
Tejashwi Yadav, the opposition leader in Bihar, said the incident had left him "deeply ashamed" and accused the government of failing to ensure the safety of women and girls in the state.
Members of Bihar's governing coalition have rejected the opposition's wider criticism of the state's law-and-order record and said those responsible for the attack would face strict action.
India's National Commission for Women has also intervened, calling for all those involved to be identified and arrested and for an impartial investigation.
The commission has asked for a report from Bihar police and urged authorities to prevent further sharing of the video clips to protect the girl's identity and privacy.
The Bihar State Women's Commission has also sought information from district authorities about the action being taken in the case.

The News
US drone logistics company Zipline will expand a three-year pilot program to deliver health supplies to a third of the Ivorian population over the next eight years, the latest sign that African governments are increasingly comfortable with using drones to provide social services.
The deal will see Zipline build nine more facilities in CÃ´te dâIvoire to add to the sole operation it has run there since 2023. After using drones to deliver nearly 4 million medical products â mainly vaccines and blood â to more than 200 healthcare centers in a region northwest of Abidjan, Zipline has now locked in a long-term contract that could serve 12 million people, roughly a third of the Ivorian population.
The Ivorian government will pay Zipline for operating costs for eight years, especially for pharmacy-grade warehousing, cold chain, digital tracking, and delivery, Caitlin Burton, Ziplineâs head of global business said in a statement to Semafor. The company declined to say exactly how much it will receive, but expects the government to make a three-fold return on its investment.
The deal will ensure health facilities in areas that are difficult to access will receive âregular and secure supply,â Amadou Coulibaly, the Ivorian communications and digital economy minister, said earlier this month.
Know More
Zipline has operated drones in Africa for a decade and aims to be an on-demand delivery service. The Ivorian expansion builds on the companyâs first steps in Rwanda in 2016, and is part of an Africa-wide expansion play. In Nigeria, it plans to reach about half of the 220 million population by adding a dozen hubs to existing operations in three states.
Nearly $2 billion from venture capital investors has underpinned Ziplineâs global business that has grown from flying medical supplies to food delivery for Uber. It is in talks to raise $1 billion from Silicon Valley investors at nearly three times its most recent valuation of around $7.6 billion, according to reports last week.
But its Africa operations â which are still mostly about human health, with a gradual foray into livestock insemination â are benefitting from government funding. Zipline will cover its infrastructure costs in CÃ´te dâIvoire by unlocking money from a $150 million grant that the US government approved for the company last year. Washington conditioned the grant on Ziplineâs ability to secure expansion contracts from African governments and get them to cover operating costs.
Notable
- Nigerian drone maker Terra Industries this month secured two contracts worth $3 million from private companies to deploy its drones and other technology for surveillance over mineral sites, including one affiliated with the Africa Finance Corporation.

Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500.
Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted.
The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest attack in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead.
All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the attack on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody.
The accused had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, including murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms.

When Donald Trump unveiled a helipad at the White House on Monday, his remarks were barely audible in live footage of the event.
This was due to a row over an institution that rarely makes the news â the White House Press pool.
Yet it is at the heart of relations between the US president and the media, and this dispute could have constitutional implications.
Coverage of upcoming presidential engagements, which include the UN General Assembly in New York, could be affected.
What is the White House press pool?
It is a group of news organisations that combine resources to follow presidents wherever they are - in the Oval Office, at state dinners, on Air Force One or on holiday.
There are separate pools for TV, photographers and print and radio outlets, as well as a "new media" category.
The idea, conceived decades ago, is that having a pool saves on costs and space and it's not practical for hundreds of media outlets to follow the president around.
Members of the pool share their material - pictures and descriptions of the president's movements - with the wider media.
The pool is always on standby in case an event requires the president to speak to the nation.
This latest row centres on the TV pool which has five members - CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC.
It began on Friday when Trump said he was banning three outlets - CNN, Politico and MS NOW - from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news" and "fictions and lies" about his team.
A day later, reporters from those organisations found that their entry badges to the White House had been disabled.
On Monday, all the major US TV networks decided to pull out of White House pool duties - in effect boycotting presidential events.
That afternoon came the first test of this post-pool era - the new helipad at the White House.
With no pool cameras present, much of the media did not carry any pictures and for those that did, there was no microphone to clearly pick up the president's remarks.
But there were no such problems at Trump's meeting later that day with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, because it was not dependent on pool cameras and lots of media were there.
Why did US networks pull out of filming Trump?
Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds the rotating role covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage" of President Trump.
In a joint statement, the five networks said: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.
"No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting."
The First Amendment of the US Constitution protects speech and press freedoms.
It forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
CNN, Politico and MS NOW have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports". A hearing is scheduled for Wednesday.
In a joint statement on Monday, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
Trump's speech to the United Nations on Tuesday will be unaffected by the boycott because it will be carried by outlets which are not part of the pool.
But the president's movements to and from his various New York events, which are usually filmed, could be subject to the blackout.
How has Trump reacted and what is Trump TV?
Responding to news of the lawsuit, Trump called the outlets "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements.
"Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He added that his team would file an appeal. Meanwhile the White House has launched Trump TV, a 24/7 stream on YouTube.
Its description reads: "Watch the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place."
So far, the channel has primarily consisted of replays of previous Trump speeches and rallies.
For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York.
Unlike the traditional pool, however, that outlet is under no obligation to share material with others and has operated unilaterally for its audience.
Have there been previous examples of White House media bans?
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.
The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.
There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.
The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.
But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. Unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS NOW and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview.

5ef0dec5e13d.text: Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) is urging Senate Judiciary leaders to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden to investigate whether presidential family ties have been used for private family gain. Why it matters: The Republican Curtis is pressing a Republican-led Senate committee to scrutinize President Trump's eldest son, arguing the same congressional oversight applied to Hunter Biden should apply to presidential families of both parties. Driving the news: The Monday letter to Senate Judiciary chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and ranking member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) asks for an investigation into "private financial benefit, preferential treatment, or access" tied to presidential family relationships. Curtis wants the committee to subpoena both sons to testify about "any instances in which their relationship to the President was invoked or understood to provide value." Catch up quick: ProPublica reported that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward Trump Jr.'s three-day wedding celebration in the Bahamas, including buying a private-island rental. Curtis also cited Trump Jr.'s ties to prediction markets. Trump Jr. is a paid strategic adviser to Kalshi and sits on Polymarket's advisory board. 1789 Capital, where Trump Jr. is a partner, has invested in Polymarket. Curtis also pointed to Trump family-backed cryptocurrency ventures, international real estate deals involving meetings with foreign heads of state, and Trump Jr.'s reported defense-sector investments. What he's saying: "A toaster is a wedding gift," Curtis wrote on X. "A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden's foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now. 'Trust us' was not enough then, and it is not enough now." For the record: The White House, Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden have not yet responded to requests for comment. Hunter Biden has denied involving his father in business dealings. Trump Jr. confirmed Kremlev hosted celebrations, describing it as a wedding gift from a friend. President Trump later defended the arrangement as "totally allowed" and said he had been told his son would repay Kremlev. Flashback: House Republicans subpoenaed Hunter Biden in 2023 as part of their impeachment inquiry into then-President Biden. The younger Biden testified that he did not involve his father in his business dealings.

The News
Saudi Arabiaâs auto manufacturing startup CEER unveiled its first cars, two luxury electric vehicles that will go on sale early next year as the kingdom doubles down on a bet that the industry can help drive its economic diversification.
The futuristic Exobot sedan and SUV have gull-wing doors and sweeping windscreens that stretch into the roof, a design that was personally picked by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Prices were not revealed, but CEER executives say the first models will target high-end buyers. Five more models at lower price points are planned by 2030.
The cars will be built at a new production plant on the kingdomâs west coast, north of Jeddah, capable of producing 240,000 vehicles. CEER was launched by the kingdomâs sovereign wealth fund in 2022 and its plant at King Abdullah Economic City is part of an emerging autos cluster that Saudi Arabia is developing in the hope of creating jobs, diversifying its economy, and boosting non-oil exports.
Production will begin in early 2027 and the first deliveries to customers are expected in March, chief executive Jim DeLuca told Semafor in an interview on the sidelines of the launch event.
âSaudi Arabia has wanted a car industry for a long time, there have been multiple attempts, and it has never come to fruition,â DeLuca said. âOur mission is to ignite that industry.â
Know More
CEER is part of a multibillion-dollar bet by Prince Mohammed to establish an auto industry after several failed attempts. Jaguar Land Rover abandoned plans for a Saudi manufacturing facility more than a decade ago and Toyota also walked away from talks in 2019.
The government has since shifted strategy. Public Investment Fund, which controls CEER in a partnership with Foxconn, invested in Lucid in 2018 and got the US EV maker to build the first auto plant in Saudi Arabia. That became an anchor for a wider cluster that includes Hyundai and suppliers such as Italyâs Pirelli, the USâs Lear, Koreaâs Shin Young, âGermanyâs Benteler, and Chinaâs Fangxin. Stellantis is also studying building a manufacturing facility in the kingdom.
CEER will initially be sold in the kingdom before expanding into other parts of the Gulf in 2028. It will face stiff competition as Chinese EV brands have been rapidly gaining market share in the region. CEERâs launch also comes at a time when many of Public Investment Fundâs other big projects have been facing budget cutbacks and a new focus on raising outside capital to help limit how much state funding they require. The fund aims to instill financial discipline and a more commercial mindset to boost returns.
DeLuca said CEER has not had any changes to its funding from PIF. âWe are fully funded,â he said, declining to comment on how much has been invested so far or when the company expects to become profitable. âThis plan to launch seven products between now and 2030 was developed and funded in 2023.â
The Exobot was supposed to go on sale in November, but supply chain disruptions from the Iran war caused a delay, he said, adding that no further impact from the war is expected.
PIF is also working on new deals to bring more suppliers into the autos cluster. That will help lift the local content in CEER cars from around 18% to 45% by 2034.
Matthewâs view
CEERâs first cars are definitely unique. The companyâs origin story is that the Saudi Crown Prince steered them into designing something unlike any other car. In that sense, they have delivered.
At Monday nightâs launch, several people compared the cars to a sci-fi movie. Car nerds in the audience broke out into applause as CEER unveiled 1,111 horsepower, a 670-km range, and zero to 100 km/h in 2.1 seconds for the top trims.
While that will undoubtedly make the models conversation starters, the key question will be whether that translates into sales. CEER executives are not giving away anything on the price yet, but given a combination of high-tech features and a complex design that may prove challenging to build in volume, it seems likely to come in at similar price levels to Lucidâs luxury EVs.
Lucid is a cautionary tale. The company has missed delivery targets, is losing more than $100,000 per car, and has required several new cash injections since PIF invested. More money will be needed.
CEER will have the advantage that being private keeps its finances out of public scrutiny. And as a strategic initiative for Prince Mohammed, CEER is likely to receive strong state support. But the management team will have their work cut out over the next few years to ensure that the kingdomâs sci-fi vehicles will hit the roads, at scale.

- Published
A 65-year-old doctor has appeared in court, the first person in the UK to be charged over the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.
Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, who is in custody, confirmed his name and address from the dock at Westminster Magistrates' Court.
He was charged following a seven year British investigation into the killings.
He was told he faced a charge of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder, as a crime against humanity.
The case was passed to the Old Bailey for a hearing on 9 October. A bail application will be considered later on Tuesday.
The 1994 killings in Rwanda lasted 100 days, during which Hutu extremists carried out a campaign of slaughter against Tutsis and other moderate Hutus.
The charges against Brown relate to an alleged slaughter in the Rugenge district of Kigali between 6 April and 13 April in 1994.
Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group, as well as intending to destroy the group "as a whole or in part."
Prosecutors said he was being charged with genocide under the 2001 International Criminal Court Act and the alleged killings were "part of a widespread or systematic attack, directed against a civilian population, with knowledge of the attack."
Three members of the same house were allegedly murdered, along with a taxi driver, a mother and her young son.
The alleged victims were Dominique Mukurarinda, Immaculee Mukankusi, Gerasi Rurangirwa, Leandre Mbogoye, Charlotte Kamaguja and Olivier Tuyishime.
Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son.
In 2006 he was worked at Praxis, a London-based charity which helps refugees from places like Rwanda.
He has also served on the Refugee Nurses Task Force, which was set up in 2003 to advise the UK government.
Senior police officers have previously stressed the UK should not be a safe haven for alleged war criminals, and investigators have been trained in international war crimes legislation.
Sam Blom-Cooper, a barrister for Brown, told the court his client denied the allegations and was intent on going in front of a jury to clear the "stains of these appalling allegations."
He said the defendant had hoped for, longed for, and prayed for the best part of 20 years, for this day."
"These are appalling crimes, terrible murders committed in 1994 but this is the beginning of the end for Dr Brown."
Inquiries continue into other alleged genocide offences in Rwanda.

610028401a6d.text: Data: Zelle New Economics of Dating Report; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Rising costs are changing dating for more than eight in 10 Gen Z and millennial daters, leaving some to stop courting altogether, per new data from Zelle. The big picture: Young Americans are pushing off milestones under cost pressures — and the milestones themselves , from getting hitched to buying a home, are getting pricier once they get there. Driving the news: For younger Americans, just planning a date is a costly ordeal, with 17% of active Gen Z and Millennial daters saying they've gone into debt trying to maintain the dating lifestyle. Nearly one-third say they've gone on fewer dates amid rising costs. A smaller share, 11%, say they've stopped dating because they couldn't afford it. Members of Gen Z are more likely to split the cost of a date because of rising costs (26%) than Millennials (18%). Daters have changed strategies to lighten the cost burden — like suggesting free activities and spending more time on dates at home, which were used by 37% and 33% of active daters, respectively. The intrigue: As costs weigh on younger Americans, perhaps it's unsurprising that checkbook chemistry plays a big role in their love stories: Half of active daters say financial compatibility has at some point mattered more than romantic chemistry when deciding to keep dating someone. Men are more likely to say that than women (56% versus 45%), as are Gen Zers (53%) than Millennials (46%). But be warned: Talking money too much can kill the mood. For example, complaining about the price of everything or chatting too much about income would both give 47% of daters the "ick." What they're saying: "Dating has always come with unspoken rules, but rising costs are forcing a rewrite," Denise Leonhard, general manager of Zelle, said in a statement. "Financial compatibility is becoming part of the chemistry test. The new flex isn't running up the tab; it's reading the room, respecting the budget and showing thought." Zoom out: It comes as nearly all younger Americans (96%) reported being concerned about the cost of rent, groceries, gas or utilities, according to a recent Axios-Generation Lab poll of 18- to 34-year-olds. With the Game of Life ahead of them, high costs are leaving younger Americans struggling to even get on the board. Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!
Alexis Nikole Nelson
Simon & Schuster, $35.00
I used to think that foraging for food would involve schlepping myself to a forest far from my urban home, a task that would demand an unpleasant car trip, practical shoes and insect repellent. But when I flipped through forager Alexis Nikole Nelson’s new book Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!, I discovered edible plants right in my neighborhood.
Linden trees, for example, are common across much of the United States, including in cities. They have edible leaves, flowers and fruits, Nelson explains. There’s one just down the block from the Science News office in Washington, D.C. And that is how I found myself, this summer, on tiptoe trying to reach as many green, pea-shaped fruits as I could hold.
And that’s not all. Dandelions, acorns, black walnuts, crab apples, roses, magnolias, serviceberries — all are edible treasures found within walking distance of my home. Nelson explains how to identify these and other plants and provides vegan recipes for dishes unlike anything found in grocery stores.
Awareness of local edible plants helps combat the “plant blindness” that pervades modern society. For many people, plants are a pleasant afterthought rather than a focal point of daily life. “Taking the time to get to know your plant neighbors helps even the most urban neighborhood … seem full of nature and whimsy, even if you have to look close to find it,” she writes.
The book’s cheeky title is a tagline Nelson uses in popular videos posted to her social media accounts, where she sometimes goes by “Black Forager.” (She uses humor to help viewers learn which plants are good for snacking and which ones might make you, uh, “unalive.”) Likewise, the joy Nelson injects into the book makes foraging approachable.
I was nervous about picking unfamiliar fruits from trees in public. Wouldn’t everyone think I was weird? But with Nelson’s encouragement I felt emboldened. While collecting my bounty of linden fruits, I had a few friendly conversations with passersby and had the opportunity to educate neighbors about the tree.
Linden is in the same family as cacao and it can serve as a chocolate substitute, Nelson explains. Following her recipe for linden ice cream, I roasted, ground and sifted my linden fruits. Then, I combined them with sugar, soy milk, vanilla and cornstarch and cooked and froze the mixture. The ice cream tasted like an earthier version of chocolate. Taste testers — some of my Science News colleagues — compared it to brownie batter, cereal milk and tea. But in fact, linden fruits are their own thing with their own incomparable flavor.
It was a fascinating project, but not a complete success. I collected just a fifth of the amount of fruit that Nelson suggested in her recipe, so I was able to make only about a cup of ice cream. And it had an unpleasantly grainy texture despite my best attempts at grinding and sifting.
But at least now I will never overlook a linden tree.

The developing El NiÃ±o climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures.
Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El NiÃ±o of 2015.
Some longer-term measures of El NiÃ±o have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year.
El NiÃ±o can cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, with the Met Office saying many of the expected impacts are already being felt.
What is El NiÃ±o and how is it measured?
El NiÃ±o is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.
Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.
Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world.
Forecasters track the development of El NiÃ±o by watching temperatures in a key region of the Pacific Ocean. When these are consistently 0.5C above normal, an El NiÃ±o is declared.
There are different ways of measuring the strength of El NiÃ±o, however.
The records that have now been broken relate to daily measurements of sea surface temperature compared with the long term historical average.
This is called the Oceanic NiÃ±o Index (ONI).
Many scientists - including forecasters in the USA and Australia - also consider an alternative measure known as the Relative Oceanic NiÃ±o Index (RONI).
This measures how warm the key El NiÃ±o region is relative to the rest of the tropical oceans, meaning it takes into account the background warming caused by climate change.
By the RONI index the current El NiÃ±o is not yet a record-breaker - but it is likely that more announcements will follow in the coming weeks.
Professor Adam Scaife, Head of Long Range Prediction at the Met Office, said: "We have been signalling for months that the developing El NiÃ±o will be an unprecedented event.
"The fact that it has already exceeded previous records â with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year â shows the enormity of this El NiÃ±o."
Impacts of El NiÃ±o already being felt globally
Every El NiÃ±o is different, therefore impacts on global weather patterns are not guaranteed.
And the unprecedented strength of this El NiÃ±o does not necessarily mean it will have unprecedented impacts on the weather.
Professor Scaife said: "Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide."
El NiÃ±o increases the odds of storms and floods in some regions and of drought and wildfires in others.
El NiÃ±o years tend to bring below-average monsoon rainfall in India, which is already being reflected in this year's data.
Statistics from the India Meteorological Department show that, until 22 September the southwest monsoon had brought 15% less rain than normal.
Another typical impact of El NiÃ±o is reduced hurricane activity in the Atlantic due to changes in wind patterns high in the atmosphere.
So far in 2026 there have been no Atlantic hurricanes, setting a new record for the latest date without a hurricane forming since satellite monitoring of storms began.
Other possible effects - some of which are already being felt - include the increased risk of floods in coastal parts of Ecuador, Peru and the southern USA, and the enhanced threat of drought and wildfires in Brazil, Australia and Indonesia.
These weather impacts can have significant knock on effects for on crop yields, food security and economies around the globe.
Will there be an impact on UK weather?
The UK is thousands of miles from the tropical Pacific and so the effects of El NiÃ±o tend to be less clear-cut than in other regions.
However, it does bring the increased chance of wet and stormy conditions across north-west Europe during the late autumn and early winter.
A forecast released by the Met Office this autumn stated that there were already "signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December.
The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El NiÃ±o, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record.
In addition to storminess, El NiÃ±o can also be associated with UK cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El NiÃ±o.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El NiÃ±o winter and that was unseasonably warm.
As this unprecedented El NiÃ±o approaches its likely peak towards the end of 2026, scientists will continue to monitor its development - and its impact on weather around the world.

A grand jury will not bring criminal charges against anyone in the death of a Mississippi teenager, who was found dead two days after a boating trip with friends on 4 July.
Ben Crump, a civil rights attorney hired by the family, had raised concerns that Nolan Wells, a black man, "ended up dead after going out on a boat with three young white men", and that there had been conflicting witness statements.
Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath said the grand jury indicated there was not enough evidence to charge someone with a crime in the death of Wells.
In a statement to US media, Crump said the grand jury result "leaves us with more questions than answers".
"Nolan's family will not rest until we know what happened to him, and neither will we," he said.
Police had said Wells accidentally drowned, with his friends saying he chose to stay back on Horn Island after they decided to leave early because of an issue with their boat.
A report from the grand jury posted on the district attorney's social media on Monday found that the "position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr Wells' body is consistent with drowning".
"There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan's death and disappearance were racially motivated," Myers McIlrath said in the video message.
According to the report, 25 grand jurors heard from 43 witnesses, including a forensic pathologist hired by Wells' family to conduct an independent autopsy.
"The grand jury finds no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026 ... engaged in any criminal conduct related to âthe death of Mr. Wells," the report said.
The report said those who travelled with Wells were fully cooperative and offered GPS devices, surveillance footage, cell phones and other evidence.
It also said it is not unusual for visitors to Horn Island to stay and leave on different boats than they came on on crowded holiday days.
Wells' mother Christine Wonsley was the first to raise the alarm that her son, who played American football at Southwest Mississippi Community College and was described by his coach as a "happy-go-lucky kid", had gone missing after he did not return on the evening of 4 July.
Authorities discovered his body off the coast of the island on 6 July, following a search that included multiple local, state and federal agencies.

An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.
That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians.
But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza.
And on 4 October, the Republic of Ireland will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia.
No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis.
So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football?
Venue changes have not quietened protests
As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza.
In May a friendly match the Republic of Ireland played against Qatar in Dublin was twice interrupted after fans threw tennis balls onto the pitch featuring the Palestinian flag.
The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott.
Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income.
As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures.
No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary.
Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly.
The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil".
Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin.
The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest.
In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years.
The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition.
Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean.
FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide".
"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."
In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity".
The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations".
Irish support for Palestinians is long-standing
The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023.
More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN).
In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice.
The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers.
On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population."
Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

The world must build more than 6 terawatts of renewable power in the next five years â more than all previous years combined â to deliver on a goal to triple global renewable energy capacity by 2030, according to a new report. At COP28 in the UAE in 2023, countries agreed to collectively reach 11.2 TW of installed renewable capacity by 2030. Last year, clean power representing a record 693 GW of new capacity was added, but that pales in comparison to the 1,200 GW needed on average every year to 2030 to meet the goal, according to the report by the International Renewable Energy Agency, the Global Renewables Alliance and the COP31 Presidency.
Delivering the extra capacity requires an additional $8.6 trillion in investment over 2026-2030, the report found. To enable the additional renewable capacity to come online, investment to expand, modernize, and build flexibility on the grid must average up to $1 trillion a year, up from $525 billion in 2025.

The defence lawyer for a Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three children has asked a judge to investigate a juror in the case.
The proceedings against Lindsay Clancy ended in a mistrial and acrimony this month after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
Her attorney, Kevin Reddington, wants the court to probe mobile phone use by "Juror Doe" during deliberations as well as a questionnaire he filled out.
A lawyer for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who wanted to find Clancy guilty, said the latest defence motion was a "Looney Tunes" attack on his client for doing his civic duty. Desronvil has said there was "enough proof that she [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing".
Warning: This article contains distressing details
The juror forewoman has claimed in a media interview that Desronvil had expressed reasonable doubt about Clancy's guilt, which would require him to find her not guilty. He denies this.
Clancy has not denied killing her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home.
Her attorneys argued she was not guilty by reason of insanity, that she was struggling with postpartum psychosis at the time.
Prosecutors said Clancy made a calculated decision to send her husband out of the house on an errand so she could strangle her children.
In his motion filed on Friday, Reddington asked the court to look at calls and texts that "Juror Doe" made between 08:00 and 16:30 local time during all the days the jury deliberated.
He also asked the court to examine the truthfulness of the answers the juror gave during the jury selection process, as well as his responses to prospective juror questionnaires.
In a separate motion, Reddington also asked for the case against Clancy to be dismissed. Prosecutors have yet to say whether they will retry her.
Facing a backlash for refusing to acquit Clancy, Desronvil has hired an attorney to represent him.
The lawyer, Edward Paltzik, said in a statement on X that the "disgusting" defence motion was an attack on the US constitutional right to a fair trial.
"If the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye," he wrote.
Several jurors have said after the trial ended that they were ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
Desronvil said last week that he had no doubt about her guilt.
"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
The jury forewoman, a retired fifth-grade teacher, said in an interview with NBC that Desronvil had admitted he had reasonable doubt, but refused to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

5acf4e28be07.text: By — Aamer Madhani, Associated Press Aamer Madhani, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-live-trump-addresses-2026-united-nations-general-assembly Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Trump addresses 2026 United Nations General Assembly World Sep 22, 2026 9:26 AM EDT WATCH LIVE: Day 1 of the 2026 United Nations General Assembly NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is set to address the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday at a tumultuous moment for the world — and for his presidency. President Donald Trump will address the U.S. General Assembly on Tuesday. Watch live in our video player above. The global economy has been shaken by his decision to launch a war against Iran. Anxiety about the social impact being wrought by artificial intelligence is surging. And questions linger about the future of the United Nations itself with Trump's scaling back U.S. financial support for the United Nations. WATCH: Press pool declines to cover Trump in protest of his ban on news outlets After his speech to the annual gathering of world leaders, Trump is expected to hold talks with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and a more informal meeting with Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez, according to the White House. He's also set to meet with leaders and senior officials from Gulf Cooperation Council nations — Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates — to discuss the way ahead with the war in Iran and growing concern about recent Iran-backed rebel attacks on Saudi Arabia. The visit to the U.N. comes when Trump's foreign policy approach — particularly his decision to start a war with Iran — has become a drag on his fellow Republicans' hopes of retaining control of both chambers of Congress during the coming midterm elections. Nevertheless, administration officials signaled Trump will make the case in his address that the world is better off for his leadership. READ MORE: Britain's Burnham to meet Trump and make UN debut after offering UK military support for Saudis "We expect the president will highlight how he has and his administration have confronted complex problems head-on around the world," Ambassador Mike Waltz, Trump's chief envoy to the international body, told reporters. Waltz also suggested that Trump might revisit some of his long-held criticism of the United Nations. The president has criticized the body as being ineffectual on issues of war and peace, has claimed the organization is perpetuating a "con job" by emphasizing the need to address global warming, and has asserted the U.N. has promoted the "invasion" of migrants into Europe. Iran war to loom large In last year's address at the U.N., Trump claimed the U.S. had "demolished" Iran's nuclear capabilities after he ordered the June 2025 bombardment of three key facilities. He returns to the General Assembly nearing the seven-month mark of a new war against Iran that he insists is necessary to address a nuclear threat posed by Iran. The war has grown more complicated even though strikes by the United States and Israel have killed much of Iran's top leadership and destroyed its air force and navy, while a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil has left Tehran in economic shambles. READ MORE: Why Trump is rolling out the red carpet for Xi after years of slamming China The passage of oil from other Gulf countries through the Strait of Hormuz has improved in recent weeks with the help of the U.S. Navy helping guide commercial vessels through the narrow waterway. Still, the flow of oil is significantly below pre-war levels. And Brent crude continues to hover around $100 per barrel, up from about the $70 range in the weeks before the start of the war. The energy market continues to be spooked. Saudi Arabia earlier this month shuttered a key pipeline that acted as a relief valve for oil blocked in the Gulf. The kingdom made the move after the pipeline came under attack by Iran-backed militants in Iraq. At the same time, territorial grabs by the Yemen-based Houthi rebels, another Iranian-backed group, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait has now made it treacherous for oil carriers to use that Red Sea shipping lane. Majed al-Ansari, chief spokesman for the Qatari Foreign Ministry, said Monday that Qatar and other mediators are trying to penetrate a "deep deficit of trust" between the U.S. and Iran and get the sides back to negotiations. "Either we sign a deal now or sign a deal 10 months away," said said al-Ansari, speaking at the Concordia Annual Summit, a global affairs forum taking place during the U.N.'s high-level week. The only difference is the number of dead and destruction that we see." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that Trump is open to meeting with Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, while he's in New York for the General Assembly. "This is a president that will meet with anybody for the most part, because he believes that engaging with people is important if you're going to solve problems," Rubio said on NBC's "Today" show. "It doesn't mean you're going to end up agreeing with them, but it's important." The administration will sign a Greenland deal At last year's General Assembly, Trump touted his record as a peacemaker and claimed that "everyone says that I should get the Nobel Peace Prize" for his administration's efforts mediating several conflicts around the globe. This year, his administration is set to sign an agreement on the sidelines of the General Assembly with Danish and Greenlandic leaders that aims to set the pathway for the expansion of the U.S. military's footprint on Greenland. The deal, announced last week, came together after Trump repeatedly threatened to "take over" Greenland, a territory of NATO-ally Denmark, by military force if necessary. Under the deal, Greenland remains Denmark's territory. Trump's frustration with Russia-Ukraine war mount

A British man has pleaded guilty to causing the death of his two-year-old son who fell from a hotel window in Cyprus.
The father, from Essex, admitted a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act at a court in Paphos on Tuesday.
The boy fell from the fourth floor of the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July, the Times had previously reported.
A further hearing will take place on 5 October when the prosecutor will set out the facts of the case and the defence will present mitigation, a court official confirmed.
The defendant's name was not given during the hearing.
The man was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral, on condition that he flew back to Cyprus last week in order for the plea hearing to take place.
His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said he would ask the court to lift travel restrictions so that his client can return to the UK to be with his wife and daughter until the next hearing.
Paphos district court was told in July that the boy fell through an open window when his father was holding him around his waist and swinging him from side to side.
The father decided to plead guilty to avoid a long trial and spare his family reliving the child's death in court, Alexandrou said.
A long trial would mean that the man was "again a victim of this tragedy", the lawyer told the Associated Press after Tuesday's hearing.
"The most important thing for him is to return to his family," he said.
The maximum sentence for the charge was four years in prison, but Alexandrou said the court should take previous cases into account where defendants had been fined or received a suspended sentence.
