Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.
Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality.
"I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.
The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.
Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.
The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.
Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.
Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda.
"As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.
He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.
Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history.
"We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.
He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.
El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031.
"As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."
Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.
Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.
Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.
The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.
Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.
Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.
Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise.
"The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.
He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.
Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.
Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.
Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.
Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.
During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.
Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.
This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations.
"We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh.
"If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Moroc

US President Donald Trump has said he would back proposals to halt American diesel exports in a bid to ease prices for drivers at the pumps.
His comments come after Republicans lawmakers put pressure on the president ahead of November's mid-term elections to curb exports, as diesel prices soar to record highs in the US.
Speaking on the sidelines at the United Nations General Assembly, Trump suggested keeping domestic supplies inside the US could also ease broader petrol prices.
"I've called for that too. I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel. That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline," he said .
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed officials were assessing "whether a full or partial ban would work" without disrupting refinery capabilities.
National average diesel prices surpassed $6.50 (Â£4.87) a gallon on Tuesday according to AAA data, a new high.
The conflict in the Middle East has constrained global oil supplies, putting pressure on pump prices.
The surge in the cost of diesel has sparked political urgency ahead of crucial mid-term elections on 3 November, with several Republicans pressing the administration to restrict the fuel's export to ease financial strain on voters.
US Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican running for Senate in Iowa, said on Monday that the state's consumers were "being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump."
In Alaska on Tuesday, Senator Dan Sullivan similarly urged for a "temporary pause of American diesel and exports" to rebuild domestic reserves.
Adding to the global market volatility, Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy facilities has knocked out the country's refining capacity.
"It is a serious hit on the Russians," Trump said during a meeting with Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday. "It's also a serious hit on the price of diesel."
Trump confirmed he would discuss the strikes with the Ukrainian president, alongside broader efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict. "I think it's going to happen," he said.
Kyiv has intensified drone attacks on Russian processing plants in recent months to choke off the Kremlin's primary source of war funding.
Because Russia ranks among the world's leading diesel suppliers, reduced refining capacity â combined with Moscow's own strict export bans â has severely squeezed global reserves.
While restricting US exports could offer short-term relief for American drivers, a ban may risk pushing up prices internationally.
The US exports roughly 1.3 million barrels of diesel per day â nearly a quarter of its refining output.
Cutting these shipments could put pressure on supplies for Western allies, including the UK and the Netherlands, which have relied on American fuel to cover deficits left by sanctions on Russian energy.

US President Donald Trump returned to the stage at the United Nations on Tuesday, where he touted his administration's policies in front of world leaders and issued pointed threats to some of those gathered in the room.
The lengthy speech was wide-ranging, covering the war in Iran, AI, Cuba and the role of America's military.
The BBC's correspondents who covered the address have picked five key moments that stood out.
1. Trump pushes message of American power
By Sarah Smith, North America editor in the room
The US president has no great respect for the United Nations â he accused it of imposing a far-left agenda â but he does relish the global platform it gives him.
He used Tuesday's speech to tout his achievements, and claim the mantle of a peacemaker, at the same time as he issued a number of pointed threats.
Iran might be annihilated, lethal strikes on small boats suspected of drug smuggling will continue and the Cuban regime may even be toppled.
The clear message was: America is still prepared to use its military might wherever Trump thinks it might be required to secure its national interests.
Trump said he was "reasserting American power" and flexed what he called the country's "unmatched military might".
"The United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere," he said.
Once again, Trump has made the full-throated assertion to the world of "America First".
2. Cubans walk out as Trump calls nation 'failed state'
By Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter in the room
Trump took aim at one of the US's closest neighbours, Cuba, calling it "an absolutely failed state" and saying his administration has been pursuing "a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba".
"It will fall," he said.
The Cuban delegation walked out of the hall as Trump continued his remarks.
Over the last year, the US president become more vocal in criticising Cuba's communist government. On Tuesday, he said it was under "enormous pressure" and "failing like never before".
The US has not, however, provided a detailed picture of what it believes change will look like in Cuba.
Cuba's foreign minister reacted angrily to Trump's comments and accused the US president of spreading "falsehoods".
"The US government is incapable of accepting that Cuba is and has the right to be a full sovereign and independent country," Bruno Rodriguez wrote on X.
3. A direct threat to 'annihilate' Iran
By Khashayar Joneidi, BBC Persian correspondent in Washington
Trump presented Iran with a stark choice at the UN General Assembly: reach an agreement with Washington and rebuild the country, or face the rapid "annihilation" of the Islamic Republic.
He then again predicted that a deal to end the war would probably follow the US midterm elections in November.
His remarks illustrated Trump's familiar strategy of coercive diplomacy - keeping negotiations open while also threatening overwhelming force.
But his language blurred the distinction between destroying the political system and threatening Iran itself.
International law experts have previously expressed concern at what they called "alarming rhetoric" used by US officials, including Trump himself, who has posted that the US might "obliterate" Iran's power plants.
References on Tuesday to leaving "no chance of survival" and "no hope" for future generations will likely have stoked similar alarm. There is also an irony in delivering this warning at the United Nations, an organisation founded to save future generations from war.
Yet the speech was not a declaration that diplomacy has failed.
It was an attempt to define the terms of possible negotiations: the US remains prepared to make a deal, but only under the shadow of an existential threat.
4. Trump hails new Greenland security deal
By Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter in the room
Trump also praised a new deal with Greenland under which he said the US would build two military bases in the Arctic territory.
"We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe," he said of the deal, which he first announced on Friday.
He added that it "very much enhances" the defence alliance Nato.
The US, Denmark and Greenland held a joint signing ceremony at the UN shortly after Trump's address.
Although Greenland is a semi-autonomous territory, it is part of the Kingdom of Denmark which primarily handles its foreign policy.
Trump administration officials are already hailing the agreement as enhancing US security at minimal cost - and with relationships intact.
Denmark and Greenland's governments, however, will be hoping it ends the long-simmering disagreement that began when Trump threatened to take Greenland by force.
That threat shook the Nato alliance and sorely tested the US-Danish relationship.
Few clear details about the nature of the deal have been confirmed publicly, and given Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, some analysts are viewing it as a quiet win for diplomacy.
5. An attempted rebrand of AI
By Nada Tawfik, New York correspondent at the UN
Trump has a penchant for branding, and in his speech he gave Artificial Intelligence a new name: Super Intelligence.
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful."
"Welcome to the new world of Super Intelligence - SI," he added.
Trump has previously argued that the US must come out on top in the AI development race, saying last week: "Whoever wins AI, wins."
The president is firmly against government regulation or introducing new guardrails - and that puts him at odds with many of those gathered at the UN.
For those who are calling for regulation, the question is whether the slow pace of diplomacy can keep up with AI's rapid development.

3c25d6671800.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/air-traffic-control-calamity-disrupts-hundreds-of-u-s-flights-spotlighting-the-aging-system Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Air traffic control calamity disrupts hundreds of U.S. flights, spotlighting the aging system Nation Sep 22, 2026 5:49 PM EDT Communications failures that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast on Monday have put the spotlight back on the aging systems that air traffic controllers rely on in the U.S. Congress already handed the Federal Aviation Administration $12.5 billion last year to overhaul technology after the deadliest U.S. plane crash in more than two decades killed 67 people when an American Airlines flight collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter over the Potomac River and a series of radar outages later that spring led to widespread cancellations at Newark Liberty International Airport. WATCH: House approves aviation safety bill The same Philadelphia facility that had the radar outages in the spring of 2025 lost both its primary and backup data lines at the same time on Monday. But that regional air traffic control center isn't alone; similar communications outages have also disrupted flights in Minneapolis and Dallas over the past year. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy quickly turned Monday's disruption that hit every major airport in the New York area into the latest example of why he's asking Congress for $20 billion more to pay for the next phase of the air traffic control overhaul. Airlines were working to recover from the outage on Tuesday, but FlightAware.com showed nearly 100 flights had been canceled by midday because a number of planes and crews were out of position after Monday's cancellations. "I have money for some of the telecom replacing old copper wires. Bringing in new fiber so it's faster. The problem is this is a 40-year-old architecture or design," Duffy said on Fox News Tuesday. "I need new money to do a whole new design — a new architecture of telecom so it will never go down." The aviation industry's Modern Skies Coalition backed Duffy's plan again and urged Congress to approve the money because the latest disruptions "demonstrate how critical it is to replace the antiquated technology and outdated systems that underpin our nation's air traffic control infrastructure." Both the primary and backup lines failed on Monday A switch on the primary communications line at the regional FAA air traffic control facility in Philadelphia failed Monday morning, but when it turned to the backup fiber optic line authorities discovered that it had been inadvertently severed by railroad construction workers. The failures left controllers without radar or communications for hours. The switch is part of the equipment scheduled to be replaced. The outage brought commercial air traffic to a near-standstill at Newark for much of the day, with no commercial flights landing at the airport from about 9:40 a.m. to just after 5:20 p.m. local time, according to flight tracking site Flightradar24. More than 200 flights into and out of Philadelphia International Airport were also canceled, while disruptions hit LaGuardia and Kennedy airports in New York. Flights had resumed by Monday evening. Technical problems that affect Newark Liberty Airport tend to get outsized attention because it's a key hub for United Airlines. During the spring of 2025, controllers in Philadelphia briefly lost radar several times and then staffing shortages at the facility prompted the FAA to restrict traffic. The Dallas outage last September disrupted American Airlines' key hub, and last month's communications failure at a regional air traffic control facility in Minneapolis halted flights across several Midwestern states and led to numerous diversions and delays. Problems at key regional control facilities affect flights nationwide Sheldon Jacobson, whose research contributed to the design of the TSA PreCheck system, said the FAA needs to make sure that its backup systems are independent of the primary line to reduce the chance that both will fail at the same time. And he said maybe the agency should look at adding a third line to have an additional backup system. WATCH: Deadly LaGuardia plane collision comes as U.S. air system faces significant stress "When any one of these systems goes down, it doesn't just affect that airport. Because these are major hubs, it affects literally dozens of other airports and literally thousands of passengers," said Jacobson, who is an engineering professor at the University of Illinois. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association said the controllers who were on duty Monday did an exceptional job making sure everyone remained safe even when they lost their radios and radar. "No controller starts their shift with the expectation that the equipment will fail them, but when it does they display professionalism and skill," the union said in a statement. Ongoing upgrades can help make the system more reliable The FAA says it has already replaced 3,346 communications lines and 190 voice switches across the country since the agency received what Duffy called a $12.5 billion down payment on the overhaul. But the plan also calls for redesigning the computer system that air traffic controllers rely on, shifting computing online to the cloud and adding a new AI-based system to help predict problems. Duffy says he doesn't have enough money for those projects yet. Robert Poole, who leads transportation research at the Reason Foundation think tank he founded in the late 1970s, said the FAA needs reliable long-term funding to complete all the needed upgrades, and that is hard to get from Congress. ae85eb3828e2.text: By — Caleb McCullough, PolitiFact Caleb McCullough, PolitiFact By — Louis Jacobson, PolitiFact Louis Jacobson, PolitiFact By — Loreben Tuquero, PolitiFact Loreben Tuquero, PolitiFact By — Samantha Putterman, PolitiFact Samantha Putterman, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/fact-checking-trumps-speech-to-the-2026-united-nations-general-assembly Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Fact-checking Trump's speech to the 2026 United Nations General Assembly Politics Sep 22, 2026 5:37 PM EDT This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. In his address to the United Nations General Assembly, President Donald Trump defended the United States' robust use of military force in Iran, Venezuela and elsewhere, saying the international community is incapable of handling threats from those countries. WATCH: Trump addresses 2026 United Nations General Assembly Undaunted by polls that show Americans tiring of the nearly-seven-month Iran war and its impact on fuel prices, Trump said in the Sept. 22 speech that the U.S. is "settling years of unfinished business. And we're doing it well." He also brushed off concerns that rapid advances in artificial intelligence could endanger humanity, saying the U.S. "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control artificial intelligence." Members of the Cuban and Iranian delegations walked out at points during Trump's speech. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was traveling to address the General Assembly on Sept. 23 — an unusual visit by a leader of a country at war with the U.S. Here are fact-checks of some of Trump's statements. Artificial intelligence "The very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming … These are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all. … This is the group that came up with the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax, the Ukraine, Ukraine, Ukraine hoax, climate change, open borders." Although some anti-AI groups may have overlaps with advocates concerned about climate change, alarms over AI are not confined to one group of people. The loudest warnings of late have come from the top of the industry itself. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a Sept. 12 essay urging a slower pace of developing AI capability. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind Cofounder and Chair Demis Hassabis and xAI founder Elon Musk agreed with Amodei, a rare concurrence in the competitive tech industry. U.S. lawmakers from both parties have introduced legislation to regulate AI. On artificial intelligence, "We're leading now over China by a lot." The U.S. has a lead over China in model capability, but key AI industry leaders and experts have said China is only a few months behind. U.S. models have rapidly become more powerful, leading to multiple safety breaches, and AI leaders are calling for a slowdown. The gap between the U.S. and China could shrink if development proceeds more slowly in the U.S., but China continues apace. "From this point forward, all United States documents and hopefully the world's will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'super' as opposed to artificial. So it's superintelligence. In other words, welcome to the new world of superintelligence — SI." Superintelligence is a specific term in the field of AI, but those in the industry say it's not an accurate description of currently available AI systems. WATCH: Trump dismisses concerns about AI risks at UN, says he won't rein it in Superintelligence is generally understood by industry experts as an AI system that is far ahead of human intelligence at nearly all cognitive tasks, including scientific research and communications. A recent paper from Google's AI lab, Deepmind, defined artificial superintelligence, or ASI, as "an artificial general intelligence that has superhuman abilities across virtually all tasks and domains of human interest and activity." Current AI systems excel at coding, math, and a lot of complex cognitive tasks. But they have limitations that place them well behind superintelligence. A 2026 international AI safety report describes current AI's performance to be "jagged across tasks and contexts." U.S. involvement in wars, conflicts "The cowards and traitors would love to say the United States is low on munitions, but that's not true. We have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using, and we're building them at levels that we have never done before." This is misleading. Several news and expert reports have found that U.S. weapons stockpiles are rapidly decreasing as the Iran war continues. A May analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a national security-focused think tank, projected that certain heavily-used munitions in the Iran war — such as the Tomahawk missile system and Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense interceptors that defend against missiles and drones — will take about three to four years to replenish. In July, NBC News reported that the U.S. military was rationing munitions and allowing some Iranian attacks because of the diminishing stockpile. Defense experts have said that aid to Ukraine under President Joe Biden's administration also reduced the United States' weapons reserve. The Biden administration started a process to expand production and replenish the stockpile, something the Trump administration has accelerated. "The United States has carried out dozens of strikes on cartel drug boats, destroying 97% of the drugs coming into the ocean and sea." False. Air and marine drug seizures have dropped since the strikes began in September 2025, but the administration hasn't provided a clear link. The Coast Guard, which oversees most drug seizures on water, recorded a 200% increase in seizures in fiscal year 2025 compared with other annual averages. Seizures show how many drugs are stopped from entering the U.S., not how many drugs are being sent to the U.

El Nino is part of a natural climate cycle of warming ocean temperatures, but this year's is expected to reach new extremes of drought, heat waves, flooding and other climate-related disruptions in South America, Africa and Asia. Southeast Asia is one of the world's most climate vulnerable regions. It's already beset by an energy crisis triggered by the war in Iran. El Nino is already fueling wildfires across farmland, depleting water supplies for major cities and hurting fish catches in the region. WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns Asian governments that have been drawing on their financial reserves to mitigate the war's ripple effects of higher energy costs and scarce fertilizer supplies have less capacity to cope with this year's intensifying El Nino, which is forecast to peak in December. The phenomenon may amplify other crises in Southeast Asia, according to Paul Teng, with Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, who said, "El Nino is only compounding all the other problems that we see." Extreme El Nino may threaten global food security During El Nino years, sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean are warmer than usual. This happens every few years and often alters global weather patterns. This year, the seas already are hotter than average, with global oceans hitting new temperature records in August as the climate warms, said Kareff Rafisura, chief of the Disaster Risk Reduction Division at the U.N. Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific. This intensifying El Nino may be the "strongest in living memory," according to the United Kingdom's national weather and climate service. Similarly, the U.S.' National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said there is a 69% chance that this will be the strongest recorded El Nino since record-keeping began in 1950. El Nino's impact will be felt differently across regions, but it is expected to jeopardize food security worldwide. It could push at least 49 million more people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, according to the United Nations' World Food Program. The problem will be worst in parts of Central America and southern Africa, with significant effects also anticipated in eastern Africa and South and Southeast Asia, warned the food agency. El Nino is already hitting parts of Asia In Southeast Asia, wildfires are torching forests and peatlands in Indonesia, sending up plumes of toxic haze. The water level of a major reservoir supplying the bustling capital city of Jakarta — the world's biggest metropolis — is dropping inch by inch. WATCH: Southeast Asia endures punishing year of extreme weather amid super El Niño As the lake dries, the ruins of one of 11 villages that had been inundated by the reservoir have emerged, as alarm grows over the need for alternative water supplies for the city of 42 million. "I would have rather not moved. There were plenty of livelihood opportunities here," said Hussen, who only uses one name, as he ferried people across the receding reservoir. This is just the beginning, said Erma Yulihastin with Indonesia's Research Center for Climate and Atmosphere, who warned El Nino has only just begun its "super phase." Southeast Asia's fisheries brace for drought Less rainfall and hotter temperatures are putting pressure on Southeast Asia's fisheries, an essential source of protein. It's a pressing problem along the Mekong, a river basin that flows through six nations and is being disrupted by mining and construction of hydropower dams. "It's one punch after another," said Zeb Hogan, with the University of Nevada, Reno, who runs the research and conservation project, Wonders of the Mekong. "If the river doesn't catch a break, we will reach a point where it's no longer going to sustain people in the way that it always has." Lower flows are especially hard on communities along the Mekong that depend on predictable water levels for fishing and farming, said Kongmeng Ly, with the Mekong River Commission, an intergovernmental group for Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. Rice and palm oil supplies are at risk Southeast Asia's wet season generally runs from June to October, when rains usually replenish reservoirs, cool overheated cities and supply water for irrigation ahead of the next planting season. Drought may force farmers to delay planting, reduce acreage or switch crops entirely, said Rafisura, with the U.N. "Agriculture is definitely on the front line," she said. READ MORE: Where have all the Atlantic hurricanes gone? El Niño might bring record slow storm season Cutbacks in staple crops like rice and palm oil can have global impacts. The world's top three exporters of rice — India, Vietnam and Thailand — are among the nations most likely to be hit hard by El Nino this year. North of the Thai capital Bangkok, rice farmers like 55-year-old Boonmark Marksuuk are already facing tough choices. - Published
Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.
The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.
The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship".
"We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it."
Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".
Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).
He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."
The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.
Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".
He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.
His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.
Torpedo exercise
For a new British prime minister, the first meeting with a US president has always been a pivotal encounter, but officials are well aware of the added jeopardy of a public appearance alongside the most unpredictable president in American history.
In advance of the meeting, the UK revealed that the UK and the US have, for the first time, fired an American torpedo from a British undersea drone in a military exercise.
The torpedo, described as "heavyweight" by UK officials, is "designed to sink ships and deep diving submarines", Downing Street said.
It was launched in UK waters last week from a 12-metre long undersea drone called Excalibur, made in Plymouth.
It is the first time either the UK or the US have launched a torpedo from an uncrewed underwater vessel, rather than a crewed submarine, and is seen as a breakthrough in attempts to protect vital infrastructure such as deep sea data cables.
"Our work together already shows what can be achieved when our two countries combine our expertise and innovation," the prime minister said.
Burnham was also asked by reporters about the UK government seeking to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.
It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.
Burnham spoke to the Mauritian prime minister, Navin Ramgoolam, on Monday.
He was asked by reporters to outline what he had told Ramgoolam, whether he supported the deal and if he had a plan to convince Trump to back it.
Burnham replied: "I said that we remain determined to secure the long-term operation of the base, which is crucial to our security and that of our allies.
"The assurance I gave was I will work towards a resolution, at the moment we don't have that, but I gave an assurance that I would commit to working towards one."

Republicans are running away from the Iran war and scrambling to curtail high gas prices as they try to keep hold of Congress â and even some who arenât up for reelection are breaking with the Trump administration in high-profile fashion.
Itâs a critical moment for the congressional GOP as the Senate prepares to empty out for election season as soon as this week, joining their House colleagues on the fall campaign trail. But as they do so, there are growing instances of daylight between President Donald Trump and the Republican Party he leads, a notable trend after so many months of muted criticism.
Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, is pushing for an investigation of Donald Trump Jr. over his business dealings while Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., reprimanded Trump for inviting Chinese leader Xi Jinping to Washington for a formal state visit this week. And looming over it all is the nearly seven-month Iran war, which is starting to generate public friction with swing state Republicans across the country. This week, Democrats are seeking to make the Senate vote on curtailing the conflict one last time before the election.
On Monday, Michigan Republican Senate candidate  Mike Rogers along with Iowa GOP Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate, called for an end to the Iran war. They were joined by Rep. John James, a Republican running for governor of Michigan, and endangered Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio.
âItâs not popular. They are in tough elections. People understand the need to have a safe nation but we also understand the need to resolve this conflict,â retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, told Semafor of her Iowa colleagues. âThe administration hasnât been clear on how to end this and I think thatâs why people are moving.â
Ernst said sheâll âprobablyâ continue voting against the Democratic-led efforts to rein in the conflict, though she wants a âclear understandingâ of the path forward.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., another retiring swing state senator, said heâd seen enough. He said the war had âmeandered for too longâ and urged GOP candidates to take the same position if thatâs what their political predicaments demand.
âThere are so many headwinds now for these candidates that I hope that the administration gets the point that you can be 90% with the president and speak about the 10% youâre not. So I think youâre seeing that distance,â Tillis said. âYouâve got a lot of people out there that want to vote for Republicans, but theyâre a little uncomfortable with one issue or another, the presidentâs tone, whatever.â
Curtis and Wicker gave Republicans further cover to find that distance. Curtis asked the Senate Judiciary Committee to subpoena both Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden, declaring that reports on Trump Jr.âs wedding and business deals raise âlegitimate questions about foreign access to members of a sitting presidentâs family.â Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, declined to comment on that request.
Wicker didnât mince words about Xiâs visit, calling Xi a âbrutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directlyâ at the United States.
Know More
Most Senate Republicans in competitive races like Husted, Dan Sullivan of Alaska, and Roger Marshall of Kansas have backed the Iran war on the Senate floor. Sullivan also threw his support behind a diesel export ban â prompting Trump himself to back it. But a few, like Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, have voted to rein in Trumpâs conflict.
Miller-Meeks and Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa, both voted last week against the war. Both Rogers and James had sounded significantly more supportive of the war earlier this year but said they want to end it this week.
âWe all want it to end as quickly as possible. I think theyâre being bold and theyâre being direct,â said Sen. Ted Budd, R-N.C., of Republican candidates. âYou have to be in sync with people in your state to get elected â in an authentic way. I think people genuinely want the war to be over; that doesnât mean you quit, you bring it to a successful resolution.â
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he was hoping he could keep Republicans from splintering on Iran right before the election: âI would hope the team could hang together on this.â
The View From the white house
Trump has repeatedly threatened to escalate the conflict only to predict a deal is close at hand. He said during his speech at the UN General Assembly that he has a âbig decisionâ to make on Iran. He can either cut a deal that helps Iran rebuild and ends the war, or, Trump suggested, he could âannihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly.â
Burgessâs view
Republicans have wanted the war to end basically since it started, but are reluctant to cross the president publicly. Thatâs clearly starting to change, but itâs one thing to criticize the war and another to vote against it.
Thatâs what makes Miller-Meeks and Nunnâs votes so interesting. And if Senate Republicans with similar views really want to show voters they oppose the war, their best chance to do so is to vote against it.

On a hot July afternoon this year, electricity generated from renewable energy briefly met over half of India's peak power demand - only the second time this happened. The first instance was around the same period a year ago.
While it was only briefly that power generated from solar, wind, hydro and nuclear sources collectively outstripped coal-based output, it was a milestone moment reflecting the astonishing growth of non-fossil fuels to the country's electricity mix over the last decade.
"It showed that renewable energy is no longer a marginal source sitting at the edge of the power system," Sumant Sinha, CEO of ReNew Power, one of India's largest Nasdaq-listed clean energy companies, told the BBC.
To be sure, coal-based power plants still continue to generate 70% of India's electricity on average because they run on a higher load factor, or for more hours than solar or wind. Yet, the country's push for clean energy appears to have reached a crucial inflection point.
A decade ago India's installed renewable energy capacity was barely 4GW. It now makes up 300GW or 54% of its total 552GW installed capacity, external - a target that's been achieved five years ahead of schedule.
For a nation long seen as the poster child for dirty coal dependence, this rapid transition points to a remarkable achievement in decarbonising its grid.
Yet, the gains are tempered by some serious challenges.
Foremost among them is a shortage of grid capacity. The renewables' build out has significantly outpaced transmission infrastructure, a point of major concern for policymakers.
"In the first quarter of 2026, transmission constraints accounted for nearly two-thirds of all renewable energy curtailment at 300 gigawatt-hours (GWh)," according to Ember, a global energy think-tank.
Put simply, that means a bulk of the clean energy that was produced in India was wasted because the country's transmission lines have been dogged by missed targets, with one out of four inter-state projects facing delays of over a year.
The difficulty lies in matching the speed of generation projects with the grid build-out, says Sinha.
"Generation projects can be constructed in 18-24 monthsâ¦ Transmission can take much longer because they involve right-of-way, land acquisition, approvals and coordination across many agencies. It is an execution issue that becomes more important as the system gets larger," he adds.
Vibhuti Garg of the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis also blames "poor planning" for the problem.
The grid was able to absorb new capacity as long as India was generating 10-15GW annually, she told the BBC. But that pace has dramatically increased, reaching a record 51GW last year, and the infrastructure is no longer able to cope.
The concentration of renewables projects in the north-western states of Gujarat and Rajasthan has also compounded the challenge of evacuating power in the face of such grid shortages.
Analysts at Ember now believe this growing mismatch between fast-moving generation projects and slower-moving transmission infrastructure, is the "most critical operational risk to the country's 2030 target of 500 gigawatts (GW) of non-fossil electricity".
A quick solution to addressing this gap would have been to build battery storage systems at renewable pooling stations to integrate the power into the grid.
"Had that been the case, India could have stored the energy and used it during evening hours rather than wasting it," says Garg.
But storage capacity has not grown because of a huge jump in the price of batteries, raw material shortages due to the war in the Middle East and a fall in the value of the Indian currency which has jacked up financing costs for Indian companies.
"Many storage projects that were meant to come up fell through as a result," Garg adds.
Yet, finance isn't a constraint merely for storage projects but an industry wide problem.
While ample global capital is available for green transition across the developed world, getting access to it remains a persistent struggle for Indian clean energy companies, despite the strides that the country has made in its renewables commitments.
Estimates suggest the country will require $400-$500bn to meet its 500GW renewables target by 2030, external. But currently, around 83% of India's finance for climate mitigation is sourced domestically, according to the government's economic survey. While the Paris Agreement clearly mandated developed countries to provide financial resources to the tune of $100bn annually up to 2025 to developing countries for their climate action, that money has been hard to get.
"Emerging and developing economies outside China receive only around 15% of global clean-energy investment, despite accounting for roughly two-thirds of the world's population," says Sinha.
According to him, while India does not necessarily need developed countries to finance its entire transition, help is needed in the form of cheaper loans, guarantees and protection against currency losses so that private investors are encouraged to put in more money into the space.
Plugging these critical gaps in finance, transmission infrastructure and storage will be critical given this transition is under way at a pivotal moment, say experts.
India is the world's third largest emitter of greenhouse gases and facing a sharp rise in electricity demand, which has grown at a compounded rate of over 7% every year. It is expected to further accelerate with the expansion of industries like data centres and chip manufacturing.
The International Energy Agency, external predicts India's electricity demand will increase by 80% by 2035, the sharpest jump among emerging economies. It also credits the country's robust expansion of its renewables as a major contributor for slowing emissions in the developed world this year, even as energy related CO2 emissions rose more strongly in advanced economies for the first time since the 1990s.

Geoff Bennett: A day after Paramount Skydance and a group of state attorneys general announced a settlement clearing the way for its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, questions remain about whether the deal does enough to protect consumers and competition. The $111 billion merger would create one of the biggest media companies in the world, bringing multiple film studios and cable channels, streaming services, and major franchises under one roof. It would also put two major news organizations, CBS News and CNN, under the same corporate umbrella. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who helped lead the antitrust challenge before reaching the settlement, acknowledged he still has concerns about the merger. Rob Bonta (D), California Attorney General: This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger. It is not a blessing of the broader merger. Broadly speaking, we believe further consolidation in markets that are central to American economic life doesn't serve the American economy, consumers, or competition well. Geoff Bennett: But Bonta emphasized several key conditions of the agreement, including Paramount being required to release 30 films in theaters per year for the first two years, a $1.5 billion investment for homegrown film production, and the creation of an editorial independence board to support CBS News and CNN. The deal itself still needs to be approved by a federal judge. For more, we're joined now by Oliver Darcy of Status. Oliver, thanks for being with us. So what ultimately led to this settlement? Was it Ellison's threat to move Paramount out of California or something else entirely? Oliver Darcy, Founder, Status News: The threat from Ellison to move out of California seems to have loomed large over this. If you remember, Rob Bonta was calling this an illegal merger for some time and really vowing to go all the way with this and saying he was comfortable going to court. And something happened in the recent weeks. And that something is David Ellison was getting very serious about his threat to take production jobs from California and move them to maybe Nashville or to Texas. And you saw the governor, Governor Gavin Newsom, and local officials really worried about this and say they would like to see a settlement. And the pressure, from our understanding, reporting on this, was really great on Rob Bonta. He really needed to settle this to make sure that David Ellison left those Paramount production jobs and potentially the Warner production jobs in California. Geoff Bennett: Of all of the conditions attached to this settlement, which is expected to have the biggest effect on the entertainment industry? For instance, the big point about they have to release 30 films a year in theaters, if you look at the fine print, they do have to release 30 films, but they can co-produce half of them. So they only really have to release 15 films on their own, and then they can co-produce the other half and get those in the theaters to satisfy that requirement. Ultimately, Geoff, this is going to result in a lot of layoffs in the entertainment sector. And that's going to happen because there's going to be a lot of synergies between Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount, the back offices, people who support communications and publicity, people who support H.R. jobs, legal jobs. Those jobs, I would imagine, would be almost immediately consolidated, and you're going to see a number of layoffs, and then it's going to just continue. This company that's going to be formed is going to be under billions of dollars in debt. They're going to need to find a lot of cost savings. And that's going to result regardless in a loss of jobs moving forward. Geoff Bennett: And Ellison has agreed to create this independent editorial board for CBS and CNN. But critics say what is described as a safeguard is in many ways hollow. Explain why. Oliver Darcy: Yes, there's a number of concerns here. One, usually, when you have an editorial board that's supposed to safeguard the CNN and CBS from management, you wouldn't have management get to select all the board members. Geoff Bennett: And, Oliver, who actually polices all of this? How quickly could the states act if Paramount decides to start testing the boundaries of this settlement? 94749f9f7a2f.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/fall-has-officially-arrived-heres-what-to-know-about-the-autumnal-equinox Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Fall has officially arrived. Here's what to know about the autumnal equinox Science Sep 22, 2026 6:31 PM EDT The fall equinox is Tuesday, when light and darkness split the day evenly. It marks the beginning of fall for the Northern Hemisphere and the beginning of spring in the Southern Hemisphere. On the equator, the sun will be directly overhead at noon. Equinoxes are the only times when both the north and south poles are lit by sunshine at the same time. READ MORE: Worsening El Nino threatens Asia with severe drought, potentially threatening global food security Equinoxes have been marked and celebrated around the world for centuries. Japan marks public holidays during the equinoxes. At the Mayan site Chichen Itza in Mexico, people gather during the equinox to watch the sun create a shadow pattern that resembles a serpent descending a pyramid called El Castillo. Here's what to know about the Earth's orbit. What is the equinox? As the Earth travels around the sun, it does so at an angle, making the sun's warmth and light fall unequally on the northern and southern halves of the planet for most of the year. During the equinox, the Earth's tilt is neither toward the sun nor away from the sun, so both the Northern and Southern hemispheres get an equal amount of sunlight. The sun rises almost exactly due east, and it sets almost exactly due west. The word equinox comes from two Latin words meaning equal and night. That's because on the equinox, day and night last almost the same amount of time — though one may get a few extra minutes, depending on where you are on the planet. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Northern Hemisphere's fall — or autumnal — equinox can land between Sept. 21 and 24, depending on the year. This year it is Tuesday at 8:05 p.m. Eastern time. Its spring — or vernal — equinox can land between March 19 and 21. The exact time of the equinox is the moment the sun is directly overhead at the equator. What is the solstice? The solstices mark the times when the Earth is tipped most extremely either toward or away from the sun. This means the hemispheres are getting very different amounts of sunlight, and days and nights are at their most unequal. At the Northern Hemisphere's summer solstice, the Earth's upper half is leaning toward the sun, creating the longest day and shortest night of the year. The summer solstice falls between June 20 and 22. The opposite happens at the Northern Hemisphere's winter solstice: the Earth's upper half leans the furthest away from the sun, leading to the shortest day and longest night of the year. The winter solstice falls between Dec. 20 and 23. What's the difference between meteorological and astronomical seasons? These are just two different ways to carve up the year. While astronomical seasons depend on how the Earth moves around the sun, meteorological seasons are defined by the weather. Meteorologists break down the year into three-month seasons based on annual temperature cycles. By that calendar, spring starts on March 1, summer on June 1, fall on Sept. 1 and winter on Dec. 1. b23b5b42feeb.text: A notorious cybercrime group is claiming they stole more than 2 terabytes of data that includes detailed personal information about thousands of FBI employees and job applicants. Why it matters : Cybercriminals and state-sponsored attackers have penetrated U.S. IT systems for years, but stealing detailed and sensitive information about FBI employees is brazen, cyber experts told Axios. Cybercriminals are known to trade leaked information on the dark web, a prospect that would leave the data up for grabs from the highest bidder. Driving the news : ShinyHunters, a group that's broken into numerous institutions, said in a post on its dark-web site Tuesday that it stole "very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job." An FBI spokesperson said in a statement the bureau is "aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating." What to watch : Cynthia Kaiser, a former top official in the FBI's cyber division, told Axios that when a hacker targets the FBI, expect the bureau "to marshal additional resources to bring them more quickly to justice." The big picture : While the breach is likely to bring more law enforcement attention to ShinyHunters in the short term, the long tail impact is greater on the FBI employees and their families whose information was stolen, Allan Liska, a threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future, told Axios. "The data is out there and has likely been repeatedly downloaded and passed around to other threat actors," Liska said. Axios has not been able to corroborate that the data stolen is legitimate or recent, but cybersecurity researchers confirmed that the attack appears legitimate. 404 Media obtained a sample of the stolen data, which appears to include information about 5,000 alleged agents. Zoom in : ShinyHunters told Axios in an email that the stolen data includes names, FBI agent statuses, emails, phone numbers, home addresses and "sometimes even spouse information," including their Social Security numbers. The group also claims it broke into the FBI's criminal justice, HR and other services. ShinyHunters also said it seized and defaced the FBI's jobs webpage via a zero-day in Oracle's PeopleSoft platform. The site was still offline as of Tuesday afternoon. Screenshot: FBI career page on Sept. 22. Catch up quick : ShinyHunters says its hack is not financially motivated. Instead, the group is pushing the FBI to retract statements it made about how ShinyHunters operates. In a May advisory , the FBI warned the hackers "commonly use harassment strategies, sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members, and in some cases, swatting." ShinyHunters claims this isn't true and told Axios that it believes these claims have been tied to their group because "other low-skilled threat actors" have been using the group's name in their attacks. Threat level: Andrew Brandt, principal threat intelligence incident commander at Huntress, told Axios that a major concern is over whether ShinyHunters chooses to sell the data to other criminal or nation-state hackers. "It doesn't take much imagination to picture scenarios where employees or their families could be threatened or harmed by this kind of information being released," Brandt said.

1906702651d8.text: Congressional Republicans are increasingly breaking with an unpopular president on foreign policy and pocketbook issues as they try to stop their majorities from slipping away. Why it matters: They aren't engaged in a full-scale revolt against President Trump, but some Republicans are testing new ways to distance themselves from him — a sign of their election anxiety. Driving the news: Trump — facing a barrage of demands from Republican lawmakers to impose a ban on diesel exports — pulled a rare about-face Tuesday, saying on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York that he'll support a ban. Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), along with Iowa GOP Reps. Ashley Hinson and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, were among those calling for a ban to ease skyrocketing diesel costs for U.S. farmers and truckers. Sullivan and Hinson are in tight Senate races. Just on Tuesday: Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) railed on the Senate floor at Trump's decision to host Chinese President Xi Jinping this week for a state dinner. Two divergent worldviews emerged from the first two national addresses on the opening day of the United Nations General Assembly’s 81st session in New York.
Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva called for decarbonizing economies, protecting forests and supporting the energy transition through technology transfer. U.S. President Donald Trump followed with a rejection of global climate and artificial intelligence regulations, dismissing warnings about global warming while presenting fossil fuel abundance and technological supremacy as foundations of national power.
This year’s General Assembly session is taking place against a slew of global challenges supercharged by geopolitical rivalries and rising planetary warming. June was the second-warmest on record globally and the hottest Western Europe ever measured. A potentially record-breaking El Niño is expected to peak around December, raising fears of drought, crop failures and global food-price shocks.
In the U.S., surging AI data center growth is triggering expensive fossil-fuel generation and grid upgrades, raising electricity bills. Meanwhile, the U.S.-Iran conflict has spread through the region, with clashes between Houthi and Saudi forces further roiling global oil markets already constrained by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
Lula framed climate policy, forest protection and technology regulation as necessary parts of a rule‑based, multilateral effort to reduce emissions and manage systemic risks. He said the planet is facing a shared, urgent climate emergency that demands decarbonization and environmental protection—not delay or denial. He called for nations to “resume the offensive and inflict a defeat on denialism,” and warned that “the glaciers in the Himalayas are melting” and “torrential rains and forest fires” are already here. The impacts, Lula said, “will hit the most vulnerable the hardest.”
He presented Brazil as proof that countries can “combine economic value with reduced emissions,” and pledged to “move forward by the roadmap for the decarbonization of the Brazilian economy.” In his view, forests and ecosystems are climate assets worth protecting and technology, including AI, must be governed and restrained, calling it an “unprecedented technological revolution with great risks and opportunities.” Lula insisted it would be an “unforgivable historical mission not to address the challenge of regulating the big techs and artificial intelligence” and criticized “technical oligarchies without rules or transparency” that bypass the U.N. and scientific oversight.
Trump presented an almost opposite worldview by downplaying climate change, celebrating fossil fuel expansion and attacking global climate regulation. He mocked those who warned about global warming as “the very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming, a name since reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming, and nobody was dead.”
Trump claimed his administration had stopped what he called an international “global carbon tax” on shipping, insisting “there is no global government, and while I’m president, there will be no global taxes.” Rather than talking about emissions or a just energy transition, he boasted that American energy is fueling the planet and claimed that the U.S. and Venezuela together hold “more than 60 percent of the oil in the world.” This alone, he said, will drive down energy costs.
On technology, he rejected any “globalist scheme to control” AI, rebranding it as “super-intelligence” and pledged his administration will “only encourage superintelligence.” On the whole, Trump’s roughly 35-minute speech treated carbon taxes, climate regulations and global tech governance as threats to sovereignty and growth, and presented fossil fuels and technological dominance as core tenets of national strength.
Environmental advocates, climate scientists and experts reacted sharply to those remarks and challenged Trump’s assertions on climate change and high energy costs.

4fe2f9a32f90.text: As President Trump fights the press over coverage, the White House launched its own 24/7 streaming channel — Trump TV. Why it matters: Trump TV gives the president a White House-run video platform to reach the public without relying on traditional news organizations. So far, Trump TV resembles a round-the-clock presidential highlight reel more than a news network. Driving the news: Trump TV launched the same day major TV networks suspended White House pool coverage — a protest that left one Trump speech airing without sound. The White House had teased the channel through cryptic videos , and it went live on its YouTube account, WhiteHouse.gov and the official White House app. Reality check: Presidents have long used White House platforms to share speeches and events with the public. What we know about Trump TV How it works: The channel launched as "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station." "Trump TV is a 24/7 livestream of the Administration's greatest hits, unfiltered," Kaelan Dorr, deputy assistant to the president, wrote on X . So far, the channel has shown curated clips of past Trump speeches and executive actions, along with live events. Catch up quick: The initial programming included Trump's July 3 Mount Rushmore speech before shifting into footage of his 2025 inauguration, per multiple reports . The Daily Beast reports 8,500 viewers were watching the stream during its first hour. Around 1,200 people were watching Tuesday afternoon as the channel aired a Trump health care announcement from August, according to an Axios review of the stream. Zoom in: The stream can also carry live events. On Tuesday, the stream carried Vice President Vance's briefing on fraud claims. But while Trump addressed the United Nations General Assembly Tuesday morning, Trump TV was replaying an earlier speech from the National Prayer Breakfast. Unanswered questions about Trump TV What we're watching: So far, Trump TV has no anchors, news ticker or headline chyrons. The stream includes banners asking viewers to text White House officials. It's unclear who staffs the channel, makes programming decisions or sets its schedule. What they're saying: A White House official tells Axios that the channel's purpose is to replay Trump's "greatest hits that the media fails to cover fairly, oftentimes on purpose." The intrigue: The White House's revamped livestream page labels its regular feed "CH 45" and Trump TV "CH 47" — references to Trump serving as the 45th and 47th president. Trump's previous streaming ventures Flashback: Trump has experimented with direct-to-audience video before. In 2016, Trump's presidential campaign launched a nightly Facebook Live show called "Trump Tower Live" that was meant to deliver campaign messaging directly to the public. Trump Media's Truth+ offers 24/7 news streams and on-demand entertainment. It appears on Truth+ apps and remains a commercial streaming service rather than an official government stream. The service began rolling out in 2024. Its lineup has included broadcasts of Newsmax, OAN and Real America's Voice.

'Super Intelligence': the president’s new term for AI, explained
A look at President Donald Trump’s relabel from artificial intelligence to ‘Super intelligence,’ and the phrase’s original meaning
President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced a rebranding of the term “artificial intelligence,” saying during the United Nations General Assembly that from now on, it will be called “super intelligence.”
“From this point forward, all of United States’ documents, and hopefully the world’s, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, ‘super,’ as opposed to ‘artificial’,” he said.
Though the rebrand may have been a surprise to many, superintelligence is already an established term in AI literature. It was popularized in philosopher Nick Bostrom’s 2014 bestseller Superintelligence, which defines the term as “any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest.” Artificial superintelligence, or ASI, thus refers to future AI systems that could be much smarter than humans, and contrasts with the weaker forms of AI that exist today.
ASI is a step beyond AGI, or artificial general intelligence, which OpenAI defines as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.” By this definition, today’s AI isn’t AGI yet, much less ASI, since we can’t yet hire AI as a reliable virtual employee.
Some experts dislike the term superintelligence, or question whether it’s a coherent concept. In the influential 2025 paper “AI as Normal Technology,” authors Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan write, “We do not think there is a useful sense of the term ‘intelligence’ in which AI is more intelligent than people acting with the help of AI.”
But others say the possible renaming contributes to an ongoing conversation about AI’s growing abilities.
“‘Super’ does align well with the fact that AI is exceeding human capabilities in a growing range of tasks and by increasing margins, which can have distinct national security implications beyond simply matching human performance,” said Caleb Withers, a research associate for the Technology and Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
For example, in early September, OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, one of the most important open problems in math.
As AI becomes more capable, it has grown increasingly central to the U.S.-China relationship. Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping are slated to meet this week to discuss trade and AI issues. Bostrom, who has warned of the dangers of fully superintelligent AI systems, said an all-out AI race increases the risk that the technology gets out of control. “If competitors are convinced that coming second [in the AI race] means the total loss of everything they care about, they will take whatever risk necessary to bypass their rivals,” he said.
Trump reportedly worries that an AI slowdown could cause a market crash, and sees “super intelligence” as a critical sector for America to stay ahead of China. “Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this, and now I say, whoever wins SI, whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins.”

Some 175,000 people in Indonesia have suffered from respiratory illness since August, its health ministry said, as it continues to battle wildfires that have raged for weeks.
More than 40,000 cases â which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia â involve toddlers.
Forest fires have blanketed parts of the country as well as neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore in toxic smog, pushing air quality indices into "unhealthy" territory.
Indonesia has deployed more than 54,000 officials and dozens of jets to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra for water bombing, but the vast territory and challenging peatland conditions make it hard to put out the fires, authorities say.
"From the air to the ground, all forces continue to move," Indonesia's Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya said on Monday.
"Everything is being done to extinguish the fires, reduce the impact of the smoke, and, most importantly, protect the public from the threat of forest and land fires."
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during its annual dry season, which usually runs from July through October.
This year, however, the fires and haze have been turbocharged by a so-called "Godzilla" El Nino, which has fuelled extremely dry conditions.
The independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas has detected around 734,000 hotspots across the country as of Wednesday - a figure that is more than 30% higher than that of 2019, one of Indonesia's worst wildfire seasons.
Since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land â nearly six times the size of Greater London â have been burned.
The wildfires have led to school closures and a surge in hospital admissions across Indonesia.
The number of people suffering wildfire-related respiratory illnesses had more than doubled to 113,336 by 9 September, up from 50,891 on 1 September, according to figures from the health ministry.
The toxic smog has also taken a toll on wildlife, including critically endangered orangutans.
Late last month, an Indonesia-based wildlife foundation shared footage showing an orangutan writhing on the ground on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan, one of Indonesia's hardest-hit provinces. The great ape, which was discovered by a farmer, was rescued and given emergency treatment for hypoxia, but later died.
Indigenous and civil society groups in West Kalimantan filed a class action suit last week against the central government and local administrations, accusing them of deliberate negligence for failing to properly tackle the wildfires scorching the province.
"This is a disaster that occurs every year. This recurring pattern proves our view that the defendants knew about the potential haze disaster and the risks of disaster from forest and land fires," the group's lawyer Glorio Sanen said in a statement at the time.
Indonesia has carried out several rounds of cloud-seeding operations in recent weeks, some conducted together with members of Japan's Self-Defense Forces who arrived in Borneo earlier this month to help with firefighting efforts.
Cloud seeding involves manipulating existing clouds, such as by dropping salt crystals or silver iodide into them, to help produce more rain. Meteorologists, however, are divided over the effectiveness of the practice.
In the Malaysian state of Sarawak, one of the worst-affected areas outside Indonesia, authorities launched a five-day cloud-seeding operation earlier this month.
Apart from tackling the ongoing haze, this exercise was aimed at boosting declining water levels at several hydropower dams ahead of a severe dry spell forecast for October.
"October might be hotter and drier," Sarawak's Deputy Premier Douglas Uggah Embas told reporters. "We want to increase the water levels as much as possible while we still can."
The haze has reached as far as parts of the Philippines, where local officials have urged residents to stay indoors as much as possible, and Singapore, where authorities have begun issuing daily haze advisories.

A rare snail found in just one lake in the UK started laying eggs on its six-hour journey from Wales to Kent, as a zoo joined a nationwide effort to save the species.
Glutinous snails are no bigger than a fingertip and used to be widespread across UK water ways.
It is thought habitat disruption and environmental changes reduced their population to such an extent that they are only now found in Llyn Tegid, a lake in Eryri National Park, also known as Snowdonia.
Wingham Wildlife Park near Canterbury has taken some of the wild population to breed and release into the wild. Samantha Eden, assistant curator, said the zoo started with six snails and recently started a new colony.
Despite their slow reputation, the breeding efforts are off to a flying start, Eden said.
"I brought 24 snails back from Wales at the start of July," she said.
"It was a six hour drive, and by the time I'd arrived back at the park I had about 12 egg pods in the carry containers that we were using. They'd laid eggs literally whilst we were driving.
"We started, with one of the ponds, with just six adult snails. We recently moved 130 babies out of that pond to start a new colony."
Hannah Ellins, head of reptiles and invertebrates, said: "We do a lot of work with exotics, but it's cool being able to help our animals here."
She added: "We'll keep breeding them and then hopefully we'll eventually then release them into the wild and help wild populations."
The scheme is part of a wider national effort to protect the very rare species.
Wingham Wildlife Park is joining Askham Bryan Wildlife Park in York and Longleat in Wiltshire, along with Dudley and Chester zoos, with the Freshwater Habitats Trust searching for suitable water bodies where the snails could eventually be released.

Top Iranian and US officials have held talks at the UN in New York on a day when the US leader said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved.
No breakthrough has been reported from the meeting mediated by Qatar and involving Iran's foreign minister and US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff - the first since a June ceasefire unravelled.
Witkoff said a round of discussions had been completed "that we hope will prove constructive and promising". Iran repeated its demand for the US to end its "acts of aggression".
The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of prices.
It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.
In his address at the annual meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime - remarks that sounded more pitched to voters the US midterms than the diplomats in the hall.
He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran - a huge contrast with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General AntÃ³nio Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples.
The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open.
Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly.
Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met Witkoff.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, quoted by state broadcaster IRNA, later said negotiations took part through a Qatari mediator who communicated Tehran's conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and to US "acts of aggression".
The BBC asked Witkoff how the meetings had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. Witkoff later confirmed on X that the talks had been held "through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day".
"They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising," Witkoff said. "The mediators will continue their work."
Since the ceasefire collapsed, both sides have intermittently exchanged fire.
Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.
The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast.
The US has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing a huge disruption to the Iranian economy.
In an effort to force Tehran to agree a deal to end the conflict, President Trump has also threatened sanctions against any country that continues trading with Iran. But so far, there has been no indication of a change of course in Iran, which insists the US and Israel end their war, including against the Iran-backed Shia group Hezbollah in Lebanon which Israel has been attacking.
Yemen's Houthis - also allied to Iran - have recently intesified attacks aimed at disrupting oil shipping from Saudi Arabia, promting an escalation of the conflict with the kingdom.
