06796907bdd6.text: The Trump administration says Americans should prepare between now and Election Day for a wave of new arrests and prosecutions over alleged non-citizen voter fraud . Why it matters: The Trump administration is deploying hundreds of federal investigators and attorneys to pursue President Trump's long-running fixation — and test a broader Republican claim that tougher enforcement will uncover far more illegal voting. "This initiative is a tier one priority," a Justice Department official told reporters on Tuesday. "It's a top priority for the attorney general and for the White House." The big picture: Across the country, there are now 1,600 open cases of potential voter fraud and 160 people have been arrested, a Homeland Security Investigations official said Tuesday. HSI agents have been requesting and combing through publicly available voter data to find cases of non-citizens registering to vote or voting when they're ineligible. The FBI has been working on these cases too. DOJ has charged 24 immigrants this calendar year following the prioritization, according to agency press releases. The accused are a mixture of undocumented immigrations and legal residents. The number of prosecutions will "rise significantly each week going forward from now until the election," the DOJ official said. Zoom in: To support these investigations, which the HSI official called agent-time intensive, Homeland Security staff have shifted work time from other priorities. HSI agents typically investigate smuggling, trafficking, financial fraud and sexual exploitation crimes. The intrigue: Staff usually focused on finding immigration fraud at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the office for legal immigration, have also been tasked with searching for possible non-citizens registered in state voter files. This staff sent referrals to HSI to investigate, according to the New York Times , and flagged the potential non-citizens by the thousands to state election officials . For three weeks, the fraud team was tasked with reviewing voter files and not allowed to do other work, a person familiar with the agency's work told Axios. The other side: Instances of mistaken registrations and cases of non-citizen voting are rare, but they've long been investigated by the federal government. The extent of this administration's efforts to prioritize searching for these cases is novel for the federal government and the local election officials involved. "It's not typical and it's not appropriate," a former senior Justice Department official told Axios in July . Between the lines: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherril revealed in July that 6,600 non-citizens were registered to vote through a software error. The DOJ official said there are also similar system errors registering people who aren't intending to register in other states. But they declined to say whether any government officials or vendors responsible for these errors would be held responsible as individual voters now are. The bottom line: "These investigations and these indictments are a major deterrent for this election" against illegal voting, Mike Davis, founder of the Article III Project, a legal affairs-focused nonprofit closely aligned with the president. "There's a new sheriff in town: His name is Donald Trump, and if illegals vote in our elections, they will be prosecuted and deported."

be434ea1d446.text: President Trump's accelerationist AI doctrine increasingly bears the stamp of the "All-In" podcast, whose tech-investor network now feeds ideas and talent directly into the White House. Why it matters: An unlikely marriage of convenience between MAGA and Silicon Valley has proved remarkably durable, deepening as Trump sheds support elsewhere and stakes more of his legacy on dominating the AI race. Zoom in: No figure has done more to bridge the two worlds than David Sacks , the "All-In" co-host who spent Trump's first year as his AI czar and remains a powerful outside adviser with direct access to the president. Sacks helped build Trump's original AI agenda around a simple premise: move fast, sweep away regulatory barriers and treat China — not catastrophic risk — as the overriding threat. Anthropic's highly capable Mythos model posed the first serious challenge to that doctrine in May, rattling the White House enough to consider pre-release oversight of frontier models. But Trump watered down the 90-day review plan after Sacks and industry leaders warned that three months amounted to an eternity in frontier AI — and could slow U.S. labs as China raced ahead. Zoom out: Sacks left the White House but not Trump's inner circle, shaping AI policy as co-chair of the president's science council while the broader "All-In" network embeds itself deeper across Trumpworld. David Friedberg serves on the same council alongside investor Marc Andreessen, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and other tech leaders — putting half of "All-In"'s core cast on the president's formal science-policy panel. Chamath Palihapitiya , another co-host and prominent Trump booster, is among the names being floated for the new AI czar job Trump announced last weekend. Brad Gerstner , a frequent fill-in on the podcast, helped conceive Trump Accounts and became one of the program's chief evangelists. The intrigue: Jason Calacanis, the show's moderator, is the political outlier — frequently criticizing Trump on Iran and inflation while otherwise aligning with his co-hosts on the revolutionary nature of AI. Between the lines: Few platforms better capture the zeitgeist of AI accelerationism than "All-In," where the movement's leading investors, executives and political allies increasingly converge. After former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon's safety warnings exploded across Washington , the hosts devoted much of their next episode to portraying the backlash as an orchestrated "doomer" campaign. Three days later, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang paused his live "All-In" Summit interview to take a call from Trump, who drew a raucous reception as he dismissed AI catastrophe fears as a "hoax." What they're saying: White House spokesperson Kush Desai said Trump "has always listened to a variety of opinions from a variety of subject matter experts" and argued that his open line to tech leaders has helped widen America's technological lead. "The fact that this President maintains an open line of communication with tech leaders instead of castigating them, as the Biden administration had done, is a major reason why America's technological and innovative lead has widened since President Trump came into office," Desai said. What to watch: "All-In" and the accelerationist wing of Silicon Valley are tying themselves unusually tightly to one president and one governing philosophy. Sacks, for example, has blessed a $ 100 million-plus midterm operation built to advance Trump's AI agenda and punish candidates who favor tougher regulation. Inside AI labs, that political fusion is feeding a deeper fear: that warnings about catastrophic risk will become coded as anti-Trump politics, turning AI safety into yet another partisan litmus test.

eb75a3157063.text: Uber is betting billions on a driverless future, but the secret to making the economics work could be — surprise! — its vast army of human drivers. Why it matters: Uber believes a hybrid network of robots and people can keep its expensive autonomous vehicles busier, and therefore more profitable, than fleets made up entirely of robotaxis. The big picture: Think of a high-tech robotaxi like an airplane: It costs money whether it's carrying passengers or sitting on the ground. The more trips each vehicle makes, the more revenue Uber and its robotaxi partners can squeeze from that expensive asset, offsetting the fixed costs of the technology, vehicle financing, insurance, depot space and other infrastructure. Between the lines: Ride-hailing is a supply-driven business, and robotaxis aren't a substitute for drivers, Uber says — they're an additional form of supply. With greater supply comes lower prices and shorter wait times, which means increased reliability. That stimulates more demand, and ultimately makes the ride-hailing pie bigger. That's Uber's theory. Robotaxi economics remain unproven , Uber's own president of autonomous mobility and delivery, Sarfraz Maredia, tells Axios. It's still early, and no company is making money yet operating them, nor is anyone yet operating them at massive scale. Whether AVs and all that's needed to support a fleet — including charging infrastructure and maintenance — will ultimately be cheaper than today's ride-hailing model "very much has yet to be proven," Maredia says. "The unit economics today have a long way to go." Uber's bet is that its mix of human drivers and AVs will produce better returns. How it works: In a hybrid network — and Lyft has a similar philosophy —AVs would handle the steady "base load" of everyday demand. Human drivers, meanwhile, would provide extra capacity during rush hour, bad weather, concerts and other demand spikes. Maredia points to late nights as an example: Uber can recharge robotaxis when electricity is cheapest while human drivers handle the bar-closing rush. So far , Uber says, robotaxis are taking shorter city-center trips, while drivers get longer, more lucrative ones. "You could argue that the AVs are getting the scraps," CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told Fast Company earlier this year. That flexibility is an advantage , Uber says. A robotaxi operator needs enough cars to handle its busiest periods — leaving expensive AVs sitting idle when demand falls. Uber, by contrast, can size its robotaxi fleet for normal demand and summon more human drivers when needed. Drivers only get paid when they're working, whereas robotaxis cost money even when they're idle. Reality check: Drivers will be displaced eventually, and Uber doesn't argue that point. Part-time drivers who use Uber as a safety net — women, caregivers and lower-income workers — will be disproportionally affected, the company acknowledges. Others will have to work longer or at different times and places to earn the same amount, the company says. But a hybrid network will help ease that transition, it says. By the numbers: Uber says trips are up in Austin and Atlanta, where Waymo AVs are sharing the Uber app with drivers, and driver earnings have stayed consistent. Uber says Waymos on its network in Austin and Atlanta are completing about 30% more trips per vehicle per day than AVs in other major robotaxi markets. Yes, but: Independent research from Gridwise, an app that lets gig drivers track earnings, expenses and mileage, had different findings. It compared earnings for Uber and Lyft drivers in the second quarter with the same period two years ago and found base pay per hour was lower in San Francisco and Los Angeles, where they are competing with Waymo. In Austin, where Waymos are exclusively available on Uber, base pay and gross pay per hour rose less than rideshare drivers in other parts of the country, Gridwise found, suggesting AV growth could already be putting pressure on driver earnings. The bottom line: Humans may make Uber's robotaxi math work. Whether the math works as well for the humans is less certain.

The US Supreme Court has refused to intervene in a custody dispute involving a surrogate who refused an abortion request from the parents who hired her to have their baby.
Justice Elena Kagan declined an emergency appeal filed by McKenna West asking the court to halt a previous ruling granting parental rights to the California couple.
The parents had asked West to abort the pregnancy after a scan at 20 weeks showed the foetus had a severe heart defect. West instead went to Texas where nearly all abortions are illegal and gave birth to the child.
The court's decision leaves in place an earlier order that granted custody to the parents.
The BBC has contacted lawyers for both parties for comment.
West has been seeking custody over the baby, which was born last month with hypoplastic left heart syndrome - a defect where the left side of the heart cannot pump enough blood to the body.
The condition often requires multiple surgeries, which are not a cure. Infants with the condition can have lifelong complications, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
West - who has been supported by several Republican officials - travelled to Texas, where the state's Attorney General Ken Paxton intervened in the case and won an emergency court order requiring that the boy receive medical care in the state. He had surgery soon after birth.
West said she denied the parents', Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, requests to have the abortion after learning of treatment options and wanting to keep "this precious baby", according to the Supreme Court filing.
West argued that the biological parents should not have custody because she worried they would not give the boy the necessary medical care since they sought to abort the child after learning of the life-threatening condition.
In a previous court hearing, Gilkar said the baby - whom they named Rumi - was "our child" and "the love of our lives", according to the Associated Press. They said West travelled to Texas without telling them and blocked their access to medical information.
A California court previously granted parental rights to Ahmed and Gilkar, while a Texas court issued a restraining order blocking West from seeing the baby.
Last month, an attorney for the California couple said the child was in critical condition and seemed to be "suffering from potential complications".
West argued that without intervention from the Supreme Court, she would no longer have access to information about the child's medical condition.
In the filing, lawyers for West suggested that the California couple could place the child in hospice care.

A Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals to people who went on to kill themselves should "rot in hell", the mother of a British woman who took her own life has said.
Imogen Nunn, known as Immy, died at her Brighton flat in January 2023 aged 25 after buying a substance online from Kenneth Law.
Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in online suicide forums. But almost 80 deaths in the UK have also been linked to him.
However, as part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.
Imogen's mother, Louise Nunn, told the BBC she was angry he would not face justice here. "I think we've been let down as families. Our children have been let down," she told the BBC.
It comes as the impact statements of UK families will be read in court in Ontario this week.
In May this year, Law pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada as part of a deal with prosecutors, who withdrew more serious charges of murder.
Authorities said Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.
Speaking at the time, families of British victims said they were angry UK prosecutors had not charged Law over the deaths of 79 Britons, which authorities said were linked to products he supplied.
The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) in the UK said it had agreed to the Canadian plea bargain on the basis Law's sentence take the British deaths into account.
A letter, seen by the BBC, revealed the CPS was concerned Law could challenge his extradition to the UK from Canada, and that including UK victims in the Canadian sentencing process was the "quickest and most effective route" to justice.
'You destroyed my whole world'
This week, a Canadian court will hear impact statements from UK victims. They will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date. It is the only opportunity for British families to have a voice in the legal process.
Speaking to the BBC, however, Nunn said part of her victim impact statement had been redacted by authorities.
"I think we had a chance to say the words we wanted to say in our impact statement, but now I've been told they've redacted my last paragraph, which felt like our only chance."
In it, she said Law destroyed her life. "You have destroyed my whole world. If Immy was here now, I know exactly what she would say to me, but I'm not Immy and I will never forgive you."
'Social media built up her confidence'
Immy was profoundly deaf and had a presence on social media where she shared a satirical look at her life.
"She found social media and I just remember how happy she was," said Nunn. "She tried to put a spin on a sad situation and she tried to take all the negative things in her life and turn it into more positive.
"It changed her, her confidence came back. Social media built up her confidence and friendships."
Responding to the BBC, the CPS said: "Some redactions are being applied to victim impact statements as advised by Canadian counsel, to ensure they are admissible within the Canadian courts.
"We recognise the profound impact of Kenneth Law's offending and are working to ensure all victims and bereaved families have the opportunity to share their individual experiences through the sentencing process."
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

Rock star Angry Anderson, whose music famously soundtracked the wedding of Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan's characters in Australian TV soap Neighbours, has died at the age of 79.
The musician, whose real name was Gary Anderson, rose to fame with rock band Rose Tattoo, which he fronted from 1976.
His solo song Suddenly became a global hit after it was played during the wedding of Minogue and Donovan's characters Scott and Charlene in Neighbours. The wedding episode was watched by 20 million people in the UK alone in 1988.
Anderson said Minogue had been "adamant" that the track was used for the scene, and he later declared that Suddenly was the best song he had ever written.
Before his death, Anderson had a cardiac arrest while on Rose Tattoo's farewell tour in Europe last month.
He was treated in hospital before going home to Australia, and the band cancelled nine live dates.
A joint statement, external from Anderson's family and Rose Tattoo remembered him as a "devoted father, and much-loved bandmate".
"His loss will be deeply felt by all those who knew and loved him both here in Australia and overseas," it said.
"We thank everyone for their prayers and messages of love and continued support."
Born in Melbourne in 1947, Anderson and Rose Tattoo first became known on Australia's rock scene, releasing five albums beginning with their 1978 debut.
After the band split nine years later, Anderson continued recording music as a solo artist, and co-wrote and released Suddenly in the summer of 1987.
It was quickly selected by Minogue for use in Neighbours for her character Charlene Mitchell's wedding to Donovan's Scott Robinson.
Thanks in large part to its use in Neighbours, Suddenly reached the top three in both the UK and Australia.
However, it was held off the number one spot in its home country by Minogue's own debut solo single, Locomotion.
Anderson released two albums as a solo artist, before Rose Tattoo reunited in 1993 to support Guns N' Roses on their Australian tour.
The band returned in 1998 for their own tour and were inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) Hall of Fame in 2006.
Anderson's other credits included playing Herod in an Australian production of Jesus Christ Superstar.
He was made a Member of the Order of Australia in 1993, in recognition of service to the community, particularly his charity work and his work as a youth advocate.

Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests.
The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in legal documents filed this week.
The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him.
In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims.
In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the case had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people.
"Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said.
"A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."
Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's security detail for the last 20 years of her life.
Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties.
In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained".
They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much."
The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell.
The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand.
In one, he said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents.
Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me."
The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees.
In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (Â£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police.
"All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint.
In his statement to TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."
But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".
The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents.
She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states.
The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment.
Parton's roadmap
Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August.
Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news.
"This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video.
Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years.
Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager.
In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career.
In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death.
"She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement.
"Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come."
The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy.

44a7bb991ab6.text:
- Published
The tech giant OpenAI will share its AI cyber defence system Daybreak for free with the Ukraine government to help it protect civilian infrastructure, like hospitals and power plants, from cyber-attacks.
According to the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), the national cyber incident response team, Ukraine recorded nearly 6,000 attacks in 2025.
Daybreak is able to quickly identify weaknesses in digital systems and help develop fixes.
Under the deal, Ukraine will get access to OpenAI's advanced GPT 5.6 Sol model - a rival to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable.
George Osborne, former UK chancellor and now Head of OpenAI for Countries, said: "Protecting civilian infrastructure means defending it against both physical and digital attacks, so people can continue to live, work and access essential services."
Reacting to the news, Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence for the cybersecurity firm Sophos, said that Russian offensive cyber operations had been "a key component" of the Kremlin's aggression against Ukraine since 2014.
"Any initiative that strengthens Ukraine's already highly capable, but heavily burdened, cyber defence efforts is a welcome development and could provide a valuable force multiplier," he said.
Jamie MacColl, a senior research fellow specialising in cyber at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told the BBC western tech firms had been supporting Ukraine for some time - partly for altruistic reasons but also because they gain very valuable data and intelligence from an active conflict.
"Given this, it's no surprise that OpenAI is now also providing defensive cyber security services" he said.
He thought access to Daybreak would be useful, particularly given the volume of Russian cyber-attacks targeting the country.
But he noted Ukraine already had access to AI tools provided by OpenAI's competitors, like Google.
Attack and defence at the frontier
The cyber-abilities of the latest, most powerful AI models, called "frontier" models in AI jargon, can be a boon for cyber-defenders, but the same abilities can also be used for attack.
Spotting weaknesses in systems, for example, is useful for defenders looking to block hackers, but also for attackers hunting for ways to infiltrate an organisation.
Anthropic has tightly restricted access to its systems on the grounds that they are too powerful to fall into the wrong hands, but OpenAI has allowed some firms in Europe, as well as UK banks, to use its most advanced cyber models.
The firm made the announcement alongside the UN General Assembly which is currently underway in New York.
AI is firmly on the agenda there, and US tech bosses including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei are due to speak at the high-level gathering.
United Nations Secretary General AntÃ³nio Guterres called for the tech to be regulated in his final address, while US President Donald Trump says it should be renamed "super intelligence".
Evidence suggests the technology is increasingly being used in the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
In a report published earlier this month, Anthropic claimed that its Claude platform appeared to have been used by a group of Russian developers to build software for a swarm of so-called "kamikaze" drones designed for attacks in Ukraine.
It said the group had activated virtual private networks - VPNs - in order to get around a geographical block put in place by the tech firm.
Anthropic also claimed AI had been used in attempts to infiltrate the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic services.
Recently, around 100 US companies signed an open letter warning governments and institutions around the world that "the window is closing" to ensure cyber defences are robust enough to withstand AI-enabled cyber attacks.
But it's not just bad actors deploying the tech that are of growing concern: in the summer, OpenAI revealed that a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls, and secretly worked together to hack to another tech firm, Hugging Face.
Anthropic, and Google subsequently revealed similar incidents.
Additional reporting by Chris Vallance

641902ec588e.text:
Timâs view
For developing countries, more green tech capital doesnât always translate to a cheaper and cleaner energy system.
Thereâs more money than ever available from private and public financial institutions for investments in clean tech in emerging economies: nearly $400 billion in 2025, according to the Climate Policy Initiative, double the sum five years ago. Itâs not enough â countries agreed at the COP summit in Azerbaijan to hit $1.3 trillion annually by 2035 â but I remember coming to Climate Week a few years ago and hearing a lot more anxiety about this subject than Iâve heard this year. One reason is that clean tech is so much cheaper that thereâs more bang for the buck. Evidence is also piling up that these investments are much less risky than many investors feared: A recent study of lending from development banks to private enterprises in emerging economies since 1994 found an average default rate of 3.5%, similar to that in advanced economies.
The bigger challenge isnât just getting more capital, but making sure it actually leads to lower poverty and lower emissions. âThereâs a lot of good intent,â Tariye Gbadegesin, CEO of Climate Investment Funds, a World Bank-backed pool of concessional capital for clean energy, told me. âBut we need to be better at converting that into outcomes.â
One lesson Gbadegesin has learned in her years in this field is that climate finance investments work best when they are coordinated with a countryâs finance ministry, rather than energy or environmental officials, which has often been the status quo. Development banks shouldnât just dump cash into individual clean tech projects, she said, but rather be proactive about helping developing countries fix their energy market regulations so they become more attractive to private investors, and so that the energy system as a whole, from generation to grids to end users, functions better. More financial innovation is also needed to mitigate the risk of losses introduced when imported hardware is paid for in US dollars, but energy is sold in local currency. âThatâs really the fundamental challenge,â she said.
Jonathan Berman, CEO of the Shell Foundation, who I interviewed at Semaforâs The Next 3 Billion event, added that more attention should focus on consumersâ budget constraints â that is, diverting more climate finance to the engineering and manufacturing improvements needed to drive the cost of clean tech down ever further. âPeople assume that if you use these billions of dollars and build these clean energy systems, that the demand will just come. Thatâs not true, and itâs less true now even than it was six months ago,â he said, as the fallout from the Iran war has weakened household budgets. Micro-lending and other financial products designed to make clean tech adoption more affordable to low-income households doesnât work in a world where each new day feels less predictable than the last, he said, so âwe probably should be driving towards no financing at all in as many of the use cases as possible.â

Local forces in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray have seized control of the airport in the regional capital, Mekelle, from federal police, local residents have told the BBC.
No flights are currently landing at the airport and Ethiopian Airlines said it had suspended flights to Mekelle and the cities of Shire and Axum because of what it called the "current situation" in Tigray.
There have been escalating tensions this year between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, fuelling fears of a return to civil war.
On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa.
A two-year war in Tigray ended in November 2022 - but both sides are now accusing each other of violating an African Union-mediated peace deal.
It was one of the most-deadly conflicts this century, with the AU's mediator estimating some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
The flight suspension follows a series of reported drone strikes in Tigray.
On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities.
The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes beginning at around 03:30.
"This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said.
Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools.
He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces.
But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun.
The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not publicly commented.
On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an open invasion on the region's residents, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity.
Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid.
It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, which formally ended the conflict in November 2022.
In July, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament.
Just before the general election in May, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy.
There have also been reports that the TPLF has forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces.

Four ancient footprints are helping scientists step into a T. rex’s shoes.
The prints form the first set of tracks probably left behind by an adult Tyrannosaurus rex, researchers report September 8 in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. Measurements of the 7-meter-long trackway suggest the ancient predator was ambling along at about 1.6 meters per second, roughly equivalent to a person’s quick walking pace.
A few single adult T. rex footprints exist in the fossil record, as do trackways possibly from T. rex juveniles or other dinosaur species, says Peter Falkingham, a paleontologist at Liverpool John Moores University in England. “But an individual track doesn’t tell you a lot. A trackway tells you more about foot placement as the animal’s moving along.” And younger and older dinosaurs probably walked differently, just as human toddlers and adults do.
“Finding an adult trackway is cool,” Falkingham says. “It’s unique. It brings something new.”
High school teacher and paleontologist Kent Hups stumbled on the footprints in 2025, while fossil hunting along a steep incline in the Hell Creek Formation in North Dakota. The tracks stick up out of the ground because sediment filled in the originally muddy footprints, which then eroded away more slowly than the surrounding rock.
When Hups saw the first track, he noted that it was three-toed and enormous, measuring 80 centimeters across. “I’m going, ‘this has to be a T. rex,’” says Hups, of Northglenn High School in Colo. and the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.
Slender toe impressions and fossils unearthed in the area signal a T. rex left behind the footprints roughly 66.5 million years ago. “There’s always the possibility that we haven’t found the skeletons of some species that we don’t know about,” Falkingham says. “But as far as our knowledge goes, T. rex is about the only track maker that could have made these.”
The team used stride length and body size to calculate the dinosaur’s speed. Unfortunately, the footprints aren’t well-preserved and estimating speed from tracks is tricky, so the T. rex may have been walking slightly faster or slower than calculated. Better tracks could have revealed whether the foot landed flat or toe-to-heel, or how foot pads supported the predator’s weight.
More tracks are sure to follow. In fact, a fifth step may be concealed in the hill. But the team is waiting for Mother Nature to wear away the surrounding rock, Hups says. “I can’t wait to get back out there and keep looking for more.”

The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis.
The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it.
Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, the company that bought the property in 2018, UrbagestiÃ³n, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from â¬500 (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650.
It subsequently lowered the new rent to â¬1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of â¬1,350.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana BelÃ©n, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti.
Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building.
In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money".
Police cordoned off a section of the street and removed people from the entrance to the building, including members of the media, striking some protesters with batons.
A representative of tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas shouted at the police through a megaphone: "Think for 10 seconds about Maricarmen, who could be your own grandmother."
"There is a police deployment as if this were a military operation," said Beatriz Duro, Maricarmen's lawyer. "This is the fourth time [they've tried to evict her] but the first time they've come right to the door of the property. It's completely disproportionate."
In June, the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called for the pensioner's eviction to be halted and for her to be offered affordable alternative accommodation. The local government said she had declined its offer of a place in an elderly care home.
The central government said UrbagestiÃ³n had refused its repeated attempts to negotiate Maricarmen's situation. The BBC has attempted to contact the company.
The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, UrbagestiÃ³n reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead.
"Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa RodrÃguez.
A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes.
In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year.
The Socialist-led government of Pedro SÃ¡nchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed".
However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

The more scientists look for chemicals that can increase breast cancer risk, the more they find.
Hundreds of potential breast carcinogens lurk in consumer goods, food, drinking water, pesticides, drugs and building materials, scientists reported in a peer-reviewed study published Wednesday in the journal Environmental Health Perspectives.
Exposure to these chemicals is ubiquitous, the authors warn, yet biomonitoring efforts are failing to measure people’s exposures to most chemicals or assess risks from compound exposures.
Chemicals found in and derived from fossil fuels accounted for some of the largest production volumes and environmental releases of potential breast carcinogens, said lead author Jennifer Kay, a research scientist at the Silent Spring Institute, which works to reduce toxic threats to women’s health. She called widespread use of petrochemicals, particularly to make plastic, “a huge problem.”
Bisphenols and phthalates, chemicals produced at high volumes for plastics, can damage DNA, trigger cell division and increase breast cancer risk or severity.
Most breast cancers occur in women 55 and older, as cells lose their ability to repair genetic damage and start dividing abnormally. Breast cancer rates have been rising in recent years for all women, with steeper increases among younger women. These trends cannot be explained by better screening or known risk factors like genetics, obesity or smoking, pointing to environmental factors as a cause.
Kay worked with her Silent Spring colleagues and University of California, Berkeley, researchers to build on her previous paper that linked more than 900 chemicals to increased breast cancer risk. Some of the chemicals cause mammary tumors in rodents, some interfere with hormones, many damage DNA and some do all three.
DNA damage that isn’t repaired before a cell divides can become a permanent mutation, a first step in tumor formation. Chemicals that trigger breast cell division—often by altering the hormones estrogen and progesterone—boost the chances of mutation.
If a premenopausal woman is exposed to gene-damaging chemicals during her normal hormonal cycle, then is exposed to hormone-altering chemicals, Kay said, “it’s just kind of hit upon hit” that sets the stage for cancer. Even after menopause, exposure to hormone-disrupting chemicals can activate cell division and increase breast cancer risk, especially if there is DNA damage, she said.
“Shocking” Number of Potential Breast Carcinogens
To understand how people might encounter chemicals with the potential to cause breast cancer, the team used more than a dozen U.S. government databases to gauge exposures.
They mapped their list of chemicals to production and import data to flag high-volume substances with potential for widespread exposure. They determined air emissions for each chemical from mobile sources like vehicles and stationary sources like factories, as well as releases into air, land and water near fenceline communities.

They also gathered information on known exposures from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey biomonitoring database. The NHANES measures only a small subset of chemicals in people, though, so the team filled in biomonitoring gaps with Environmental Protection Agency models that estimate daily exposure to chemicals. Finally, they compiled lists of chemicals used in everything from toothpaste to vinyl flooring.
The team found 500 chemicals linked to breast cancer in consumer products like cosmetics, plastic goods and detergents, and nearly as many in pesticides and dietary sources. Many of the potential breast carcinogens found in human blood and urine samples were detected in more than 90 percent of the population, but NHANES doesn’t monitor most of the chemicals.
It’s critically important to highlight the sheer ubiquity of these breast-cancer-related chemicals in the U.S. population, said Rashmi Joglekar, science policy director of Stanford University’s Health and Toxics Policy Lab, who was not involved in the research.
In 2019, the year with the most recent data available, manufacturers produced more than 5 billion pounds of potential breast carcinogens, including bisphenol A, used to make polycarbonate plastics and resins, and 10 chemicals that cause mammary tumors in rodents, including styrene, benzene and vinyl chloride.
It’s “really, really shocking” that some of the chemicals produced and released into the environment in the highest volumes are established mammary carcinogens or genotoxic chemicals, Joglekar said. Seeing millions of pounds of known carcinogens released into the environment in a single year highlights the failure of U.S. regulatory agencies to protect people, she said.
The study identifies chemicals the authors believe warrant additional research and potential regulatory attention, a spokesperson for the American Chemistry Council, which represents nearly 200 companies in the chemistry business, said in a statement. “The authors themselves note that many of the exposure estimates used in the analysis are based on predictive models that rely on limited data and assumptions and are subject to significant uncertainty.”
That uncertainty includes a universe of chemicals that aren’t being tracked. The authors flagged more than 340 potential breast carcinogens that aren’t included in EPA’s Toxics Release Inventory, even though a quarter of them were produced or imported in excess of 1 million pounds in 2019. And the study likely underestimates exposures, the authors noted, because their calculations are based on EPA models of average daily intake, rather than on estimates of the most exposed groups.
Some people could be exposed to certain chemicals at levels 10 to 100 times higher

South Sudan President Salva Kiir has dissolved the transitional government, three months before the country's first election since its independence in 2011.
The country has previously postponed elections twice and extended the transitional period several times.
Under the amended law, signed on Monday, Kiir removed the country's five vice-presidents and dissolved parliament, as well as national and state governments.
Kiir is the presidential candidate of his Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM). No prominent figures have announced plans to challenge him in the December poll. The main opposition leader Riek Machar was sacked as vice-president last year and charged with treason.
He is under house arrest.
Machar had been named vice-president as part of a 2018 peace deal to end a five-year civil war between forces loyal to the two men.
Kiir will remain in office with full constitutional powers until an elected president is sworn in. He also reappointed some ministers and governors in caretaker positions until the 22 December elections.
Ahead of Tuesday's announcement a heavy security presence was reported in the capital, Juba. Soldiers from the army and national security services blocked access to government ministries. Soldiers were also seen patrolling parts of the city.
A senior government official told the BBC that staff arriving for work were turned away and told to return the following Monday.
UN agencies in Juba also asked staff to work remotely while the situation was monitored.
Kiir last week dismissed the chairman of the national elections commission, Abednego Akok Kacuol, without giving a reason. He was replaced by the commission's secretary-general, Gabriel Bol Deng.
Akok had said in August that the commission needed $250m (Â£190m) to conduct the election but had received only $21m.
In June, the main opposition group, the Sudan People's Liberation Movement in Opposition (SPLM-IO), the party of Machar, warned people not to take part in poll preparations.
"Anyone coming to register voters and campaign in territories controlled by the mighty SPLM-IO, you will be a prisoner of war," Nathaniel Pierino, acting chairperson of the group, said in a post on Facebook.
The body which oversees implementation of the 2018 peace agreement, the Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (RJMEC), said South Sudan had entered a "critical phase".
It said several key talks under the agreement remained incomplete and urged the parties to agree on a path towards credible elections and a peaceful end to the transitional period, which has lasted since independence.
The latest 24-month extension was due to end on 22 February 2027.

READ MORE: As China and U.S. compete for AI dominance, both have shared concerns over safety The White House has not released many details about Wednesday's greeting, but Trump is expected to participate in an arrival ceremony at the base with Xi and his wife. The salutation will kick off a three-day visit that's expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate for the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump's May visit to China. But it also is a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan. Beyond using the visit to try to keep "strategic stability" between the two countries, Trump seems to be pulling out all the diplomatic stops to show off for Xi. Trump has lavished praise on Xi as a "great leader" and described a warm relationship with the man he has called a friend. That is all while he has given Xi a pass on many issues. Sen. Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, criticized the "lavish welcome." Wicker, R-Miss., said during a speech Tuesday in the Senate that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader "based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party." Wicker archly suggested a list of topics that Trump could discuss with Xi at the state dinner, such as "the purposes of China's massive military buildup, or about China's clear support for Iran," saying that "during every minute of dialogue" Trump should keep in mind that "his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America." Trump has made it clear he wants to wow Xi, telling reporters in recent weeks that he was delighted his new "work of art" helicopter landing pad would be ready for the visit while bemoaning that his massive White House ballroom would not. On Wednesday, Trump is expected to try to match the pageantry he was met with in China earlier this year. Xi was not at the airport to meet Trump — Chinese Vice President Han Zheng was there instead. But there a red carpet was rolled out to meet Air Force One in Beijing. A military honor guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths waving Chinese and American flags and chanting, "Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!" also were present. The children wore white and light blue uniforms that mirrored the traditional paint colors of the presidential plane. Trump's airport ceremony for Xi will be followed on Thursday by more formalities, including an arrival ceremony at the White House and a review of troops. Before the black-tie dinner, which will feature tech industry leaders like Nvidia's Jensen Huang and SpaceX's Elon Musk, the two leaders are expected to dive into the weighty issues behind closed doors, even as expectations are low that the trip will produce any major breakthroughs in the relationship. On Friday, Xi and Peng will be back at the White House for a private tea with the Trumps before joining them on a tour of the National Archives in Washington. The White House has said they will view historic documents underscoring the relationship between the two countries. Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report. This development could change poetry forever. Roses are red and now they’re also blue.
True blue roses were once thought impossible. Roses can make red and yellow pigments but don’t have an enzyme needed to make blue pigments. At least they didn’t until 2004, when researchers at the Suntory Global Innovation Center in Kyoto, Japan, genetically modified a rose to produce blue pigments. The team inserted the gene for an enzyme that can produce a blue pigment called delphinidin. But those roses were purplish, suggesting it takes more than blue pigment to make flowers blue.
Naturally blue flowers, such as irises, make blue pigments like delphinidin. But they also need almost colorless “co-pigment” molecules called flavone C-glycosides to create their blue hue. Those helper molecules stabilize pigments and make them appear deeper blue. Roses also lack genes for making the co-pigments.
This time, Suntory researchers inserted four genes from other blue flower species into a light pink rose. A gene from Canterbury bells (Campanula medium) allowed the engineered roses to produce multiple blue pigments. Two genes from wishbone flowers (Torenia x hybrida) and one from clustered gentian (Gentiana triflora) made enzymes that produce the colorless helper molecules. The combination of the blue pigment malvidin with a helper called isoorientin made bluer flowers than roses producing only delphinidin, the company announced August 25 at the 32nd International Horticultural Congress in Kyoto. The higher the level of co-pigments in the petals, the bluer the flowers, the researchers found.
Roses making the co-pigments are rated as violet blue based on a flower color chart. The rose bushes continued to produce blue flowers for seven years in greenhouse tests in Japan and three years growing in fields in Colombia.
The achievement is sweet. And the team hopes to further enhance the hue.

US President Donald Trump has disclosed millions of dollars' worth of stock market trades made during July, including in firms from Elon Musk's SpaceX to tech and AI giants such as Microsoft.
According to official documents, between $6.5m (Â£4.8m) and $31m worth of stock in Microsoft was sold on behalf of Trump, while they show purchases of between $165,000 and $400,000.
Across more than 1,000 trades, shares were bought and sold in AI company Nvidia and software firm Palantir, a contractor with the US defence department and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the filing shows.
A White House spokesperson said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties.
The spokesperson told the BBC: "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold.
"There are no conflicts of interest."
According to the filing, thousands of dollars' worth of stock was also bought and sold in SpaceX, the rocket, satellite and AI company led by Musk - who was once in charge of the US Department of Government Efficiency.
SpaceX listed its shares on the US-based Nasdaq stock market in June.
Its share price has fluctuated since then, sharply declining in July and August, but it is currently trading 14% higher than its stock market debut.
Shares were also bought and sold in Tesla, Musk's electric vehicle-maker, on behalf of Trump.
Trump has previously publicly disclosed thousands of stock market trades since he returned to the White House in January last year.

French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying.
His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov.
Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev.
However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe.
It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list.
Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns.
Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years.
Usmanov was cited by the EU in its 2022 listing, external as having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine".
The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans".
Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men.
Foreign Minister Baiba BraÅ¾e said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive". Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative".
French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations.
Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon.
Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government.
Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China.
"I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court.
Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Mamedli was not among the 20 prisoners pardoned by Aliyev.

Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.
In a victim impact statement in court, his accuser, Miriam Haley, said the assault had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".
Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions".
Weinstein has already spent six years in prison as the cases against him play out, and he has a separate conviction for sex crimes in Los Angeles. He has faced three trials in New York over rape and abuse allegations.
He was originally convicted and sentenced in the Miriam Haley case in 2020. But in 2024, New York's highest court overturned the conviction, ruling Weinstein did not get a fair trial. He was retried and convicted again in the case last year.
Weinstein was a high-flying Hollywood producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, before reports in 2017 detailed allegations of sexual assault against him stretching back decades, sparking the #MeToo movement.

b6921a661b6e.text: By — Megan Janetsky, Associated Press Megan Janetsky, Associated Press By — James Brooks, Associated Press James Brooks, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/polo-off-mexican-coast-is-among-the-strongest-storms-ever Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Polo off Mexican coast is among 'the strongest storms ever' Nation Sep 23, 2026 12:11 PM EDT MEXICO CITY (AP) — Polo has grown into one of the most powerful Pacific cyclones in decades and was expected to skirt Mexico's southwestern coast as a major hurricane, while another Pacific system, Odalys, strengthened Wednesday from a tropical storm to a hurricane without threatening land. LIVE MAP: Track the path of Hurricane Polo The U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami has called Polo an "extremely dangerous" storm and forecast the system would turn sharply to the northwest before moving west-northwest over the next several days. Polo was about 165 miles (266 kilometers) south of Zihuatanejo and 320 miles (515 kilometers) southeast of Manzanillo, the center reported. It was moving slowly north with maximum sustained winds of 150 mph (241 kph). That put it at Category 4 strength, after earlier being a Category 5 storm. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Fluctuations in intensity are expected, but Polo is expected to remain a very powerful major hurricane during the next few days," the NHC said. Odalys was a Category 1 hurricane and was about 1,295 miles (2,085 kilometers) off the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula of Mexico, moving east-northeast at 9 mph (15 kph) with maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (120 kph), the hurricane center said. Waves, flooding and mudslides are all risks Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said experts indicated Polo was not likely to touch land. Still, hurricane-force winds extend up to 40 miles (65 kilometers) from the storm's center and tropical storm-force winds up to 105 miles (169 kilometers) from the eye, the U.S. center said. Tropical storm conditions were expected along the Pacific coast in Guerrero, Michoacan and Colima states Wednesday into Thursday. READ MORE: Polo has rapidly intensified to a hurricane and is expected to impact Mexico Polo on Tuesday became the third Category 5 hurricane of the Pacific season, following Genevieve and Lowell earlier this year. Category 5 is the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale, reflecting that a storm has maximum sustained winds exceeding 157 mph (253 kph). The hurricane set residents along Mexico's Pacific coast on edge once again after being walloped by a number of powerful cyclones in recent years. Beaches emptied and dark clouds swirled above choppy seas, while Mexican authorities temporarily suspended classes Tuesday in a number of areas. Mexico's navy shut down ports in the states of Guerrero and Michoacán and warned civilians and fishermen to take care. Concepción López Villegas was busily preparing her seaside restaurant for what may come. Strong waves were already lapping at the coastline of her city Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán. As men and children watched the stirring waters behind her, López Villegas said she feared powerful waves would destroy the small business she has worked decades to build. "We're worried and trying to protect our businesses," López Villegas said. "And of course, we're sad because it's our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed." U.S. National Hurricane Center data shows Polo's winds reached speeds comparable to only a few hurricanes in the region in recent decades, primarily Hurricane Patricia, which had winds that reached 215 mph (346 kph) in 2015. "This is one of the strongest storms ever in the (Pacific) Basin," said Kristen L. Corbosiero, professor at the University at Albany's Department of Atmospheric & Environmental Sciences. Heavy rain could produce flash flooding and mudslides. About 3 to 6 inches (8 to 15 centimeters) of rain was forecast for Guerrero and Michoacán states, with smaller amounts possible for coastal portions of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco states. El Nino fueled rapid intensification The U.S. Embassy in Mexico issued a weather alert, instructing citizens to avoid water and beaches and to heed warnings from Mexican authorities. "Even if the storm does not make direct landfall, heavy rain may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Hazardous ocean conditions — intensified by storms — may result in deadly rip currents and rogue waves," the embassy wrote in a statement. READ MORE: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns The rapid intensification of the storm has stunned scientists and authorities alike, with the NHC writing in a report that it was "truly remarkable" how quickly Polo gained strength in 24 hours. Philip Klotzbach, research scientist in the Department of Atmospheric Science at Colorado State University, attributed the intensification to the weather phenomenon known as El Nino, which has fueled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region. In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes, he said. "There are all the ingredients that hurricanes need to get really strong really fast," Klotzbach said. No Atlantic hurricanes have formed yet this year, and this year has set a record for the longest start to a season without a hurricane. The effects of this year's El Nino crush storms before they get going. Brooks reported from Atlanta. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Yinkaâs view
For decades, the debate around Africaâs natural resources has largely been over who gets the value from what the continent digs up and ships out. But at Semaforâs The Next 3 Billion summit in New York this week, the recurring theme was more nuanced. The question was what economic ecosystems can African economies build around their resources before they leave the continent?
That means moving beyond extraction toward processing, manufacturing, infrastructure, energy, and the jobs that can come with them. It also reflects a changing approach to foreign capital. African governments increasingly want partnerships that build domestic capacity, rather than simply finance projects or provide an exit route for commodities.
Nigeriaâs trade minister Jumoke Oduwole put the ambition plainly when discussing the countryâs talks with US companies on critical minerals, saying her government is looking for âpartners that will make sure that the value chain development [and] the jobs are created on Nigerian soil.â
DR Congoâs Prime Minister Judith Suminwa described diversification of both the economy and its foreign partners as a priority, saying partnerships should âbring a plusâ to the country. The implication is that the choice is not necessarily between China, the US, Europe or the Gulf, but whether competition among them can be used to secure more lasting economic capacity.
There is a compelling logic to that strategy. Countries that remain primarily exporters of raw materials are vulnerable to commodity cycles and capture relatively little of the value created farther down the supply chain. More refining, processing, power generation and transport infrastructure could create wider economic spillovers.
But there is also a danger in making âvalue additionâ the answer to every development problem. Processing minerals or refining oil requires enormous amounts of reliable electricity, transport infrastructure, capital, and technical expertise. In some cases, importing finished products may still be cheaper than producing them locally. And building a factory does not automatically create a competitive industry.
The more interesting test, then, is whether Africa can turn its resource advantage into productive capacity without turning industrial policy into an expensive exercise in symbolism. The opportunity is real. The harder question is what African economies can build that will remain competitive after the foreign partners and commodity boom move on.
Notable
- Dangoteâs Lagos refinery is one of the starkest examples of the economic power of domestic production: It netted $1.8 billion in profit after tax in the first half of this year, more than its total revenue for 2025. The companyâs recent IPO was the largest in Africaâs history.

Millions of lettuces are set to be wasted as farmers are grappling with a record outbreak of aphids that has devastated the end of their growing season.
Growers are facing losses of Â£10m, as 30 million heads of lettuce will be rendered unusable, according to the British Leafy Salads Association (BLSA).
The organisation says that warm and dry weather has produced "ideal conditions" for the bugs, with as much as 30% of the UK crop between now and the end of October set to be wasted.
Homegrown lettuce dominates the market in the summer and early autumn weeks before a transition that sees more imports filling shop shelves.
But imported lettuces are now likely to be on the shelves in the UK a couple of weeks earlier than usual.
Farms in many parts of England - the Midlands, East Anglia, the south-east, south and north-west - have been impacted by the outbreak.
Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, BLSA spokesman Dieter Lloyd described the issue as "serious", while not affecting all of the UK crop.
He said people have been eating salads from UK products "all summer" but added: "The issue though is serious, the aphids bloom in June and again in August/September."
"What we're talking about here is the loss of the crop over the course of the last couple of weeks and the couple of weeks ahead."
He said that "this is not all of the heads in the UK, but it's a significant percentage of it" and producers are "looking at not using 30 million heads of lettuce at the cost of Â£10m to the growers".
Over the course of the season, UK growers produce around half a billion heads of lettuce.
Asked if weather is a factor that has contributed to the issues, Lloyd said that short-term weather patterns and regional variations do have an impact.
"We had a problem with aphids last year, we've had a mild winter which traditionally might affect the aphid populations and then they do like warm weather."
The National Farmers' Union said that they are looking to support growers and researchers amid the outbreak.
Martin Emmett, the organisation's horticulture chairman, said: "This summer's warm and dry weather created a number of challenges for growers and the effects are still being felt, with rising levels of pests and disease now adding further pressure to farming businesses following an already difficult period.
"While growers are working hard to tackle record high numbers of aphids, the NFU is supporting the work of grower groups, plant breeders and researchers."

The Scoop
UN agencies are putting a premium on diversifying where they source technology and computing power â away from solely American providers. Last yearâs US sanctions on the International Criminal Court, and Anthropicâs Mythos model cutoff earlier this year, provided a âwake-up callâ about relying on single â mostly American â companies, the chief information officer of the International Telecommunication Union said.
Some UN groups are exploring shared computing and data infrastructure, which could give them more control over their sensitive data, leaving them less dependent on US cloud and AI companies, Khuloud Odeh told Semafor. Agencies are also thinking about exit plans for tech agreements that could be upended. Odeh leads tech and AI strategy at the UN agency that sets international tech standards, giving her a unique vantage point into how the UN system is adopting AI.
One concern is that the Trump administration has shown a willingness to restrict access to chips and AI models as part of its foreign policy, potentially disrupting the UN agenciesâ or non-US companiesâ operations.
Countries around the world are increasingly discussing tech sovereignty â a broad term that generally means having control and choice over data and tech systems â but the UN is in a particularly precarious spot given Washingtonâs retreat from global bodies and disdain for some specific groups.
âWeâre all being asked, what is our game plan if something like this happened? What would be an exit plan?â Odeh said. That doesnât mean a âwhole radical moveâ away from all US technology, she added, but rather making backup plans, creating more choices, and sorting systems by sensitivity.
âItâs something I think about with every choice I make now,â she said, adding that itâs a âcoreâ consideration for CIOs across UN agencies, which each have their own tech budgets and vendor relationships.
At a meeting of the UN technology chiefs in Valencia in May, officials discussed âsanctions-driven service suspensionâ and âextraterritorial data accessâ as risks to the UNâs cloud arrangements, according to a report.
Know More
Much focus, especially during this weekâs UN General Assembly session, is on how the international community, including the UN, could set global rules around AI. The UN and its dozens of agencies, funds, and programs â which collectively employ some 120,000 people â arenât often thought of as major enterprise users of AI.
A UN registry counts more than 1,000 AI use cases, including projects aimed at reducing hunger and getting more schools connected to the internet. Odeh said the conversation is shifting from experimentation to determining where to put more resources.
âItâs not really about a proof of concept. Now it needs to be a proof of value,â she said.
Some of the UNâs data is especially sensitive, like refugee records and health information, raising the stakes of where it is stored and processed.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian has told the UN General Assembly that it will never "bend the knee" after almost seven months of war with the US and Israel, but is ready for a diplomatic solution to the conflict.
Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, Pezeshkian said: "He must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying."
He also insisted any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ships and ports.
"It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access," he said.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed since the start of the war in late February due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US blockade.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoy Steve Witkoff held indirect talks brokered by Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Witkoff said he hoped the discussions â the first since June â would "prove constructive and promising", adding that the mediators would continue their work.
But Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said the talks were "not anything new" and that Araghchi had maintained Iran's conditions, including the end of the US blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
