Sisak, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/harvey-weinstein-is-sentenced-to-15-years-in-prison-for-2006-sex-crime-in-new-york Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Harvey Weinstein is sentenced to 15 years in prison for 2006 sex crime in New York Nation Sep 23, 2026 11:57 AM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison in a #MeToo reckoning redux after the disgraced movie producer's original conviction was overturned and a retrial last year ended with a jury again finding him guilty of a serious sex crime. Weinstein's sentencing Wednesday for sexually assaulting one-time TV production assistant Miriam Haley followed a legal odyssey spanning more than six years after he was first convicted and sentenced in 2020. In 2024, New York's highest court erased Weinstein's conviction and ordered a new trial, ruling that Weinstein was prejudiced by testimony from other women whose allegations weren't part of the case. READ MORE: Harvey Weinstein's lawyers question accuser Miriam Haley at rape retrial Tried for a second time last year, Weinstein was again convicted of a first-degree criminal sex act for pushing Haley into a bedroom at his Manhattan apartment and sexually assaulting her in 2006. The charge carried a maximum penalty of 25 years in prison. Weinstein, first publicly accused of wrongdoing in 2017 and arrested in 2018, has already served more than six years in prison as his case has cycled again and again through the criminal justice system. He has repeatedly denied raping or sexually assaulting anyone. This is a breaking news update. AP's earlier story follows below. NEW YORK (AP) — The first time Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to prison, reporters, advocates and the curious public crammed the courtroom to witness the disgraced Hollywood honcho's #MeToo reckoning. Hours later, the world began shutting down as the COVID-19 pandemic raged. Now, after an overturned conviction and two retrials, Weinstein is set to be sentenced again on Wednesday for one of the same crimes — more than six years after his first sentencing in March 2020. Weinstein, 74, faces up to 25 years in prison for sexually assaulting a one-time TV production assistant, Miriam Haley, at his Manhattan apartment in 2006. He has already served more than six years as his case has cycled again and again through the criminal justice system. Haley gave her account of the assault at two trials and spoke again in court Wednesday just before Weinstein was to be sentenced. "Having been sexually assaulted by Harvey Weinstein has had a devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away. Making the decision to speak up will have me looking over my shoulder for years to come," Haley said. "It's a life sentence for me." "I've been further traumatized in exercising my right to hold him accountable. All of this traces back to his actions," she said, adding that she thought about ending her pursuit of justice many times. Minutes later, Weinstein apologized in court to those he may have hurt. "I do have remorse for Miriam Haley's pain, but I have to reiterate my innocence," he told the judge while seated in a wheelchair. Why Weinstein is being sentenced a second time The Oscar-winning "Pulp Fiction" and "Shakespeare in Love" producer was originally sentenced to 23 years in prison after a jury convicted him of assaulting Haley and raping an aspiring actress, Jessica Mann, in 2013. But New York's highest court erased those guilty verdicts in 2024, ruling that Weinstein was prejudiced by testimony from other women whose allegations weren't part of the case. Tried for a second time last year, Weinstein was again convicted of a first-degree criminal sex act for assaulting Haley, who has also gone by the name Mimi Haleyi. In a messy split verdict, the jury acquitted him of forcibly performing oral sex on another woman, Kaja Sokola, and could not reach a verdict on a rape charge involving Mann. After another retrial ended in a hung jury in May, Manhattan prosecutors dropped the rape charge rather than pursue a fourth trial after Mann said she could not bear to testify again. That decision cleared the way for Weinstein's sentencing. Weinstein's health issues are central to the defense's plea for leniency Manhattan prosecutors asked for 20 years in prison — which would keep him behind bars until at least his late 80s. Defense lawyer Jacob Kaplan asked that Weinstein receive a sentence of three more years on top of the six years he's already served, saying a longer sentence would make it more likely that Weinstein dies in prison. Weinstein is in failing health and has been in the hospital six times since 2025, Kaplan said, while dealing with blood cancer, congestive heart failure, and kidney issues. He has used a wheelchair now for several years. Weinstein has denied raping or sexually assaulting anyone. Once he's sentenced, he can appeal. "I will be proven innocent. That I promise you," Weinstein told The Hollywood Reporter in a jailhouse interview in March. Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate rape case in Los Angeles. A California appeals court upheld the 2022 conviction but threw out his original 16-year sentence because the judge had considered his New York convictions that were later thrown out as an aggravating factor. After shuffling between state prison, where he tested positive for COVID-19 early in the pandemic, and New York City's notorious Rikers Island complex, the ailing Weinstein is now housed at a medical unit for jail inmates at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan. His health issues in recent years have included chronic myeloid leukemia, diabetes and walking difficulties that necessitate a wheelchair to get in and out of court, his lawyers said. Maymead, a company that plans to build a controversial asphalt plant south of Winston-Salem, North Carolina, is suing a consulting firm and one of its former employees, alleging they committed fraud, civil conspiracy and deceptive trade practices in spearheading opposition to the project.
The former employee, Chris Hopkins of Tennessee, used an alias, Chris Sanderson, to infiltrate a neighborhood group in Clemmons near the proposed plant, Inside Climate News reported in early September.
Although Hopkins told neighbors he opposed the plant for environmental reasons, Maymead alleged in court documents filed in Forsyth County Superior Court that he and then-employer Land Use Strategies were working on behalf of an unnamed competitor to thwart Maymead’s project.
“There was no legitimate business purpose in defendants’ attempts to manipulate citizens and to use them as agents to manipulate the market for asphalt,” the legal complaint reads.
The company alleged that Hopkins’ subterfuge was intended to “protect his client’s market position and competitive and pricing advantage,” and “to create opposition where opposition did not exist, to disseminate information known to be false, misleading, or inaccurate about asphalt plants.”
Hopkins did not respond to text messages from Inside Climate News seeking comment for this article; an email bounced back. In a brief interview last month, he denied that Sanderson was an alias but refused to provide identification to prove his identity.
At the time, Hopkins was a partner with Land Use Strategies, which specializes in “grassroots coalition building,” strategic communications and public affairs on behalf of mining interests, data centers, landfills and other industries, according to the firm’s website.
After Inside Climate News emailed documents to Land Use Strategies showing Hopkins’ dual identities, the firm responded that he was no longer an employee. The firm also told Inside Climate News in an email that it didn’t know about the situation in Clemmons.
Land Use Strategies did not respond to an email and a phone call seeking comment about the lawsuit.
Tom Terrell, an attorney representing Maymead, told Inside Climate News that Hopkins and Land Use Strategies were not engaged in “protected political speech.”
“It was an illegal attempt to manipulate supply and demand to control market prices,” Terrell said.
Maymead is asking the court to force Hopkins and Land Use Strategies to pay attorney’s fees and more than $25,000 in financial damages. With court approval, Maymead plans to identify the competitor it alleges Hopkins was aiding once the name is disclosed in the discovery phase of the litigation.
Maymead is under contract to buy land along Gun Club Road for the plant, but it needs county approval of its air permit application before constructing the project. The application is still under technical review; if the county approves a draft permit, the public can comment on it before the final version.
Residents are petitioning Forsyth County officials to deny Maymead’s application over concerns about air pollution, truck traffic and noise. Each year the plant would emit 7 tons of health-harming particulate matter, 4.8 tons of cancer-causing formaldehyde, a half ton of cancer-causing benzene and many other air pollutants, according to the application.
The plant would lie within 2 miles of eight elementary schools, several parks, churches, day cares and hundreds of residences, including a mobile home community.
Several Clemmons residents previously told Inside Climate News that they felt “invaded” and “betrayed” by Hopkins.
Few neighbors knew about the proposal until Hopkins, posing as Sanderson, formed an anti-asphalt-plant Facebook group and an online neighborhood discussion list. He visited neighbors in their homes and emailed and spoke with local government officials. He ordered and paid $700 for flyers, stickers and signs. A resident looking at the flyer metadata found “Christopher Hopkins” listed as the document creator.
Therese Vick is a long-time community organizer with the nonprofit Blue Ridge Environmental Defense League who lives in Johnston County, southeast of Raleigh. She said she encountered company operatives who were trying to disrupt local opposition when fighting a hazardous waste incinerator in Northampton County in the 1990s and during the rapid expansion of the hog industry in eastern North Carolina.
Industry moles often leave clues that they are not who they claim to be, she said. Impersonators might suggest or advocate for violence, interfere with a group’s strategy, make big promises or try to undermine an organization’s leadership.
Other tells include “someone new who shows up during a contentious issue, whom no one knows, and who has no verifiable local connections, is evasive about where they live, has a vague background, foments division and has unreasonable curiosity about leaders,” Vick said.
Hopkins gave differing accounts of where he lived, residents told Inside Climate News, and said he had experience dealing with mining and asphalt issues, but was vague about the details.
“Grassroots community organizing isn’t new to North Carolina,” Vick said, “and neither are the pressure tactics that come with high-stakes industrial development.”
About This Story
Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert.
Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo.
It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately.
Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.
By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.
In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar.
Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added.
A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato.
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.
"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said.
"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."
French President Emmanuel Macron said shortly afterwards that his country had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks, vowing that this would not be left "without a response".
Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
There have recently been a number of suspicious fires and blasts at defence facilities in a number of European Nato members from Italy to Bulgaria to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.
Earlier this month, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig airport - an accusation denied by Moscow as "absurd".
And earlier this week, Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC that his country had already made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they would "not surrender" if attacked.
Ukraine said the drone's target "could have been the diplomatic train", while the Russian military said only that it had struck "railway infrastructure".

Paramount, looking to firm up its financial picture as it digests Warner Bros. Discovery, is looking for fresh sources of cash. Executives at the company have discussed asking Elon Musk to become part of a syndicate of equity investors into Paramount, according to people familiar with the matter.
Muskâs name is one of a number of wealthy individuals that Paramount CEO David Ellison has considered tapping for the syndicate, the people said. Musk and David Ellisonâs father, Oracle founder Larry Ellison, have long been close, and it is in part the elder Ellisonâs money â and connections â that made Paramountâs takeover of Warner Bros. possible. Larry Ellison has personally guaranteed more than $40 billion of the equity financing for Paramountâs acquisition of Warner Bros.
Larry Ellison invested $1 billion in Muskâs 2022 deal to take X, formerly Twitter, private. He also invested in Tesla in 2018, and served on the companyâs board of directors for years.
The size of a potential Musk investment could not be determined. A spokesperson for Paramount declined comment. Musk did not return a request for comment.
Rohanâs view
An investment from Musk would be a significant vote of confidence in the combined Paramount Warner Bros. from a businessman who also has a devoted retail investor following. A check from Musk or other big financial backers would also give Paramount a more diversified investor base, and reduce Larry Ellisonâs financial burden.
But having Musk in this deal would also be politically fraught: Muskâs dollars and political influence were concerning to Democrats during the 2024 election, given his control of X. The possibility of him having even partial ownership in CNN and CBS would likely raise alarm bells in Washington, even though it is unlikely Musk would have formal input over the companyâs operations.

US President Donald Trump will host Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Washington, with AI, trade and Taiwan expected to be on the agenda for the leaders of the global superpowers.
Xi will be greeted personally by Trump at Andrews Air Force Base on the eve of a White House state dinner and a military flyover.
The three-day trip marks Xi's first state visit to the US since 2015 and his third meeting with Trump in the past year.
Adding to the high-stakes state visit, a US-China trade agreement reached last year is set to expire in November.
The trade truce - reached in October 2025 as Trump and Xi met in South Korea - saw Washington suspend steep tariff increases on Chinese goods while Beijing eased back from restricting rare earth exports critical for manufacturing.
Experts said they will be watching for some sort of announcement around an extension of this agreement during the forthcoming state visit.
Xi's trip to Washington, which ends on Friday, will have plenty of pomp and pageantry, and includes lavish dinners, private tours and performances.
He will be accompanied by First Lady Peng Liyuan who is expected to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art with US First Lady Melania Trump on Thursday.
David Sacks, a fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the planned extravagant welcome by Trump as "really unprecedented".
"From meeting Xi Jinping at Andrews Air Force Base to having a flyover for Xi as well, this is not something afforded to any US ally," Sacks said, "much less an adversary like China.
"It's quite, quite stunning," he continued.
Trump is expected to address several issues as he meets Xi, particularly on tariffs and trade.
The US president has long criticised his country's trade deficit with China, which stands at more than $91bn (Â£68.2bn), according to the latest US Census Bureau data, external.
Also, Chinese rare earth exports to the US are down, external despite the agreement last October.
US and Chinese officials held trade talks on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, but failed to make meaningful progress ahead of the Xi visit, multiple sources told the BBC.
The talks focused on finding areas of agreement around non-tariff trade issues and agricultural exports, according to sources familiar with White House thinking.
US negotiators were expected to continue talks with Chinese counterparts in Washington on Wednesday after Xi's arrival.
Another likely talking point between Trump and Xi is artificial intelligence, a topic that David Firestein from the Bush China Foundation said has "climbed rapidly toward the top of the agenda" ahead of this visit.
China and the US are competing in what has been described as an AI arms race. But after a series of recent high-profile security incidents involving the emergent technology, there has been growing pressure on the Trump administration to regulate AI and slow its development.
Senator Bernie Sanders wrote on X this week: "For the sake of all humanity, Trump and Xi must negotiate a treaty NOW to pause AI and ban superintelligence before it's too late."
Trump's former White House adviser Steve Bannon and some Republicans in Congress have also warned about dangers posed by AI.
The president, who views the technology as vital to the US economy and a battleground in a global struggle for power, has been reluctant.
He views defeating China in the AI race as a primary objective. "Whoever wins AI, wins," Trump has said.
Firestein told the BBC he expects Trump and Xi to discuss ways for AI collaboration.
On Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, and said the two had "very successful" talks on trade and AI.
Several AI and tech industry titans will attend a White House state dinner on Thursday, according to US officials.
Open AI's CEO Sam Altman, Jensen Huang, whose company Nvidia makes chips that power AI, and X boss Elon Musk are some of the dinner attendees.
Experts who spoke to the BBC said any major breakthroughs on AI or other issues are unlikely to occur during the Trump-Xi meetings this week.
Then there is Taiwan, which remains a diplomatic thorn.
The US Congress has approved a multibillion-dollar arms sale to Taiwan that awaits Trump's signature. He has held off for now, viewing the move as a bargaining chip with China.
Beijing has long vowed to "reunify" with self-governing Taiwan and has not ruled out the use of force.
Firestein said he expects Xi will be looking for Trump to either commit to extending the delay of the arms sale or somehow avoiding the sale altogether.
Xi - like Trump - is also facing economic headwinds at home, and is expected to use this visit to discuss deepening US-China trade.
However, that presents a potential political problem for Trump. Some members of his cabinet and his supporters view China with deep suspicion.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued a letter, external to Ford Motor Company in September, urging the company to cut ties with China due to national security concerns and protection of American jobs.
Regardless of the clear hurdles that remain before any new US-China deals are inked, it is clear that Trump views personal contact with Xi as vital to the process.
"Trump has made a decision that no matter what, we need to not have a confrontational relationship with China," Stephen Orlins, president at the National Committee on US-China Relations, said.
"He believes that the more he and President Xi meet, the less confrontational that relationship will be," Orlins continued, "and he is right."
With additional reporting by Daniel Bush, Washington correspondent

c3264e8dabfc.text: Chicago could halt new data center development within city limits for a year. Why it matters: Data centers' growing demand for electricity and water could affect residents' utility bills and the environment, and city leaders want more time to study those impacts. The latest: Mayor Brandon Johnson, along with a group of alders, is pushing for a 12-month moratorium while the city develops a "comprehensive regulatory framework" for data centers. There are 39 active data centers in Chicago, according to the city. Details: The proposal would give Johnson's Data Centers Task Force time to study the industry's impacts on clean air, clean water and energy use. What they're saying: "Chicago is open for business, but we are not for sale," Johnson said in a statement. "We welcome innovation, investment, and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents." Context: The announcement comes as other alders, including Ald. Bill Conway (34th), push their own ordinance to regulate data centers. "The Mayor's proposal risks months if not years of debate and litigation, all while data centers keep building, polluting, and spiking utility bills with zero community input," Conway said in a statement. Conway's ordinance would immediately subject data centers to additional zoning requirements and community and environmental reviews. Zoom out: Chicago wouldn't be alone. At least a half-dozen major U.S. cities, including Seattle, Charlotte, Baltimore, Cincinnati, Cleveland and Oklahoma City, have temporarily halted or restricted new data center development while considering new regulations. At the state level, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has paused new tax incentives for data centers, but has said he doesn't have the authority to impose a statewide moratorium on construction. Illinois cities like Bloomington, Carbondale, Effingham, West Chicago and Mattoon have already paused new data center development or expansion. The other side: "As the City of Chicago faces significant and continuing fiscal and budgetary challenges, it's important to recognize that data centers are net revenue generators that provide billions of dollars in economic investment," Data Center Coalition's Brad Tietz said in a statement. "Unfortunately, the Mayor's proposed moratorium sends another signal that Chicago is closed for business." Friction point: Communities across the country are pushing back against proposed data centers over concerns about electricity demand , water use, pollution and other impacts. President Trump has criticized efforts to restrict them, writing on social media: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign." What's next: Both proposals will now make their way through the City Council, setting up a debate over how the city should regulate new data center development.

September's full Moon will be visible in UK skies this weekend, just days after the autumn equinox.
Known as the Harvest Moon, it will reach its fullest point at 17:49 BST on Saturday 26 September.
At that time it will still be below the horizon for much of the UK, but it will rise shortly afterwards and appear almost completely full throughout Saturday evening.
It gets its name from being the full Moon closest to the autumn equinox, which this year took place on Wednesday.
Why is it called the Harvest Moon?
September's full Moon is traditionally associated with the harvest, because historically, the additional moonlight after sunset was useful to farmers gathering crops.
The Royal Observatory Greenwich also lists the Corn Moon as another common name, reflecting the crops traditionally harvested around this time of year.
However, it does not always fall in September and if October's full Moon is closer to the autumn equinox, it takes the title instead.
Why can the Harvest Moon look red?
If you catch the Moon as it rises it may appear yellow, orange or even reddish.
This is not a special feature of the Harvest Moon, but simply that when it lies low in the sky and is close to the horizon, its light has to travel through more of the Earth's atmosphere before reaching our eyes.
More of the shorter blue wavelengths of light are scattered, allowing the yellows, oranges and reds to become more prominent.
Will the weather be clear enough to see it?
The current forecast suggests Saturday could bring some drier and brighter weather, particularly across parts of England. However, there is some cloud further west and rain for parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland by the evening.
The best chance of clearer skies currently looks to be across some southern and eastern parts of the UK, while conditions are expected to be more changeable elsewhere.
The exact times of the moonrise will vary across the UK but will be shortly after it reaches its fullest point.
Keep up to date with the weather where you are online or on the BBC Weather app.

373965b7010b.text: In his first-ever meeting with Venezuela's new leader, President Trump emphasized the need to keep oil flowing, relations warm and that country's elections on the horizon, White House sources tell Axios. Why it matters: Trump did not insist on a future election date in his meeting with Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodriguez , but he emphasized their importance as a crucial final step in Venezuela's evolution into a full-fledged democracy, the sources said. "You have to have elections at the end of the day," Trump said to Rodriguez at one point, one of the sources briefed on the meeting said. Zoom in: Trump held the roughly 15-minute meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York to thank Rodriguez for their good working relationship after the U.S. ousted her one-time socialist ally, Nicolas Maduro, on Jan. 3. Since then, the Trump administration has struck oil and gold-mining deals with Venezuela, which had been a U.S. adversary for more than a quarter-century. Venezuela has one of the world's largest sovereign debt problems of $300 billion — larger than its gross domestic product — which needs to be restructured before the country holds elections, U.S. officials say. "The country can't succeed until that is solved," a White House official said. What they're saying: "We held a historic meeting with the president of the United States, Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security," Rodriguez posted Tuesday night on X. The post included a photo of Rodriguez holding up two fingers in a "V" (for Venezuela) and Trump giving his characteristic thumbs-up. Friction point: The photo outraged the small but vocal Venezuelan diaspora community in the U.S., where critics want to hear more about Venezuela elections and less about deals. On the same day Trump and Rodriguez met, allies of Venezuela opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Marina Corina Machado went public to complain that she has been blocked from re-entering the country. In the Miami area, home to both Secretary of State Marco Rubio and a sizable population of Venezuelan exiles and expats, Rubio's 2024 U.S. Senate opponent, former Democratic Rep. Debbie Mucarsel Powell, posted the image on X and urged people to register to vote. "Tell every single member of the South Florida delegation that you are done with the lies and the blatant corruption. No Mas!" she wrote . Between the lines: The U.S. wants Venezuela's elections to be called by Venezuelans via the country's new National Reconciliation Council, which represents various political parties in the country. It's a three-step plan: Change the composition of the Venezuelan Supreme Court to make it more representative of the country. The opposition is going to get to nominate justices, an official said. Reform the National Electoral Commission to ensure there's not a repeat of 2024, when it manipulated the vote count and stole the election from Edmundo González on Maduro's behalf. Announce an election date. Trump, however, pointedly did not say when he wants that to be. Inside the room : Trump and Rodriguez were joined by two Venezuelan officials as well as Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. Trump did most of the talking and also regaled Rodriguez with a description of the precision U.S. military operation that ousted Maduro. "It was warm. It was friendly. But it was also direct," one of the sources said about Trump's discussion of the importance of future elections. "She acknowledged it. She said she wants elections too," the source said. Zoom out: The multiple challenges Venezuela is facing from the legacy of socialist mismanagement to the earthquakes that damaged the country this summer make calling an election date even more complicated, U.S. officials say. "We don't want to have an election, have a democratically elected government take over and inherit an economic catastrophe within six months," said one. "A democratic government is going to be facing massive street protests over inflation, the economy. It could threaten the entire thing." The intrigue : By process of elimination, insiders say a Venezuelan election in the summer or fall of 2028 makes more sense because it would give the country more time to repair its finances and electoral system. Trump also would like to leave office with the legacy of removing a dictator, fixing a country and fostering democracy — but he might want to wait until the final months in office so the U.S. could still exert outsized influence on Rodriguez's government. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) has called for Venezuela to hold elections on July 24, 2027, but Trump administration officials and allies say that might be too early. "If can be in '27, that would be great. We would like that," an official said, cautioning that Venezuelans need to lead and need to fix their debt problem first. "Whether the date for those conditions to be met are 2027 versus 2028 is still up in the air," the official said. "It certainly can't go on indefinitely."

Bernie Sanders unveils bill to ban artificial superintelligence and create Department of AI Politics Sep 23, 2026 2:10 PM EDT Washington (AP) — Two leading progressive lawmakers, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar, are unveiling legislation Wednesday that would ban artificial superintelligence and create a federal agency to oversee advanced AI as some of the industry's own leaders urge Congress to impose guardrails on the advancing technology. The bill, provided first to The Associated Press, would also pause advanced AI development until guidelines are implemented while creating the Department of Artificial Intelligence. Multiple employees at leading AI companies are endorsing the bill. WATCH: Trump dismisses concerns about AI risks at UN, says he won't rein it in "It doesn't take a genius to say, 'slow it down,'" Sanders, I-Vt., said in an interview with AP. "Do we really want to develop a super intelligence that when it becomes smarter than human beings could act independently of human control? I don't think we do." Please check your inbox to confirm. Congress has so far done little to rein in the AI industry even as some of its most prominent leaders warn about potentially catastrophic risks. President Donald Trump has resisted recent calls for greater government oversight, putting him at odds with tech leaders including Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and xAI's Elon Musk. The bill aims to dramatically slow down AI development The legislation would permanently prohibit artificial superintelligence, which it defines as a system that exceeds human cognitive ability or has sufficient capabilities to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity. READ MORE: Voters don't like data centers. They really don't like them close to home It would temporarily pause development of the most advanced AI systems until new federal safety rules are established by a new Department of Artificial Intelligence. Advanced AI systems would then need federal approval before they could be deployed. Violations could carry significant penalties, including up to 20 years in prison in some cases. A number of current employees at AI companies and experts signed on in support of the bill, according to a statement shared with AP. Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe, a researcher in OpenAI's Safety Systems, said in a statement supporting the bill that "superintelligence could either go extremely right or extremely wrong" and that "we shouldn't be playing such games." WATCH: Steve Bannon says 'we have to rise' above partisanship to address AI 'hinge in history' Swante Scholz, a software engineer at Google DeepMind who said he was not speaking on behalf of his employer, said on the current path of development, the "most likely outcome is an existential catastrophe for humanity." "A ban on superintelligence development would be a positive change for the foreseeable future," Scholz said in a statement. The bill faces long odds but draws a line in a growing fight The bill from Sanders and Casar faces long odds in the Republican-controlled Congress, where lawmakers have struggled to coalesce around even less sweeping AI regulations. But it offers a window into how the progressive wing of the Democratic Party is approaching AI regulation ahead of November's midterms and a 2028 presidential campaign in which the technology is expected to be an increasingly prominent issue. Casar, a Democrat from Texas, is the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Potential 2028 presidential candidates have rushed in recent weeks to release proposals showing they're taking the issue seriously. Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore announced a plan to regulate AI on Tuesday, while California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order to accelerate implementation of a California law that calls for independent oversight of AI companies last week. Sanders, a two-time presidential candidate who is now 85, has especially focused on the issue in recent months. In June, he introduced legislation to create a sovereign wealth fund financed through a one-time tax on the stock of the largest AI companies. Last week, he hosted colleagues for a briefing with experts and also attended a conference focused on the issue alongside Republicans, including former White House adviser Steve Bannon. The debate over AI regulations has scrambled political alliances both in Washington and for voters across the country. Americans have grown more concerned about the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence over the last year, according to a recent poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago. The survey data say about half, 53%, of Americans are "extremely" or "very" concerned about artificial intelligence's environmental impacts. That is up from 41% last year. Democrats are driving much of the increase in environmental concern, but the poll also reveals broader worries about the local impact of data centers, which power AI and cloud computing. Trump has shown little interest in curbing AI risks While some industry leaders have called for new safeguards, Trump has pushed in the opposite direction. On Tuesday, Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that artificial intelligence will be renamed "super intelligence." (AP) — Police in Mississippi have arrested a second man in the death of a Black woman found hanging from a tree and have issued an arrest warrant for a third suspect. Jackson police said late Tuesday that they arrested 25-year-old Earnest Lloyd Jr. in the death of 29-year-old Tasia Fortune, whose body was found hanging behind an abandoned home in the city on Aug. 3. READ MORE: Man pleads not guilty in the hanging death of Tasia Fortune in Mississippi Like Fortune and the first man arrested, 51-year-old Jarques Ratliff, Lloyd is Black. He appeared at a brief hearing Wednesday in Jackson. Fortune's mother Christy Spivey, who attended the hearing, said afterward that she was ecstatic to see arrests made in her daughter's death. She said that neither she nor several of her daughter's friends knew Lloyd, and she cautioned that everyone is innocent until proven guilty. "My family is not the only family that this is affecting," Spivey said of the defendants' families. "I feel for them as well. The only difference is that mine can never come back. At least they can have telephone visits." "I'll never truly have peace," she said Ratliff was arrested in September on murder charges. He pleaded not guilty and remains jailed without bond. Police said in a statement that they issued an arrest warrant for a third suspect, but gave no details about that person's identity or alleged link to Fortune's death. They also said they expect to issue additional warrants. READ MORE: What we know about the death of Tasia Fortune in Mississippi After Ratliff's arrest, Jackson's police chief, RaShall Brackney, said Ratliff had an "association" with Fortune, but she didn't elaborate. Although police haven't suggested a possible motive for the killing or said whether they think race played a role, the case has attracted widespread attention because the manner of death recalled lynchings in the Southern state. A Kentucky native, Fortune had four children and had been living in Jackson for about a decade, relatives said. Spivey previously said her daughter struggled with homelessness in recent years, and that she wasn't sure where her daughter was living at the time of her death. She said that before her death, her daughter had talked about starting a cleaning business and was trying to get her life in order. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The Scoop
As the midterm battleground map expands deep into red territory and Republicans fret about the deteriorating national mood, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., is reassuring GOP senators that they can still outperform the environment and hold onto the Senate.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee chairman gathered Senate Republicans on Wednesday for a final meeting before they scatter across the country to fight for their political lives. He likened their potential fortunes to those of Democrats in 2022, when then-President Joe Biden was deeply unpopular but Democrats ended up gaining a Senate seat even as they lost the House, according to a person in the room.
âWeâre in the fight for our lives with a record number of toss-up races,â Scott told his colleagues.
Scott also argued that Republicansâ position on the general ballot is improving and that GOP voter enthusiasm for the election has increased 20% in the past two months, citing new polling from Peak Insights, the person said.
He also told Republicans up for reelection in deep red states to run like they are behind, explaining that the NRSCâs spending on Senate races will focus on the surplus of toss-up races across the country. He singled out contests over Democratic-held seats in New Hampshire and Michigan and GOP-held seats in Maine, Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and Alaska.
At this pivotal moment ahead of the midterms, Senate Republicans are increasingly breaking with an unpopular President Donald Trump with the fight for the Senate majority hanging in the balance in such unlikely places as Texas and Iowa. Republicans can afford to lose up to three Senate seats and keep control of the chamber, but doing so will require the party to shore up its position in a number of battleground states. Republicans have some offensive opportunities, but they have to balance those with all the states theyâre defending.
Scott said the partyâs polling showed the gap narrowing in North Carolina while Minnesota is also tight. One Republican super PAC cut some of its ad reservations in North Carolina; the party is debating whether to scale back investments in Georgia, where Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is favored to win re-election.
NRSC staff also told senators that the party is capitalizing on the Supreme Court rulings that loosened restrictions on coordinated spending between candidates and campaign committees and allows those coordinated ad buys at discounted candidate rates. Republican committees ramped up their coordinated spending in August and further accelerated that practice in September, essentially matching well-funded Democratic candidates.
Democratic candidates are set to outspend Republicans $32.8 million to $2.3 million on TV September in six key states, but Republicans are set to augment that with $29.3 million in coordinated spending, according to the data presented to the GOP. Thatâs important because GOP super PACs that are pouring money into the Senate battlegrounds receive worse ad rates. Democratic candidates have enjoyed a persistent fundraising advantage this cycle.

0aee986d0918.text: The left's push to rein in AI is taking shape on two fronts: slowing advanced development at home, and weakening China's progress abroad. Why it matters: The nation is locked in a moment of mass anxiety about runaway AI, but the range of views on how to regulate it are as varied as the what-ifs about social, economic and security impacts. There's agreement among the left something has to be done, but a series of Wednesday events demonstrated there are multiple priorities — but not a clear leading voice — on AI. Driving the news: Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders (Vt.) and fellow progressive Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) introduced legislation Wednesday to ban superintelligence and pause advanced development until a new, Cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence sets guardrails. "I understand that I may be called an alarmist for introducing this bill," Sanders said in a Wednesday call with reporters, "but I'd rather be called an alarmist than a father and grandfather who is asleep at the wheel." Casar emphasized that "we cannot wait for an international agreement to pause dangerous development in the United States. China trains their models off of American models, so stopping dangerous AI development in America will slow down dangerous advancements in China." Zoom out: Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) took up another regulatory approach Wednesday, focused on restricting foreign AI capabilities. " President Trump must draw a hard line. Do not weaken America's export controls. Do not give China greater access to the advanced chips and chip-making equipment it needs to close the gap," Schumer said in a plea to move forward on related bipartisan legislation . Schumer argued that calls to pause AI research and the focus on winning the AI race "are not at all contradictory." Casar said the goal of his and Sanders' legislation is to "stop the race towards disaster." Sanders has been forceful in calls for immediate congressional action, saying Wednesday that "we cannot simply sit by idly and wait for advanced AI to cause the next 9/11 or Chernobyl." Between the lines: Even within the progressive camp, there's not complete cohesion on the specifics of confronting the AI buildout, Axios' Maria Curi writes . Warren has backed a pause on advanced artificial intelligence, but she's stopped short of endorsing a ban on superintelligence, like Sanders. Possible 2028 contenders diverge as well, with several stopping short of echoing Sanders' call to pause development. Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel previously told Axios that "a pause is fine — but then what?" Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), another member of the party's progressive wing who has called to ban self-improving AI, is also set to convene a virtual hearing Wednesday calling for a U.S.-China agreement to pace AI development — yet another potential regulatory approach. State of play: The three proposals come as Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping, with AI a likely focus of the talks as the rival nations discuss ways to manage shared risks, per Axios' Courtenay Brown. Trump has insisted the U.S. must keep an edge over China, warning that "whoever wins" the AI race "wins." The bottom line: Which idea (or ideas) Democrats in Congress champion could become a key issue for the November midterms . Go deeper: AI boom can withstand a development slowdown

7739d3826683.text: By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press By — Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administrations-ban-of-three-prominent-news-outlets-from-white-house-is-in-court Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration's ban of three prominent news outlets from White House is in court Politics Sep 23, 2026 4:19 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The extraordinary showdown between President Donald Trump and media outlets whose coverage he dislikes moved Wednesday to a courtroom in the nation's capital, where a judge is hearing arguments on whether the president's move banning three news organizations from White House grounds violates the Constitution. The administration has doubled down on its contention that it has the right to decide who can set foot in the White House. "Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right," it said in a court filing late Tuesday. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. It also argued that the reporting of the three outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — poses a threat to national security. In his early comments about the case, Trump focused not on national security but on negative coverage by the outlets and allegations of "fake news." The proceedings are historic, said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University. READ MORE: CNN, MS NOW, Politico sue over Trump denying White House access "No president has taken this explicit of a step" to ban entire news outlets because he doesn't like their reporting, she said. "There have been various presidents throughout history who have grumbled about the press or threatened to take more major steps, but really there was nothing at this level before Trump." The case is being heard by U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, whom Trump appointed in 2017 and who ordered a CNN journalist's access restored in a similar case in 2018. The Trump administration outlined 'reporting incidents' of each news outlet In the filing, administration lawyers argued that the ban does not violate the First Amendment, which guarantees the right to a free press. It contended that the outlets, in their reporting, violated "standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues and publishing sensitive or classified information." The administration went on to detail letters that were sent to each outlet that identified "a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents, including those that have threatened national security and spread falsehoods." WATCH: Trump says he's banning 3 outlets from White House in his latest attack on press freedom The "reporting incidents" cited in the filing included: CNN reporting on "'top-secret' construction details related to the East Wing bunker"; MS NOW reporting "on an alleged leak investigation"; and Politico publishing "a document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements." Further examples were given in individual letters. Politico's letter detailed six incidents of reporting, including in June citing a "senior administration official … granted anonymity" predicting whether a preliminary deal would end the conflict with Iran. That item appeared to reference a background briefing set up by the White House, where an official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House itself. Several other outlets also reported the official's remarks. The news outlets argue that the ban blatantly violates the First Amendment Trump began to emphasize the national security argument Tuesday, when he said negative coverage was dangerous for the country. "I think we have a right to clean out fake news," he told reporters at the United Nations, defending the ban, which was suddenly announced Friday. The next day, journalists for the three outlets arrived at work to find their entry badges disabled. WATCH: Trump's attacks on free press echo rhetoric used by autocrats, Jodie Ginsberg says On Monday, the outlets filed their joint lawsuit, alleging they were singled out because of the content of their coverage — in other words, viewpoint discrimination. They called this a "blatant violation" of the First Amendment and asked the court to immediately restore their access. The ban prompted other media outlets to take action in solidarity. The five-network U.S. network press pool — a rotating cast of news outlets that covers the president, and to which CNN belongs — decided to suspend coverage of Trump events until further notice. The Associated Press joined a group of organizations that refrained from publishing photos of the president Monday. On Wednesday, the network pool was again missing from a daily White House press schedule. WATCH: Press pool declines to cover Trump in protest of his ban on news outlets The ban and subsequent lawsuit are part of a long-running conflict between the president — especially in his second term — and media outlets he finds unfavorable. Trump has responded in the courtroom, or with regulatory action. He's also lashed out at individual reporters in personal terms. Trump filing gives anecdotes on past presidents The administration's filing to the court also relies on historical anecdotes to argue that a president can decide which news outlets to grant favorable treatment. It says, citing books on the subject, that in the early 20th century, President Theodore Roosevelt "began a practice of regularly inviting reporters into the Ova

ed67b1bf0030.text: By — Ali Swenson, Associated Press Ali Swenson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-focus-on-noncitizen-voting-has-led-to-160-arrests-that-shows-its-rare-experts-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say Politics Sep 23, 2026 3:56 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The Trump administration's whole-of-government effort to find and prosecute noncitizens illegally on state voter rolls has resulted in about 1,600 voter fraud cases that have led to 160 arrests, Homeland Security Investigations senior official Matthew Millhollin said in a press briefing Tuesday. The numbers unveiled just six weeks before Election Day provide a rare status update on an initiative that has redirected federal resources and hundreds of employees to search for foul play in elections at the direction of President Donald Trump. WATCH: How the Trump administration is trying to reshape how elections are run They fall far short of the hundreds of thousands of noncitizen voters that Trump and the Department of Homeland Security have previously suggested were on the rolls. They also represent a tiny fraction of the country's more than 211 million active registered voters, underscoring what former election officials and election law experts say is a proven fact: Voter fraud, including voting by noncitizens, is rare. Please check your inbox to confirm. "They have tried to manufacture evidence of widespread noncitizen voting, and every time they do, their numbers are incredibly small, even when they're overstated," said David Becker, a former U.S. Justice Department attorney who leads the nonprofit Center for Election Innovation and Research. "They confirm what we've known for years, which is that states have been doing an extraordinarily good job of keeping noncitizens off their voter lists." Millhollin shared the arrest data at a joint press briefing with the Justice Department and the U.S. Postal Service about DOJ charges against a Utah postal worker for throwing out more than 300 mail ballots during the state's June primary. In the same briefing, Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said the DOJ had charged 70 people since the start of the administration with "unlawful voting and registration offenses." WATCH: DOJ threatens to arrest state election officials if noncitizens vote The DOJ's figure represents defendants formally charged with unlawful voting and registration offenses, Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels said in an email. HSI's 160 arrests, she said, "originate from voter fraud investigative leads, but many result in charges for related offenses, such as false claims to citizenship or false statements, rather than the voting statute itself." The federal actions represent the period between January 2025 and September 2026, according to the Justice Department. Ahead of November's midterms, which will determine control of Congress for the final two years of his term, Trump has taken extensive measures to try to crack down on noncitizen voting. It's something he claims is rampant and marring elections across the nation, but research shows it is incredibly rare. READ MORE: How Trump's mail voting claims are affecting voters He signed two election-related executive orders designed in part to address the issue, both of which are tied up in legal challenges. He also has pressured states to use a controversial federal voter database that has been blocked by a federal judge for violating Americans' privacy, and tried repeatedly to get lawmakers to pass a stagnant documentary proof of citizenship bill. In a last-ditch effort to hunt for noncitizen voters without detailed data from all states, DHS in August ordered a group of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services staff to pivot to a full-time manual investigation of state voter rolls, according to a federal whistle blower's report. The whistleblower said the effort is directing federal employees to misrepresent themselves on state voter lookup tools in a way that could violate state laws. The person also warned the initiative leans on unreliable data that could wrongly implicate U.S. citizens in federal documentation. WATCH: Whistleblower warns USPS rushing new system that could jeopardize mail-in ballots State election officials in Texas investigated registered voters who were flagged as noncitizens on their voter rolls by Trump's federal voter database before a judge blocked its use. Of the 2,724 registered voters, it referred 117 cases to the Texas attorney general's office for investigation. In mid-September, seven people in the state were charged with illegally voting in federal elections or falsely claiming citizenship. Texas has about 18 million registered voters. Becker said examples like that are characteristic of what often happens when potential instances of noncitizen voting are investigated: The real numbers are consistently small. "No system is perfect," he said, adding that he was not aware of a single election whose outcome was altered by noncitizens voting. McCotter, in Tuesday's briefing, argued that even a small number of fraud cases can be significant. "The right of American citizens to have their votes properly counted is vital to determining the rightful winner of an election," McCotter said. "But the actions of even one malicious actor on the ground can fatally undercut that security." Kathy Boockvar, the Democratic former secretary of state of Pennsylvania who now runs a nonpartisan election security firm, said there are real consequences for election officials when Trump and others make hyperbolic claims of fraudulent voting. a237f83a1c7c.text: Senate Majority Leader John Thune says President Trump is "not really dug in" against guardrails for AI , despite Trump's public campaign against restricting the technology. Why it matters: Thune told Axios he spoke privately with Trump as the AI issue was getting "pretty hot" a few weeks ago and believes some of Trump's strong pushback is against public "paranoia and noise around the subject." Thune reads Trump's position as a preference for companies coming up with ways to secure their systems, rather than Congress or the administration. That approach relies more on experts to provide guidance. Trump has called recent fears around AI safety a "hoax." "I do think that the threats are real," Thune told Axios in an interview on Wednesday at his Capitol office. Zoom out : Thune has Trump's skepticism in one ear and tech leader alarm in the other. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called Thune to discuss AI safety before sounding his latest public alarm on the risks of AI, Thune told Axios. The two also talked about Thune's AI bill. What to watch: "I think you have to have at least some sort of a plan and some guardrails around it, which is what I think our bill does," Thune said, referencing the bill he has introduced with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) in past years. "But I do also think that there are people who are... doing a lot of fear mongering," Thune added. Thune's bill, which has not yet been reintroduced this Congress, puts the onus on tech companies to mitigate AI risks. It also requires AI companies to report on any serious risks with frontier models and to come up with plans to address the concerns. Thune said Klobuchar is trying to get more Democratic co-sponsors on board — including Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) — before re-introducing the bill. The details: Democrats have two main sticking points, according to Thune: Pre-deployment testing is something companies can opt into in the bill language. Democrats want it mandated. Cantwell is asking for AI rulemaking authority at the Department of Commerce. Thune worries rulemaking authority could give the executive too much power. The bottom line: Thune is able to pull on experience working on AI policy. If he had not become leader, he would have again chaired the Commerce committee, which has jurisdiction over much of the issue.

2798d13c3aaa.text: Senate races in Georgia , Kansas and South Carolina were reclassified with a nudge toward Democrats in the latest analysis from the closely watched Cook Political Report. The big picture: To win the Senate, Democrats must net four seats in November. Tighter races in Republican strongholds like Kansas and South Carolina could force the GOP to devote resources beyond the core battlegrounds. The latest: In the latest Cook ratings, Kansas moved from "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican." South Carolina shifted from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican." Georgia and the seat held by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) changed from "Lean Democrat" to "Likely Democrat." By the numbers: There are six Republican-held Senate seats rated by Cook as a "Toss Up" or better for Democrats. The Georgia shift makes a Republican pickup there less likely, while the Kansas move expands the map of competitive seats for Democrats. Zoom out: The midterms environment is improving for Democrats amid voter discontent about gas prices, the cost of living and the broader handling of the Iran war. Flashback: Last month, Cook shifted Senate and gubernatorial races in Texas and Iowa in Democrats' favor.

US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45 billion (Â£1.85 billion) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs.
But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280 million handed over so far. The board estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4bn over the next decade.
Jared Kushner, Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded the project faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason".
"The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders.
He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said the group had made "real progress" over the past year.
"All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added.
In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinians officials.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate press conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that".
In August, a senior official on the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the Palestinian armed group Hamas.
In August, Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.
At least 1,381 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".
The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year.
Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats.
In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which will see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza.
But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.
The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide.

1f40424747d5.text: A judge on Wednesday appeared skeptical of Trump administration arguments justifying the White House barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico, but he did not immediately grant the news outlets' request for a temporary restraining order. Why it matters: In declining to rule right now, the White House has no legal mandate to remove the ban. That means the broader press boycott will likely drag on, leaving the American public without key visual coverage of the White House. Outlets that weren't banned stood in solidarity with their peers, vowing to suspend video and photo distribution until their peers' access was restored. Zoom in In a statement, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said the president's sudden move to strip reporter credentials appeared to violate legal precedents that require journalists to be given notice, per Politico . He said he planned to issue a ruling on the plaintiff's request for injunctive relief soon. Catch up quick: The banned outlets sought a temporary restraining order to restore access while the case is litigated through a lawsuit filed on Monday. A ruling in their favor would mark a huge win and indicate the judge believes their case would likely hold up in court. In their complaint , the outlets argued the White House violated their First Amendment rights, by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoints, and their Fifth Amendment rights for banning them without due process. The other side: In a court filing Tuesday, the Justice Department argued press access is a privilege, not a Constitutional right, and that it revoked the plaintiffs' press passes for national security reasons. Zoom out: The news industry has broadly supported the banned outlets. The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, along with 50 news outlets — including Axios — filed a court brief in support of the plaintiffs. Flashback: Kelly oversaw a CNN lawsuit against the White House over blocked access in 2018. In that case, he granted CNN a temporary restraining order that required the White House restore then-correspondent Jim Acosta's press badge, ruling that pulling his credentials without notice or an appeal process violated his Fifth Amendment rights. While the outcome of that case isn't binding, it does hold weight in informing Kelly's decision-making. CNN, MS NOW and Politico referenced that case in their lawsuit. Zoom out: Press freedom lawyers argue the plaintiffs have a strong First Amendment case, given a binding legal precedent set by a higher court. In 1977, a federal appeals court ruled that the White House could not revoke a journalist's press credentials based on their coverage or viewpoint. In that case, journalist Robert Sherrill sued the White House for being denied a press pass with no explanation. That court ruled that once the White House opens up a space as a public forum and lets journalists in, it cannot selectively remove access for select journalists based on their viewpoint or coverage under the First Amendment. What's next: Trump had previously indicated that he intended to appeal the injunction ruling, if not in his favor. Note: The author of this article is a paid contributor for CNN.

The FBI says it is investigating a reported breach of its system after a cybercrime group claimed to have stolen sensitive information on thousands of bureau personnel.
The hackers, Shiny Hunters, say they now hold private data on all the bureau staff - around 38,000 people - including anyone who applied to join the investigation agency.
The group says it has every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address, phone numbers and spouse information.
In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was aware of the claim and the agency was "actively and aggressively investigating the matter".
The criminals claim to have breached the FBI's servers on Monday night and began contacting reporters on Tuesday sharing samples and screenshots of the stolen data.
The BBC has seen a small portion of the data which appears to be genuine.
According to Reuters, some of the data contains details about officials' âjob assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence and drug cartels.
ShinyHunters is an international collective of hackers, believed to have originally started in France. It has been behind a number of high-profile breaches including on Rockstar Games in April and a highly disruptive hack on education platform Canvas in May.
The group claims to have found a vulnerability in the Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI to breach multiple systems including FBIJOBS, FBI BEAST, which does background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which holds agent's medical records and FBI BICS, which holds investigation information.
In its message on darkness web, the group said it did not hack the FBI system for money.
Instead, the cybercriminals are asking the agency to retract an advisory that it issued about the gang, saying it was "offended" by its characterisation.
That FBI's public service announcement, external described ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims".
"They target major companies across tech, finance, and retail, often stealing millions of customer records at once," the advisory said.
ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations or they would publish the full databases.
The FBI did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the BBC.
In its statement on X, the agency said it was trying to determine whether or not the hackers had breached its systems or a third party.
"We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk," the post said.

- Published
A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vulnerability.
Elisabeth Belien told the four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, Canada she had been at her lowest ebb when he sold her toxic chemicals when she was just 23.
Belien, who until Wednesday had not been known as one of his customers, said she had physically recovered after being successfully given an antidote by medics.
But as she faced him as he sat in the glass-panelled dock, she revealed she had suffered "survivor's guilt" after learning from police others had died.
Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in suicide forums online. But there are almost 80 deaths in the UK that have also been linked to him.
As part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.
But impact statements from their families are being read during the sentencing hearing this week.
Belien told the court: "I had struggled with my mental health for a long time before this. Kenneth Law made it a lot easier to act on that despair.
"I continue to struggle with intrusive thoughts and flashbacks of that day.
"I made a full recovery. However, emotionally and psychologically, the effects are far more long lasting.
"I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived It has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened.
"I felt like the purchasing from Kenneth Law, I enabled him to continue his business, supplying his products, to other people who might have been vulnerable, like I was. I felt guilty for surviving."
Belien, who said she took the poison in January 2023, said being in court reminded her "how easily" it could have been her own parents there talking about her.
"I'm learning that things can get better," she said.
"I'm learning to be excited to see what the future holds for me. But the gratitude I'm feeling for being alive today doesn't take away from the trauma of the experience."
Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.
He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US.
David Parfett, whose son Tom died in October 2021, said in a victim impact statement: "Since Tom died, I've struggled with my mental health.
"Initially, in the months after he died, I didn't properly mourn him, because my focus was on understanding, and then exposing the harm caused by the internet platforms that allowed Law to trade suicide to kids.
"I'm still, after five years, unable to fully process Tom's death. I'm a very different person to who I was before Tom took his own life, having previously been gregarious, outgoing. I find it difficult to enjoy life."
A statement was also read from the parents of Henry Tucker, a 14-year-old British boy who died in October 2021.
Kate and Henry Tucker said Henry had been diagnosed with autism but actually had a neurological condition that could have been treated with antibiotics.
"The realisation that his suffering and his death could have been prevented is a weight that is impossible to bear," they said.
"The death of a children under these circumstance is a heavy burden to carry for the rest of our lives.
"We will carry it however with Henry's blessings until we meet again. We love you Henry."
Norson Harris, the father of British victim Ashleigh Harris, read a statement in person on the agony of losing his daughter.
He said: "The circumstances of Ashleigh's death have been incredibly tough to bear.
"We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashleigh's death.
"Rather than offer the help needed that individual Kenneth Law sold her a chemical that Ashleigh took to end her life.
"I still hope over time Mr Law will recognise the answer to Ashleigh and the myriad of others who reached out to him should have been that they were loved and there was help available to them."
Earlier Stephen Mitchell Sr, the father of Canadian Stephen Mitchell Jr, told of the aftermath of his death on March 25 2023.
"He was ill, he needed help, and I tried my best to bring him that help," he said.
"Mr Law robbed my son of that chance to be well."
Mr Mitchel Sr, addressing Law in court, said: "I'm willing to accept that during Mr Law's time in incarceration, he might have had brief moments of regret, or even despair and helplessness.
"Perhaps he may have even thought during those moments: my life is meaningless, what is the point of living.
"That was the same thoughts that my son Stephen had before he took the chemicals that Mr Law sold him.
"When my son was well, he would have gladly helped Mr Law work out his depressive thoughts, if asked, because he believed in the value of people."
Sandra Scott, whose daughter, Amara Scott, died on February 9 2022 aged 25, said she and her family were trying to help her through a mental health crisis.
"Our efforts were cut short when, in her most vulnerable state, she made contact with the accused, she said.
"The day I and her friends found Amara, and the way that she died â it broke my heart.
"It was a blessing and an honour to be Amara's mother."
The hearing continues.
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line
