More than 451,000 people are projected to die across the globe in the next six months from the additional heat brought by a super El Niño, according to estimates from climate scientists released Wednesday.
The El Niño—the warm phase of the Pacific Ocean’s recurring cycle, when heat from the ocean is released into the atmosphere—began in June. It can intensify and affect storms, fisheries and rainfall patterns far from the Pacific, raising global land temperatures.
In the new estimates, scientists at the University of Chicago Climate Impact Lab project the hotter land conditions brought by El Niño will resemble the higher temperatures climate change is predicted to deliver in 20 years.
The estimated heat death toll, the scientists warned, are on top of the impacts from droughts, wildfires and flooding, expected from hotter temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns in a world already superheated by greenhouse gases.
Michael Greenstone, a co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab and an economics professor, said scientists have long been able to predict the impacts of higher temperatures on crops. But now, they can predict the impact an El Niño can have on deaths.
“This is such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbors, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives,” Greenstone said in a statement. “This report allows decisionmakers to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives in the coming months.”
The countries most affected by land temperatures increased by 1.2 degrees Celsius over the next six months are Nigeria, Indonesia, Sudan, India and Brazil. Collectively, the five countries account for more than 97,000 of the projected heat deaths. The U.S. is in the top 20 most affected nations, with 3,500 projected additional heat deaths, according to the study.
As El Niño conditions began affecting the Asia Pacific in June, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said in a statement that local chapters are already working to prepare for and respond to these evolving climate risks. Their preparations include strengthening early warning systems, providing cash and livelihood assistance and promoting climate-resilient agricultural practices.
Intensifying heat, drought and pressure on agriculture, water and energy systems could further amplify risks, a statement from the humanitarian network said, making extreme weather more intense, less predictable and more disruptive for vulnerable communities. Alexander Matheou, IFRC’s regional director for Asia Pacific, said there still is a window to act.
“We know where the risks are emerging, and we have the tools to respond early,” Matheou said. “What is needed now is the commitment to invest ahead of the crisis—rather than paying a far higher price later.”
This El Niño, which could be the strongest on record, could permanently push the planet’s average annual temperature past the 1.5 degrees Celsius warming threshold enshrined in scientific documents and political agreements as a turning point for potentially irreversible climate impacts.
The warm conditions from June 2026 to February 2027 will resemble the higher temperatures that climate change is projected to deliver in 20 years, leading to 44 percent more extremely hot days than expected in a normal year. Forecasts suggest El Niño will remain beyond February 2027 through spring 2027, potentially pushing death counts higher.
The study authors wrote that El Niño is effectively leapfrogging the world into the future, causing temperatures which won’t be the norm for another two decades and before countries have time to adapt and protect themselves.
The report combined peer-reviewed methods on the relationship between temperature in more than 24,000 regions across the world and mortality and seasonal temperature forecasts. The death projections were compared to the same months of an average year between 1996 and 2025.
Time-sensitive projections can guide multilateral and humanitarian organizations’ decisions about where to direct emergency funds to avoid tens of thousands of deaths, the study said. It can also inform governments of all levels where to target their resources.
The climate lab’s adaptation inventory finds that heat warnings, health outreach to vulnerable populations, cooling centers and hydration stations, worker protections and expanded health system capacity can help people cope with extreme heat.
Tamma Carleton, faculty head of research for the Climate Impact Lab and an assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley, said increasing emergency response and better targeting efforts can save many lives this year.
“But 20 years from now, once today’s extreme temperatures become the new normal, we don’t want to be in a constant state of emergency,” Carleton said.

Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.
The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA.
The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down.
That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it to manufacture coating for frying pans until 2012.
Sam and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result.
"When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale.
"I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said.
'It's quite emotional, a shock'
Forever chemicals are a group of substances, also known as PFAS, that are resistant to water and oil and are in thousands of everyday products, such as clothing and cookwear.
But because they do not break down easily they have raised health concerns. PFOA has been banned in the UK since 2020 because it was classed by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as a Group 1 carcinogen, which means there is clear scientific evidence it can increase the risk of cancer.
The Environment Agency and Wyre Council have been testing the area close to the AGC Chemicals factory since 2024 to determine if it has been contaminated.
They found PFOA at elevated levels in the soil, eggs and locally grown vegetables. Two allotment sites have now been closed and are due to be classified as contaminated land, while residents within 1km of the factory have been advised to peel any fruit or vegetables grown in their gardens.
Those investigations concluded the PFOA was likely to have come from the factory having been carried in the air.
Residents previously asked the council to test their blood for the chemical. But according to the UK Health Security Agency, PFAS monitoring is not currently recommended because "tests are unlikely to provide clear information for individuals".
Instead independent tests were offered by Manchester Metropolitan University, paid for by investigative journalists Watershed and Law for Change - which funds cases covering environmental issues.
Forty-nine residents volunteered, and they were told their blood test readings on Wednesday.
Andrew Molloy found out he was in the highest-risk category.
"I was half expecting it to be just normal," he said. "Because the investigation here has all been focused on - you're only really being at risk if you eat fruit and veg from the garden or grow your own eggs - which I don't."
Andrew's home was built on land that used to be part of the factory. He underwent the tests because he was worried about persistent health problems in his family.
"One of the first things I'm going to do is take [the results] to my GP and at least get it on my record. They seem to refuse to do anything related to this, but now I have hard information and data," he said.
Mario Panteli, who was visibly shaken by his results, which were among the highest, said it was "quite emotional, a shock". He added: "I bought a property, assuming that this is our forever home. I'm going to have to stop my children from going in the garden, front and back. I feel constricted, like I'm in a cage now."
Dr David Megson, who carried out the testing at Manchester Metropolitan University, said the results made him feel sick.
"To me, it shows something seriously wrong has happened to that community in that area, that the levels were far higher than anything we would have ever expected to see in the general population."
The UK does not have any recommendations about acceptable PFAS levels in people, although the US and Germany do.
Of the 49 residents tested, 70% had readings that could leave them at increased risk of adverse health effects, according to these countries' guidelines.
Possible effects include a higher risk of reduced thyroid function, kidney cancer, testicular cancer, elevated cholesterol, pre-eclampsia and ulcerative colitis.
Having elevated forever chemicals in their blood is not a guarantee residents will develop these conditions, but US and German authorities have suggested anyone with elevated levels should be offered further health screening.
Factory to close later this year
More than 100 residents, including those who had their blood tested, are now considering taking a group legal action against AGC Chemicals to claim damages for the contamination
Sarah Moore, partner at law firm Leigh Day - which is representing some residents - said compensation could be sought for financial losses on residents' homes and the impact it has had on their use and enjoyment of the land.
She said damages could also be sought "in relation to the health risks, which we now consider to be a significant issue as a result of the testing we've been doing locally".
The case would be "groundbreaking in the UK," she added and would be the first time a community has brought a legal claim over contamination from forever chemicals in the country.
Overseas, one of the biggest legal cases over PFOA contamination was in West Virginia, in the US, which was depicted in the 2019 film Dark Waters. In that case, DuPont and Chemours Co settled more than 3,500 PFOA lawsuits for a total of $671m (Â£526m). Both companies have always denied any wrongdoing.

9f25246ed73c.text: Executives from leading artificial intelligence organizations urged global cooperation Wednesday to address risks from increasingly autonomous AI systems during a UN Security Council meeting. The big picture: AI capabilities are advancing faster than governments are developing safeguards, raising concerns about whether humans can maintain control over increasingly autonomous systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appeared in person at the meeting, while Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue joined by video conference. Driving the news: " We have a choice in front of us," Altman said. "AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray." He outlined the risks of AI systems becoming increasingly autonomous, warning "they could move faster than our institutions, concentrate power in too few hands, or make decisions that people no longer understand or control," fears he noted become increasingly urgent as AI systems move toward self-improvement . "It doesn't matter whether people put the risk of catastrophe at 10% or 1% or 12% or 0.1 percent," he said. "None of these levels are remotely acceptable, and we should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we'll be able to keep under human control." State of play: A recent Hugging Face breach and newly disclosed AI safety incidents have intensified concerns about monitoring and security standards. The UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI warned that the present AI firewalls are "unravelling." Last week, OpenAI disclosed six new incidents where its models concealed mistakes, sought unauthorized credentials or committed other misbehaviors — making it clear the Hugging Face breach was an eye-opener, not a standalone fluke, Axios previously reported. " To better understand and mitigate these emerging cybersecurity risks, the global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure," Delangue said Wednesday, reflecting on the summer breach that triggered a cascade of new questions about AI capabilities. Zoom out: AI's current trajectory needs to continue for only one or two years before reaching what Amodei called "a country of geniuses in a data center," he said in his remarks. That holds massive opportunity, he said, pointing to a discovery announced Wednesday that was led by his company's LLM, Claude: an enzyme system hidden in bacteriophage DNA. Amodei also noted serious risks of the technology, such as misuse by bad actors to create biological weapons or loss of control over advanced systems. Managing that risk depends on global cooperation, he said, calling for an agreement to ban the use of AI to make biological weapons; new evaluation and verification systems; common standards for testing models for risks; and a notification system for global security concerns. Catch up quick: Industry leaders have raised fresh alarms in recent weeks about the rapid advancement of their technology and the need to slow its pace. President Trump , who appeared before the UN General Assembly Tuesday, vowed not to hamstring AI development. The bottom line: Altman warned, "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone." He added, "They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve." Go deeper: Exclusive: Thune believes Trump is willing to listen on AI guardrails

The company has taken a number of steps to address the concerns, including cutting its default video retention window from 30 days to seven days.
The company has said its cameras have helped save thousands of lives and reduced crime in the communities it operates in. âIn public safety, the benefits far, far outweigh the concerns,â Flock board member David Ulevitch said on Semaforâs Compound Interest show earlier this year. f19036426e93.text: By — Patrick Whittle, Associated Press Patrick Whittle, Associated Press By — Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/maine-dems-hammer-collins-over-report-of-pay-to-play-probe-gop-senator-calls-it-completely-false Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Maine Dems hammer Collins over report of pay-to-play probe. GOP senator calls it 'completely false' Politics Sep 23, 2026 6:17 PM EDT PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Maine Democrats on Wednesday assailed U.S. Sen. Susan Collins over a news report that the FBI investigated how much she knew about illegal campaign contributions that sent one of her donors to prison. The ProPublica report, published Tuesday, states that the FBI in 2024 planned to launch an investigation into Collins' dealings with Navatek, a Hawaii defense contractor and donor to her campaign. The investigation, which focused on an alleged pay-to-play scheme, failed to commence after President Donald Trump took office after winning the election, according to ProPublica. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The report arrived six weeks before an election where Collins is seeking her sixth term against Democrat Troy Jackson. Democrats have targeted the seat, in a state that Trump lost in 2024, as the party tries to win control of the Senate, making it one of the most competitive races on the November ballot. READ MORE: How Troy Jackson went from Maine logger to Democratic nominee for Senate against Susan Collins Collins on Tuesday called the entire story "absolutely outrageous" and said it is frustrating and unfair to have such claims made against her so close to the election. Her campaign manager, Steve Abbott, also said Wednesday the allegation that "we charge people to have meetings" is categorically false and Collins accepting campaign cash for contracts "did not happen." Jackson called the allegation "corruption of the highest order." He was not present Wednesday when a group of Maine Democrats held a news conference near Collins' Portland office, but said the allegations are a betrayal of trust. "I cannot stress enough here today the seriousness of these allegations. Maine people deserve clear and real answers from Susan Collins right now," Maine Democratic Party Executive Director Devon Murphy-Anderson said. FBI says allegations were already investigated The ProPublica report stated that the head of a Collins super PAC met with executives from defense contractor Navatek in 2019 and asked them for a $500,000 campaign donation. The company's CEO, Martin Kao, sent an initial $150,000 donation using a shell company, the report stated. ProPublica reported that it reviewed an internal company email from Kao in which the CEO later told Navatek executives that Collins committed to getting the company $32 million in Navy contracts. Kao and two other Navatek executives were later indicted on charges of funneling illegal donations to Collins. Kao sought to reduce his jail sentence by revealing to the FBI the full scope of illegal contributions to Collins, ProPublica reported. Collins said Kao is "a liar" whose story is untrustworthy. "He has been twice convicted in separate federal court cases. He's been convicted of money laundering. He's been convicted of bank fraud. He has been convicted of false submissions to the FEC. He's being convicted of a lot of crimes," she said. An FBI spokesperson said in a statement that the allegations "had already been investigated by the FBI years ago and ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins' campaign. Any suggestion otherwise is totally false." The ProPublica article also states that Trump's return to the White House left the Justice Department unable to perform the investigation. Corruption investigations have decreased in Trump's second term The number of FBI agents and Justice Department prosecutors specializing in corruption investigations plummeted in the first months of the Trump administration. The Justice Department, for instance, decimated its elite Public Integrity Section in early 2025 while the FBI disbanded a white-collar fraud and public corruption squad based out of its Washington field office. The administration has also fired numerous law enforcement officials who participated in investigations into Trump, including over his efforts to undo the 2020 presidential election he lost and his retention of classified records at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida. READ MORE: AP report: FBI fires agents who worked on Trump classified document investigation An email seeking comment was sent to the Justice Department on Wednesday. Collins said she first learned of the company through the University of Maine because of the research the Navy found to be valuable, which had to do with 3D printing for production. She said the Justice Department has already reviewed the matter. "I'm telling you this is completely false," Collins said. Senate Majority Leader John Thune dismissed the idea that Collins would be implicated in a pay-to-play scheme, calling the allegations "a political hit job." Mascaro reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Mary Clare Jalonick and Eric Tucker in Washington, D.C., and Kimberlee Kruesi in Providence, Rhode Island, contributed to this report. 8ff5008d1164.text: President Trump welcomed Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews for the Chinese leader's state visit to Washington D.C. Wednesday evening. Why it matters: U.S. presidents typically receive visiting foreign leaders at the White House, making Trump's airport welcome an unusual diplomatic gesture. The latest: Trump met Xi at the foot of the stairs after the Chinese leader's jet landed at Joint Base Andrews, the U.S. military base 13 miles southeast of the White House in Maryland. Zoom out: It's much more common for U.S. presidents to greet visiting leaders at the White House. In February 2025, Trump welcomed Volodymyr Zelensky at the West Wing entrance to kick off the Ukrainian leader's tense visit. In April of this year, King Charles III was received at the White House's South Portico. The big picture: Presidents in recent decades have occasionally greeted visiting popes at D.C.-area airports, but airport welcomes for other foreign leaders have largely fallen out of use. President John F. Kennedy personally welcomed several foreign leaders at Washington-area airports in 1962, including Ivory Coast President Félix Houphouët-Boigny. More recently, President George W. Bush greeted Pope Benedict XVI at Andrews in 2008, and President Obama greeted Pope Francis there in 2015. What they're saying: "President Xi hosted President Trump in China for a historic summit this summer, and President Trump is reciprocating his hospitality by welcoming the Chinese delegation for a reciprocal visit this week," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Axios. "The President will forge relationships with anyone in order to advance our national interests and make good deals for the American people." The bottom line: Trump's tarmac greeting revived a presidential practice that has become uncommon outside visits by popes.

"Whoever wins AI, WINS!"
US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China.
His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view.
"China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies.
You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not.
For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he has described as "a hoax".
China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all.
It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world.
Is the US in the lead?
There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured.
American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.
In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%", according to researchers at Stanford University, external.
Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models.
The stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies.
So that might partly explain why President Trump sees AI as key to US success.
Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models.
China's advantage
Despite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all.
Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans.
The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software.
This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms.
Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months.
Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable.
Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said.
"AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous."
AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesati told Tech Life on the BBC World Service.
"Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said.
In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become the world's biggest manufacturer of robots, with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated.
The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House.
Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said.
But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms.
China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit".
Safety concerns?
China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different.
While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war.
Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president.
"We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution".
Washington has prioritised innovation and sought to reduce regulation in an effort to "keep American labs ahead", said information security officer Jayant Dave from cybersecurity firm Check Point Software Technologies.

Scotland's waste sector is on the verge of a crisis which could see rubbish piling up on the streets, experts have warned.
They say the combination of significantly reduced landfill space and a breakdown of Glasgow's main incinerator have created a "perfect storm" which could see waste left uncollected.
Industry representatives are due to meet ministers to discuss their concerns but say there's no obvious short-term solution to avoid the crisis.
The Scottish government said was working with stakeholders to maintain resilience and identify contingency arrangements should they be required.
Landfill capacity in Scotland has been shrinking as operators wind down their operations ahead of a forthcoming ban on sending black bag waste to landfill sites.
That had been due to come into effect at the start of this year, but was delayed until January 2028 after a Disclosure investigation reported that 100 lorry loads of waste would have to be sent to England by road each day.
Last year there were 10 sites which took in most of Scotland's residual waste â the material left over after recyclable and compostable materials have been separated out.
However, that has now been reduced to just three, one of which is in administration.
The problems have been exacerbated by the breakdown of Glasgow's main incinerator at Polmadie, which has been out of action since April.
Welding cracks were identified during routine inspections and the facility is not expected to resume operations until next March.
Much of the city's household waste is currently being diverted to a large landfill site at Mount Vernon - but its operator, Patersons, says it only has a few months of space available for burying the rubbish.
The amount of rubbish being processed there has increased from about 2,000 tonnes to 5,000 tonnes a week.
An application to extend the site has been refused on appeal by the Scottish government.
The operator estimates that it will be full by the end of the year.
The ban on sending black bag waste to landfill was designed to encourage more recycling, with the residual waste being sent instead to incinerators where it is burned to create electricity.
The proposals sparked a rapid rise in plans to build waste to energy facilities, which led in 2022 to a ban on new applications
This was introduced because of concerns that Scotland would end up with more incinerators than needed to deal with the available waste, particularly if recycling rates increased.
But the amount of household waste being recycled has barely changed in a decade.
A fresh report published last month by Zero Waste Scotland concluded that most incinerators are operating well below their maximum capacity, which suggests the capacity gap might have been miscalculated.
Several more sites are under construction, including the South Clyde Energy Centre at North Cardonald, but are not expected to be ready quickly enough to address the current issues.
Several sites in the north of England, some of which are understood to have received waste from Scotland, have been shut down by the Environment Agency following investigations into suspected illegal waste activity.
'We can't see a solution'
Landfill manager David Balmer, who works with Mount Vernon's operator Patersons, said it was possible that Scotland would quickly run out of landfill space.
He said the Polmadie breakdown had created a perfect storm.
"Could you see waste on the street? Absolutely," he said.
Balmer said councils and waste management contractors were under an obligation to collect the rubbish.
"But if they can't process it further down the line, what's the easier solution?
"The easier solution is to leave in the streets at the moment, pending a solution. The problem is we can't see a solution."
Waste consultant Alasdair Meldrum, of Albion Environmental, says he has not seen such a looming crisis in almost 40 years of working in the industry.
He says there are already commercial operators who are struggling to find outlets to send their waste, with some being sent hundreds of miles to locations in England.
Meldrum added: "There's no easy solution. There are a number of landfill sites that could develop more void space but you can't do the engineering work in the winter.
"There's no real short-term solution. We've got ourselves into a real problem."
One possible solution is for householders to reduce the amount of black bag waste they generate by sending more for recycling.
However, rates of recycling have barely changed in Scotland over the last decade.
Zero Waste Scotland has estimated that more than half of domestic residual waste could be recycled.
One of the biggest elements is food waste which, if collected separately, could be processed through anaerobic digestion.
However, environmental group Friends of the Earth Scotland believes its policy which is to blame rather than the actions of individual households.
Kim Pratt, circular economy campaigner, says there has been far too much focus on incineration and not enough on reducing how much waste is in the system.
She added: "That makes all these problems much easier to solve. It reduces the expense for households, it makes it easier to meet the landfill ban and it reduces the need for incineration."
Glasgow City Council said general waste was being disposed of at a range of alternative sites, including other energy from waste facilities.
A spokesman added: "We are satisfied there is sufficient capacity in the overall system to ensure general waste is disposed of appropriately while the Grrec is offline for repair.
"Residents should continue to use their household bins as normal. Recycling services are unaffected by the current issues."
The council and Viridor, which operates the incinerator, say they are working to bring the facility at Polmadie back on line once repair work is complete.

As of Wednesday, the national average for a gallon of diesel was $6.52, according to AAA. That's up from an average of $3.69 this time last year. "The average person, including myself, doesn't typically buy diesel fuel," said Kenneth Gillingham, professor of environmental and energy economics at Yale University. "But diesel fuel is crucial for so many parts of our economy." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Energy and economics experts who spoke with PBS News said Americans can expect higher costs across the board as a result of the record high diesel prices, at a time when consumers are already struggling with stubborn inflation. In August, while diesel prices were nearly $1 cheaper than they are today, consumer prices rose by 3.4% compared to a year ago, according to a Labor Department report. WATCH: News Wrap: August inflation report shows consumer prices up 3.4% Here's what to know about diesel prices, which industries rely on the fuel and how rising costs are expected to be passed down to consumers. Why are diesel prices so high, and why are they expected to remain that way for a while? Ongoing global conflicts have led to rising prices across multiple industries, and the cost of diesel is no different. However, diesel is "suffering from a two-pronged attack," Gregory DeYong, a professor at Southern Illinois University and expert in supply chain management, said in an email. The U.S. war in Iran has affected the supply of crude oil, from which diesel is produced. In early September, the price of a barrel of oil again surpassed $100. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major shipping route for the world's oil, and the bombing of oil facilities and alternate shipping routes in Saudi Arabia have contributed to the rise. WATCH: Iran-backed Houthis seize island at entrance to Red Sea, threatening Saudi oil exports Diesel supply has also been affected by the loss of refineries in Russia amid its war with Ukraine. Russian oil facilities, including refineries that produce diesel, have been hit by Ukrainian strikes, straining the industry. After the U.S. and China, Russia has been the third-largest producer of refined oil products in the world, according to a September International Energy Agency report. In June, the amount of oil going through Russia's refineries dropped to its lowest levels in more than 20 years, the report found. Even though an end to the global wars would ease the strain on the oil market, it wouldn't immediately solve the rising costs, experts said. WATCH: Trump says oil prices will come down after midterm elections Repairing and building refineries takes several months to years to complete. And existing refineries are already running near capacity. In the U.S., refineries were running at 97% capacity as of Sept. 11, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. "It will still take some time for prices to come back down, simply because inventories will have to be rebuilt, refineries will have to be put back up and running, and the standard flow of trade would have to be reestablished," Gillingham said. What runs on diesel? Even though fewer than 3% of passenger cars in the U.S. run on diesel, much of the economy does. "Diesel is the fuel that moves the economy," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a statement. Some of the industries that rely on diesel include: Shipping and logistics: Most vehicles used in transporting stuff to and within the U.S. — such as trucks, trains and large boats — run on diesel. This includes trucks that transport gasoline to gas stations. Home heating: About 4.8 million homes in the U.S., mainly in the Northeast, use heating oil in the winter as their primary heating fuel, according to the Energy Information Administration. Heating oil is "essentially identical to diesel fuel," DeYong said. Agriculture: Heavy machinery used in agriculture, irrigation pumps used on fields and trucks that transport food from farms to stores rely on diesel. Many fertilizers and chemicals that farmers use on crops are also petroleum-based. "Every part of the food system uses diesel," said Jeffrey Dorfman, a professor of agricultural and resource economics at North Carolina State University. Construction: Trucks that deliver construction material to worksites run on diesel, as do the heavy machinery used to carry out "demanding construction work, such as lifting steel beams, digging foundations and trenches, drilling wells, paving roads, and moving soil and rocks," according to the Energy Information Administration. A worker fills his truck with diesel fuel at a corporate filling station in San Diego, California, May 18, 2026. Photo by Mike Blake/Reuters How are diesel prices passed down to consumers? Because so much of the economy relies on diesel, the rising cost of the fuel will lead to further increased costs for consumers. But how much or how quickly prices will rise vary based on the product and the industry. "High diesel prices primarily affect consumers indirectly, as firms along the supply chain make decisions about whether to absorb higher diesel prices or pass these along to their buyers," Jason Miller, supply chain management professor at Michigan State University, said in an email. A federal court in Michigan has tossed out a pioneering antitrust lawsuit brought by the state of Michigan against four major oil and gas companies and their largest U.S. trade association that alleged a conspiracy to forestall the transition to renewable energy and electric vehicles in order to maintain market dominance of fossil fuels.
Michigan failed to bring a viable claim under federal antitrust law because the state could not prove the higher prices that residents have been paying for a fossil fuel-dependent energy system were specifically caused by the oil companies’ alleged conspiracy, the court said.
The ruling on Tuesday, from the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan, was based on the threshold issue of standing, or the right of a party to bring a case to court. In this case, the court ruled that Michigan lacked standing to bring its antitrust claim because the state did not adequately allege that its harm—overcharges for energy—was caused directly by the fossil fuel defendants’ conduct.
“The distance is too great between the alleged conspiracy and Michigan’s and its residents’ overcharges to find that the conspiracy proximately caused the overcharges,” U.S. District Judge Jane M. Beckering wrote in her decision.
Michigan filed its lawsuit in January against BP, Chevron, ExxonMobil, Shell and the American Petroleum Institute, claiming that they engaged in collusive anticompetitive conduct to suppress the development of renewable energy and EV technologies for the purpose of protecting their fossil fuel business and boosting profits.
This conduct resulted in consumers having fewer choices for fueling their cars and powering their homes and having to pay more for energy, the lawsuit argued, since renewables are now the cheapest form of energy and do not come with externalized costs like public health and climate damage. The case was brought under federal and state antitrust law, and it was the first suit brought against oil companies focused entirely on antitrust theories in the context of the energy transition.
“By colluding to delay the energy transition away from fossil fuels, defendants have deliberately imposed
staggering external costs on Michigan and the People of Michigan,” the state asserted in its complaint. But Beckering said these kinds of costs, like increased home insurance premiums and climate adaptation expenses, were not relevant to the antitrust claim. The only viable harm the state alleged under antitrust law was overcharges in the energy market, the court determined.
And that harm could not be proven to be caused by the alleged conspiracy by Big Oil to suppress renewables and EVs, according to the court, given there may be other factors or “market forces” involved. “The alleged conspiracy’s success at entrenching supracompetitive fossil fuel prices depends on numerous market forces besides defendants, such as technological developments, other investors, and the public’s interest in renewable energy, as well as the supply of fossil fuels,” Beckering wrote.
The court dismissed Michigan’s federal antitrust claim, and declined to even consider the state antitrust claim, essentially tossing out the entire case.

“Michigan’s lawsuit was part of a coordinated campaign against an industry that is vital to everyday life and serves as the engine of America’s economy. Climate policy is a federal, not state, issue, and we are pleased with the court’s decision,” Ryan Meyers, API senior vice president and general counsel, said in a statement.
BP declined to comment, while Chevron, ExxonMobil, and Shell did not respond to a request for comment.
Michigan has not yet announced whether it will try to appeal.
“The Attorney General disagrees with the opinion and order issued on the energy affordability antitrust case the Department brought on behalf of the People of the State of Michigan,” Danny Wimmer, press secretary for the Michigan attorney general office, said in an emailed statement. “Our office is reviewing the opinion in full and considering our options.”
The ruling comes after the same judge dismissed a lawsuit brought by the Trump administration last year to try to preemptively block Michigan from suing Big Oil over climate harm. Since that lawsuit was filed before Michigan had brought any sort of case, the alleged harm was too speculative, Beckering ruled.
The dismissal of Michigan’s antitrust case is the latest legal win for major oil and gas companies that are facing mounting demands for climate accountability through state laws and lawsuits. A federal court in Syracuse, New York, recently struck down New York’s landmark Climate Change Superfund Act that sought to make large fossil fuel producers pay for a portion of the staggering hundreds of billions of dollars the state is expected to incur to adapt to climate change. In March, the Maryland Supreme Court sided with fossil fuel companies in upholding a lower court ruling dismissing climate tort lawsuits brought by the cities of Baltimore and Annapolis and Anne Arundel County..
The U.S. Supreme Court, meanwhile, is slated to take up a climate tort case filed by Boulder, Colorado, against oil companies Suncor and ExxonMobil, in a hearing on Oct.5 that legal experts say could be “incredibly consequential” for the more than two dozen other climate lawsuits pending against the fossil fuel industry. If the court rules in favor of Suncor and Exxon on the question of whether federal law preempts state climate lawsuits, it could put an end to many of these cases.
“With the [climate] tort cases [the fossil fuel industry] has won some and lost some,” said Michael Gerrard, founder and faculty director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University.

e919428e4bc4.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/fbi-investigates-hackers-claim-to-have-stolen-employee-data-compromised-jobs-website Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FBI investigates hackers' claim to have stolen employee data, compromised jobs website Nation Sep 23, 2026 5:37 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI said Wednesday it was investigating a criminal hacking group's claims that it had stolen "very sensitive data" belonging to thousands of agents and applicants and that it had compromised the bureau's jobs website. "The FBI is aware of a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information," the FBI said in a statement. It said that while the "point of breach" was undetermined, "we are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk." WATCH: Patel explains why FBI no longer considers bestiality an automatic hiring disqualifier A message that circulated online from a hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the hack. The jobs website, the main portal for prospective employees to learn about the FBI and initiate the application process, remained offline as of Wednesday afternoon. "We have compromised the FBI. We hold very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI Agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job," said the ShinyHunters message, which was directed to FBI Director Kash Patel and Brett Leatherman, the assistant director in charge of the bureau's cyber division. The claims could not immediately be verified. An email to an address associated with ShinyHunters was not immediately returned. In its message, ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations contained in an FBI public advisory from May that described the organization as a "cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion." That public service announcement characterized ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims," commonly harass or threaten victims and "may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist." ShinyHunters said in its message to the FBI that it was "offended" by those characterizations and demanded that the FBI remove those claims. It did not say what would happen if the FBI did not do so within a week. "This is not a ransom, coercion, or extortion. Your federal policies do not apply here. This PSA is NOT financially motivated," the hacking group's message said. The FBI, the nation's premier federal law enforcement agency, has been a common hacking target. In March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating "suspicious activities" on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of Patel's and posted online what appear to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work resume and other personal documents dating back more than a decade. The FBI described the compromised information as "historical in nature" and said it involved "no government information." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 21c29e036c8f.text: By — Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ai-firm-leaders-tell-un-security-council-that-it-could-be-a-risk-to-all-humanity Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AI firm leaders tell UN Security Council that it could be a risk to all humanity World Sep 23, 2026 5:23 PM EDT UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to set controls over the burgeoning technology they are designing in order to save the world — or, at least, its people. WATCH: Trump dismisses concerns about AI risks at UN, says he won't rein it in "If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," said Dario Amodei, the chief executive officer of Anthropic. "We could lose control of the future to AI," said his competitor, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI. Both said the countries of the world, though the U.N. Security Council, where they testified Wednesday afternoon, have to set safeguards, which would be actual controls to prevent the technology from getting too powerful to rein in. They also called for the world to make sure that the power of AI isn't concentrated in one company or country. For world leaders, one key question about AI is this: Who should control life-and-death decisions — human or machine? The United Nations Security Council on Wednesday huddled with top technology leaders to figure out if the increasing abilities and pervasiveness of artificial intelligence should be controlled and, if so, by who. Other lingering questions: How could it be done? When might it be just too late? The day before, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of "killer robots." Experts and European leaders said that's not hyperbole but something that's already a reality or at least perilously close. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 1b9ca9079822.text: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian forcefully rejected President Trump's portrayal of Iran as a source of terrorism at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, insisting instead that Iranians are "victims of terrorism." Why it matters: Pezeshkian used one of the world's biggest diplomatic stages to directly challenge Trump on U.S. soil — as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran rages on. What he's saying: "The United States president described us as terrorists," Pezeshkian said in a roughly 18-minute speech. "We have been the victims of terrorism… Those who are terrorists and train and protect terrorists describe us as such. We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists." "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength," he said. "We live in a world in which the powerful, instead of thinking about humanity, justice, fairness, and democracy, they seem to be the protectors and creators of instability and destruction." Zoom in: Pezeshkian cited attacks that he blamed on the U.S., including strikes that killed children. He pointed to the deaths of more than 150 Iranians at an elementary school in Minab, including more than 120 children. A recent UN report found "reasonable grounds to believe" the U.S. committed a war crime in the strike. While the U.S. has not released findings of an investigation related to the attack, the AP has found evidence that at least one U.S. missile struck the school. Pezeshkian also mentioned the alleged deaths of children playing at a sports hall and an adjacent school after they were struck by a U.S.-made ballistic missile. Between the lines: The same UN report found that Iran's crackdown on protesters likely constituted "crimes against humanity." The report cited tactics including "murder, imprisonment, torture and other inhumane acts" as "part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians." What to watch: U.S. and Iranian officials held three hours of indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN on Tuesday, with Trump calling the meeting "very productive" and suggestions a deal remains possible. Iran has downplayed the breakthrough, saying its negotiating position has not changed — underscoring how far apart the two sides remain even as diplomacy continues. Go deeper: UN report: U.S. may have committed war crimes in Iran

216d3036e739.text: A district judge tossed an election interference lawsuit by President Trump against the Des Moines Register, parent company USA Today Co. (formerly Gannett) and pollster Ann Selzer , rejecting claims that its inaccurate pre-election poll amounted to consumer fraud. Why it matters : The dismissal is an early court test of Trump's broader push to use litigation against media organizations over coverage he disputes. Zoom in : In his ruling, Judge Scott Beatle said the plaintiff's attempt to use fraud law to allege liability on the poll was not a valid legal argument because political speech is protected by the First Amendment . "As such, the only question before the Court is whether the Petition states a claim the law recognizes," Beatle wrote. "At its core, the Plaintiffs' Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability." "After considering the parties' arguments, the Court must conclude that the protection is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed," he wrote. What they're saying : "Today is a victory for the First Amendment—and for the essential role of a free press in American democracy. We are gratified that the Court recognized what this meritless lawsuit sought to obscure: that claims of "fake news" are little more than an attempt to punish news outlets for coverage those in power do not like," said Polly Grunfeld Sack, USA TODAY Co, Chief Legal Counsel. "A free press is fundamental to an informed public and a vibrant democracy. This decision reaffirms the enduring First Amendment principles that empower journalists and sends a message to those who think they can intimidate the press through legal action." The big picture : The lawsuit is part of a broader effort by Trump and his Administration to target media companies with legal action for what they believe is unfair coverage. To date, the courts have mostly sided with media companies, citing the strength of the First Amendment. What we're watching: The White House referred Axios to Trump's personal lawyers, who did not respond when asked whether they plan to appeal.

696e1d6a5988.text: The president of Iran told the United Nations General Assembly his country won’t bend to U.S. intimidation. Masoud Pezeshkian spoke one day after President Trump threatened to escalate the war from the same stage. On the sidelines, U.S. and Iranian officials signaled no breakthroughs in mediated talks. Nick Schifrin reports. Amna Nawaz: The president of Iran told the United Nations General Assembly his country won't bend to U.S. intimidation just a day after President Trump threatened to escalate the war from the very same stage. Geoff Bennett: On the sidelines, U.S. and Iranian officials signaled no major breakthroughs in mediated talks. Nick Schifrin has the latest after another busy day in New York. Nick Schifrin: It is a building on U.S. soil, an organization dedicated to peace, and never before has it hosted the leader of a country at war with its host until today. Masoud Pezeshkian, Iranian President (through interpreter): Yesterday, the United States president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism. Nick Schifrin: And on the same dais where President Trump yesterday delivered this threat... President Donald Trump: Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Nick Schifrin: ... Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian delivered his own defiance. Masoud Pezeshkian (through interpreter): We will never bow our head or bend at the knee. Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force. Nick Schifrin: Within minutes, the sole member of the U.S. delegation had heard enough and walked out of the room. But, inside Iran, Pezeshkian leads the faction that advocates for negotiation and economic integration with the West. He's losing that argument to hard-liners, who today threatened Iran's neighbors after they cooperated with U.S. sanctions banning Iranian airlines. Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iranian Supreme National Security Council (through interpreter): If any country joins the United States in this adventure, its airports will no longer be able to operate flights. The choice is yours. Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State: Do they want to be a country or do they want to be a revolution? Nick Schifrin: Speaking right after Pezeshkian, Secretary of State Marco Rubio called yesterday's indirect talks between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and American mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner significant. But he said Pezeshkian's speech was the pot calling the kettle black. Marco Rubio: Slaughtering 10,000 of your own people in protests is a violation of the U.N. I hope it's a violation of the U.N. principles. I think sponsoring terrorist organizations in the region to attack your neighbors, attack energy infrastructure, attack civilian sites is a violation of the U.N. system. So I don't know what standing Iran has to lecture anyone on human rights or the international system when they habitually violate it. Nick Schifrin: But Rubio acknowledged that another violator of the international system, Russian President Vladimir Putin, is invited to Florida in December, when President Trump hosts the G20 in his Doral resort. Marco Rubio: We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president, but with other world leaders. We hope that's an invitation he will accept. Nick Schifrin: But, today, Kyiv was filled with the sound of Russian drone strikes. Authorities said at least two people were killed and dozens injured... Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President: De-escalation steps are important, are needed before winter, now. Nick Schifrin: ... as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned the war could escalate. And as Ukraine begins to rely on autonomous weapons, Zelenskyy warned the AI future could become the present. Volodymyr Zelenskyy: As early as next year, there is already a real possibility that AI, not only people, will begin -- will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield. And we need peace before we reach that point. Dario Amodei, CEO and Co-Founder, Anthropic: That AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole. Nick Schifrin: Today, the Security Council held its first ever U.N. General Assembly AI meeting, including warnings from American AI leaders. Sam Altman, CEO, OpenAI: No one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their world view on everyone else. Nick Schifrin: But, in this chamber, the flawed but still only international body whose resolutions are legally binding, it fell to the co-chair of the U.N.'s independent AI panel, Yoshua Bengio, to warn the world it must police AI companies and issue a clarion call for collaboration. Yoshua Bengio, Co-Chair, U.N. Independent International Panel on AI: Today, a handful of companies and countries are acting in their self-interest by taking reckless risks with humanity's fate. Our future, all of us, our future is at stake. Decisions that affect us all should be made by us all. The choice is still ours, but we must act now to correct the trajectory. Nick Schifrin: This year's U.N. General Assembly theme is Restoring Trust, a U.N. that delivers for all. This week, that sentiment has been fleeting, as many here are worried the future feels fractured and uncertain. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Nick Schifrin.

c915484c7943.text: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. At the same time, a federal judge heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning the outlets from the White House. Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington this evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. And at the same time, a federal judge today heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning them from the White House. Our Liz Landers is at the White House covering both stories, and she joins us now. So, Liz, we will start with this state visit. What is the focus of it? Liz Landers: Yes, Geoff, President Trump is greeting leader Xi right now at Joint Base Andrews here in Washington for an arrival ceremony that has all the pomp and circumstance of this major state visit. This is the first time that Xi has been to the White House since 2015. And President Trump visited China back in May and was not awarded this same kind of pomp, circumstance and arrival. In particular, Xi did not greet him when he landed there in China back in May. You're seeing some of those images now. I will remind our viewers that those images are from several months ago because the White House TV pool is still not covering the president's events today. We believe that there are going to be a number of issues that will be addressed during this visit. A senior administration official told us earlier that AI, artificial intelligence, of course, will be on the top of the list, also some of these export controls that the United States has on our computing chips and selling those to China. The possibility of reducing tariffs on some goods is apparently going to come up, and also political prisoners. Several China watchers and experts that I have spoken with don't really think that this meeting is going to be so much about deliverables as it is about continuing to forge that personal relationship that President Trump has with leader Xi. I spoke earlier today with Kyle Chan. He's a fellow at the Brookings institute. And he was actually talking about these export controls, saying that matters less and less for the Chinese government because they are going all out to build their own AI chips themselves. And when it comes to artificial intelligence in particular, you heard some of that addressed from the U.N. today in Nick's story. China is not interested in a joint slowdown of AI development, according to Chan. He says that they're more worried about cyber risks, hacking companies, and they don't share, China does not share the same concerns that we have heard from U.S. AI companies and leaders recently that robots, AI may kill us all in the near future. Geoff, one more thing I want to add. Not everybody is happy about this visit and all of the accoutrements that are being laid out for President Xi. Republican Senator Wicker, he's the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, says that he would have advised against this lavish welcome to what he calls a brutal dictator. Geoff Bennett: And, Liz, there's a state dinner tomorrow evening. Who is expected to be in attendance? Liz Landers: Well, Geoff, as you would imagine, with all of this talk of AI and technology, there are leaders from several major business companies and AI companies that are going to be at the White House tomorrow. A senior administration official says that Jeff Bezos will be there, as well as Elon Musk, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, a chipmaker, and Sam Altman of OpenAI. The first lady, Melania Trump, said in a FOX News interview today that President Trump wanted to have the state dinner because they have a great relationship. She said that she's been involved in every detail of the planning for the state dinner tomorrow night. And she also -- and I'd also just add that this is only the second state dinner that President Trump has now had in his second term in office, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: All right, Liz, in the minute we have left, bring us up to speed on this lawsuit involving the three news organizations that were banned from the White House by President Trump. Liz Landers: There was a hearing on this, this afternoon, and the judge in this case, a district judge here in Washington, said right off the bat that he was skeptical of the argument that the Trump administration, that the Trump White House is making here on due process grounds. It sounds like the judge believes that the due process of these news organizations was violated. The government is arguing in a filing that they issued late last night that news organizations failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House. This has now turned into a conversation about national security. That is what the president and the administration are arguing is at stake here, that these news organizations somehow violated national security there. The judge also seemed skeptical of that, Geoff. We still do not have an answer from the judge as to whether the ban on Politico, CNN, and MS NOW will be lifted. Geoff Bennett: Liz Landers outside the West Wing at the White House for us tonight. Liz, thanks so much. Liz Landers: Of course.

An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI "infiltrated" an Australian government website in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said.
The agent gained unauthorised accessed to a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive Medicare information", Albanese told a news conference at the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Medicare refers to Australia's universal healthcare scheme. The breach is among the first publicly reported AI-led hacks of a government website in the world.
OpenAI said it only became aware of the incident in August "during an ongoing review of OpenAI misaligned model activity", and informed Australian officials on 10 September.
While the review is ongoing, a spokesperson for the AI firm said that it is not believed that any patient records were accessed.
Albanese said the breach occurred in June this year, but OpenAI only informed government officials via email on 10 September.
The prime minister said he spoke directly to CEO of OpenAI Sam Altman to say that it had taken "too long" to inform authorities and "to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident".
He said the agent accessed both public and non-public files and a "forensic investigation" is under way to find out if other government systems were affected.
The investigation will be led by the Australian Signals Directorate, the country's cybersecurity agency.
The public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal is administered by Services Australia, the main hub to redirect users to government services.
He told reporters: "No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing.
"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable."
Earlier this year, OpenAI revealed a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls and secretly worked together to hack another tech firm named Hugging Face.

8f0099869568.text: Meta on Wednesday debuted "Muse Charm," a new, keychain-sized AI handheld device it will use to bring its viral Muse assistant to the masses. Why it matters: Meta's has raced ahead of OpenAI , Apple and other companies that are racing to build a new crop of small AI devices, revving up the massive market interest that Muse has generated in the market. Driving the news: The Muse Charm will be available for purchase by December, and the company is the first tech giant to unveil its plans for an entirely new category of device. OpenAI has spent billions to build a hardware division, so Meta's advance on the category is likely to stun many analysts and investors. Meta has also poured billions into hardware, most notably VR, an effort that most analysts have written off as a waste. Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has long held that a convergence of those investments with AI could make that bet pay off. Catch up quick : In addition to Charm, Meta announced new Muse capabilities including live video chat, real-time voice conversations with custom voice options and an e-mail address for each person's agent. Meta announced new retail partners, including Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Wayfair and more, a growing list that makes Amazon's decision not to allow Muse stand out. Muse has prompted a stock selloff in recent days as investors fear an end to stickiness between brands and customers. Meta said Muse is coming soon to its AI glasses, though it declined to be more specific than "in the coming months." "I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives," CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during his Meta Connect keynote on Wednesday. Zuckerberg said that Meta's business model behind Muse is a novel one. "We believe that Muse will make you money, and we're standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions," he said. Beyond Muse, Meta used the event to debut a range of new hardware along with new privacy options that could make the gear more palatable to the mainstream. Meta's first audio-only glasses aim to appeal to those who want the benefit of open-air sound and an always available AI assistant without the cost and potential creepiness that comes from the camera-equipped version. The new models, which will be available later in October, start at $349. Meta is also updating its Meta Ray-Ban and Meta Glasses lines with modest improvements and new designs. The more radical shift is coming on the VR side of things . Meta previewed a much slimmer, $1,299 headset due out next spring. The Meta VR glasses shift the computing, battery and storage to a separate, wired puck, allowing for a 5K display in glasses that weigh just 100 grams. The headset relies entirely on voice, hand gestures and eye gaze to control a range of apps across games, entertainment and productivity. The big picture: Meta has invested heavily in glasses and AI over the last several years. Now it sees those giant bets converging. "It just feels really clear that [AI]'s what's going to enable the next big platform," said Alex Himmel, Meta's vice president of wearables. "You're really starting to see that vision of VR and AR converging into glasses, starting to happen sooner." Between the lines: Meta is continuing a big shift on the privacy front. The company had already said it is working on a confidential virtual machine option for the Muse assistant. On Wednesday, Meta added that it is also readying "Private Processing" for AI glasses, a system designed to keep data protected even while it is being processed in the cloud, similar to Apple's Private Cloud Compute.
