Brian McNamara spent six years running the group behind Advil, Centrum, and Sensodyne before GSK spun off its consumer health division in 2022. Perhaps a fifth of that job is comparable to what his role is now, as CEO of Haleon, he estimates, such was the difference in responsibilities.
As CEO of a standalone company with its own London listing, he needed to educate a new board, manage a debt overhang, and make capital allocation decisions across a far bigger strategic playing field than the one that had been open to him under his former parent company.
McNamara also wanted to create a performance-focused, consumer-centric drive in a business that had grown up under the umbrella of a more cautious pharmaceutical company. But he discovered that âthe organization was quite tiredâ after its efforts to separate the company from GSK, and before that, to integrate two large mergers.
âThe team that took us through separation did a phenomenal job,â McNamara says, but he concluded that he needed to bring in new skills and energy. His response was to change 13 members of his 15-strong leadership team, bringing in fresh talent from leading consumer brand companies like Procter & Gamble, EstÃ©e Lauder, Unilever, and LâOrÃ©al.
With the initial sprint to define a new company and strategy behind him, hereâs how he describes the lessons from its spin-off, and why you shouldnât see such a milestone as a finish line.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: The split from GSK was four years ago. How do you think about this moment in the story?
Brian McNamara: I think about the journey of the company in phases. Phase one was to separate, build all the corporate functions, and deal with our leverage. At about the two-year mark, we got through all that. Then the next phase was laying out the new strategy, with our ambitions of reaching a billion more consumers and delivering industry-leading shareholder returns. Now, the last phase for me is to create a truly agile, performance-focused, consumer-centric company.
What was the culture you inherited? And what are you trying to do with it?
GSK was a great owner, but it was a pharma company, and the speed of a consumer business is very different. I joined GSK in 2015 through its Novartis joint venture, but we spent three years integrating that business. Then we announced the next deal, with Pfizer, and spent two years integrating that business. Then we spent a year separating [from GSK], and then we had to stand up [Haleon as a new] company. These are all incredibly internally focused things. So we needed to step back from that and create the right external focus and the right growth mindset and the right performance culture.Â
Whatâs changed in your own leadership role?
I ran this business for six years as a division of GSK. I think there was maybe 20% of that role that was the same. Itâs that big a difference. [Other CEOs] would talk to me about what itâs like to be a listed company CEO. And to a person, they said, âListen, Brian, logically, we can tell you. But until youâre in the seat, you really wonât understand it.â And they were absolutely right.
I had a fantastic board, but they were relatively new to the business, so they needed to be educated on it. Despite all our efforts to separate and have everything set up the way we wanted to, these things are hard and theyâre a little messy, so we needed to make some changes.
The other change was my external role, ensuring that Iâm staying current on technology changes and whatâs happening geopolitically, and talking with other CEOs on how theyâre navigating these situations. I found people are extremely generous with their time. When youâre in that kind of role, itâs a unique place to be, and you need a different kind of support and advice.
You said the organization was quite tired. What have you learned about injecting energy at those moments?
As we moved to separation, I think a lot of people viewed it as the end, like we were getting to the finish line. And, by the way, they probably had an unrealistic view of how great it was going to be as our own company. I was the division head for 21 quarters, and I got maybe 10 questions [on GSK analyst calls] over those 21 quarters, so we were a bit protected by the umbrella of GSK. If I could do it over again, I might change a bit of the messaging for people going into this. Because I probably didnât realize in my gut how different it was going to be, to be a listed company.
What I found is that purpose was really important to this company. So as we created the purpose, to deliver better everyday health with humanity, this organization connected to that. As we created a business that we wanted to be more agile, more consumer-focused, more performance-edged, for some people that really worked, and some people decided to make a different choice. But thatâs part of the evolution of the company.
Is your strategy of pursuing âinnovation-led premiumizationâ while expanding your reach to low-income consumers a bet that the economy will stay K-shaped for a while?
Thatâs right, and we see that on the premium side, thereâs tremendous opportunity. On the low-income side, thereâs tremendous opportunity. In the middle, thereâs quite a bit of stress and pressure on the consumer. Thatâs a US thing, but thatâs also a Europe thing, and weâre seeing that more globally.

I feel fortunate that weâre in consumer health because health really matters to consumers, and in health, brands really matter. The News
The diesel export ban that President Donald Trump is mulling in a bid to bring down record-high prices would backfire in two ways â further dividing Hill Republicans while risking even pricier gasoline.
Itâs not clear that the Trump administration will impose diesel export limits, which the president said this week that heâd explore as average national prices push past $6.50 per gallon. If Trump does push ahead, his main cheerleaders will be GOP candidates in tight races this fall who are eager to market more ideas to lower costs before the midterms.
But most congressional Republicans want nothing to do with the idea, no matter how close they are with the administration.
âThe better policy would be for states like California to lift the restrictions that theyâre imposing on the exploitation and the refining of diesel,â Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., told Semafor. âTaking down domestic barriers that have been exerted by states â that, to me, is a far better approach.â
US oil executives have fought hard against a ban, warning it would push prices higher worldwide; the European Union recently echoed their concerns, as its own diesel costs climbed following Trumpâs remarks. Energy analysts are just as critical, describing it as a Band-Aid at best â even if the constraints are nonbinding, as Energy Secretary Chris Wright suggested they could be in Pennsylvania on Thursday afternoon.
âThe diesel export ban, even if in a strong-armed âvoluntaryâ form, is a desperate idea that promotes inefficiency and ultimately higher prices,â said Skanda Amarnath, a former Federal Reserve economist who now helms the left-leaning organization Employ America.
The frosty response from Trumpâs own party is particularly notable after a year that began with Republicans stiff-arming his earliest ideas to lower the cost of living. Soon after, Trump pursued an Iran war that has since dragged on past the seven-month mark, straining the global economy and leaving voters increasingly pessimistic.
GOP lawmakers instead proposed alternatives like cutting gas taxes or tapping oil reserves: âWe should be looking at multiple solutions,â Hagerty said.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., lamented that âwe always keep skating to where the puck is at the expense of getting to where the puckâs going to be,â calling the ban âjust another example where, even in the White House, I think thereâs disagreements about the pros and cons.â
âThe president always makes the decision that is best for the American people,â a White House official told Semafor, adding that he âis evaluating all the options on the table.â
Know More
GOP Senate candidates like Ashley Hinson in Iowa and Mike Rogers in Michigan say a ban is necessary to bolster their statesâ struggling agricultural producers.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who also faces a tough race, said she hasnât âhad the chance to look atâ the proposal. Like Hagerty, she proffered a different solution: releasing heating oil from a federal reserve ahead of the winter.
Oil-state Republicans are harshest of all in their criticism: Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, derided it as âa gimmickâ that âwonât work.â
As plummeting consumer sentiment emboldens Democrats to push farther into GOP-held territory despite a cash deficit in some key races, they see the export ban as proof of the GOPâs desperation this late in the cycle.
âRepublicans can try one gimmick after the other, but they refuse to deal with the source of the problem,â House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters this week. âGo tell Donald Trump to end that war in Iran that no one in America asked for in the first place.â
While there is already legislation that would restrict diesel exports, the Trump administration doesnât need Congress to act, legal experts told Semafor. Trump can impose a ban unilaterally thanks to sweeping authorities provided by the International Emergency Economic Powers Act â the same law that provided his initial authority for tariffs since struck down by the Supreme Court.
âThis would be a very straightforward thing to do under IEEPA,â said Georgetown Lawâs Peter Harrell, a former State Department official who later oversaw supply chains on former President Joe Bidenâs National Security Council and National Economic Council.
Trump needs to declare oil shortages a national emergency, Harrell said, and sign an executive order restricting diesel exports. The order could allow the Energy Department to make some exemptions âin case there is some unforeseen adverse consequence,â he added.
Trump also has the option of wielding the Defense Production Act, as he did to crack down on exports of critical minerals and protective equipment. âBut that would be more complex,â Harrell said.
Room for Disagreement
The small group of Republicans who have called for a ban to tamp down prices say itâs a necessary step to shield farmers and consumers from the Iran warâs economic fallout.
Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, said on the Senate floor this week Trump should impose the embargo by executive order to âhelp family farmers who feed and fuel the world.â
Eleanor and Nickâs View
Democrats see the response to Trumpâs latest idea as proof that Republicans are flailing, but we see the clearest sign yet of what our colleague Burgess identified earlier this week: A GOP long in this presidentâs thrall is suddenly moving past him at an increasingly fast clip.
The degree of blunt talk we heard from Trumpâs party about the economic and political downsides of a ban â at least, on the record â would have been unimaginable last year.

e939e712fa60.text:
Ashleyâs view
The White House and its allies are lonely in their insistence that AI development in America must accelerate without governments setting ground rules.
At the UN General Assembly in New York City, as well as in meetings with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington this week, President Donald Trumpâs team was clear: US companies are the leaders in AI; they plan to keep it that way; and they reject any international attempts to rein in the technology.
Trump, with his call to leave AI âexactly where it isâ contrasts with Xi, who said responsible AI development is necessary â as other Chinese officials said this week that they support a global governance framework.
Without official support from the US, however, any such agreement will be difficult to execute. White House science and tech adviser Michael Kratsios rejected global efforts in a UN address that he called an âintervention.â
As a result, nations may be left setting nonbinding rules and best practices without the buy-in of the biggest companiesâ home country. Meanwhile, frontier labs are pushing forward with their own self-regulatory schemes, which will ask them to agree on testing standards in a highly competitive environment.
Yet even AI CEOs are more aligned with the UN than with Trump. Companies are pushing for coordinated âAI pacing,â saying they support global efforts to coordinate on safety and affirming that they cannot set the standards for responsible AI use on their own.
âThe international community will need to establish a common framework to manage the risks associated with frontier AI models,â said Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot, the French official who chaired the UN National Security meeting on AI featuring the CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face.
Polling shows Americans are largely skeptical of claims that the US must beat China at AI development, and that people are generally worried the technology is moving fast enough to pose a risk to their jobs and livelihood. Those surveys show worries about AI acceleration across party lines.
Trumpâs AI isolation from the world, and much of the electorate, puts congressional Republicans in a strange position, too. Theyâre advocating for AI safety and slowdowns and sponsoring bipartisan legislation to regulate AI, while their party leader presses the gas.
As Semafor first reported on Thursday, Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., has asked Secretary of State Marco Rubio to convene National Security Council meetings with cyber experts and AI developers about potential national security threats, including possible AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure.
âThe United States should continue to lead the world in the development and deployment of artificial intelligence,â Young wrote to Rubio. âMaintaining that leadership also requires ensuring that our government keeps pace with emerging capabilities and understands the risks they may present.â
Room for Disagreement
Trumpâs allies often see ulterior motives behind much of the current advocacy for stricter AI safety rules. Some argue that companies as big as OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic are seeking âregulatory captureâ by trying to shape legislation that only their companies will have the means to comply with, therefore giving themselves a leg up.
Others decry âdoomerism,â or the belief that AI could kill off humanity or eliminate jobs, as hysterical and speculative. Criticizing the effective altruism community, which many AI safety groups have connections to, is another burgeoning White House tactic.
But the core of the presidentâs message is simple: The US should do nothing that might give China, with its cheaper open-source models, an advantage in the AI race.

Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has announced that he is helping to fund a new $660m (Â£500m) fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and Djibouti
The project will include a 120km- (75 mile-) pipeline connecting Djibouti's Damerjog port to a distribution facility in Dewele, Ethiopia, as well as storage capacity of about 400 million litres.
It is expected to begin operations within 18 months.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said the pipeline would reduce the time needed to transport fuel from Djibouti's port to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, from five days to one.
The first phase will transport key petroleum products, including jet fuel, diesel and petrol.
Speaking at the ground-breaking ceremony, Dangote, Africa's richest man, said the project would strengthen Ethiopia's energy security and make its fuel supply chain more resilient.
Landlocked Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti's port for imports, including petroleum products. The new infrastructure is expected to reduce pressure on existing transport systems supporting industries, including transport, aviation, agriculture and construction.
Djibouti is also expected to benefit from increased port activity, job creation and higher government revenues.
The project is part of Dangote's wider expansion of infrastructure and manufacturing businesses across Africa.
Dangote Cement has production capacity of about 55 million tonnes a year, while his oil refinery in Nigeria currently has capacity to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day and is seeking to double that to 1.4 million barrels a day.
The refinery recently listed 4.1 billion ordinary shares on the Nigerian stock exchange, aiming to raise about $1.63bn (Â£1.2bn).
In Kenya, the company is due to break ground next week on a proposed 700,000-barrel-a-day crude oil refinery in Lamu.

1c298c9e5509.text: With midterms 39 days away and the outlook for President Trump 's party looking increasingly bleak, top Republicans say they're focused on three big questions for the final stretch: Are their attack ads working? Republicans expect a wave of private polling in early October to reveal whether their massive financial advantage is cutting into Democrats' leads. GOP groups had spent more than $450 million through Sept. 23, more than twice what Democrats had spent, according to campaign finance expert Rob Pyers. But Republican strategists say they aren't sure yet whether the barrage is working amid voter anger over high prices, data centers and Trump's war in Iran. Trump's political operation didn't begin pouring its $416 million war chest into attack ads until around Labor Day, and Republicans argue the ads need time to sink in. Strategists are particularly watching the Texas Senate race, where national GOP groups have sunk more than $100 million into helping Ken Paxton against Democrat James Talarico. Several polls have shown Paxton — whom GOP leaders have long viewed as a problematic nominee — trailing Talarico. "September tests whether your messaging moves the needle in races — and early October is when the map locks in," a Republican strategist told Axios. 2. Who gets cut loose? Republicans concede they'll have to make painful spending decisions by early October. That could complicate things for GOP Senate contenders Mike Collins in Georgia and Michael Whatley in North Carolina, who have consistently trailed Democrats Jon Ossoff and Roy Cooper despite millions in Republicans' spending. If Collins and Whatley's numbers don't improve, Republicans say they could redirect money to Michigan and New Hampshire, where the party is playing offense. Republicans also may have to spend more in traditionally red states such as Kansas, where polls show GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in a tight race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Hamilton would be the first Kansas Democrat to win a Senate seat since 1932. The race is tight enough to have drawn Vice President Vance to the state for a recent visit to try to give Marshall a boost. Trump's political operation, meanwhile, has begun spending to defend a South Carolina House district that Trump carried by 13 points in 2024. 3. What does Trump do? The president and his political team remain one of the midterms' biggest question marks. Trump's team said early this year that he'd campaign weekly for GOP candidates. That didn't happen. Trump now says he'll spend the final 30 days campaigning for candidates in 35 key Senate and House races. By early October, Republican strategists expect to see whether he'll follow through — and, if he does, where he goes. Where Trump doesn't go could be just as telling. Some Republicans in competitive races are keeping their distance from the unpopular administration . When Vance visited Iowa last week, GOP Senate candidate Ashley Hinson didn't appear, citing previously scheduled events. Then there's the question of how much Trump's willing to spend. Strategists say that should become clear in early October.

fa0bc73d38bb.text: A new analysis of the AI buildout shows its staggering scale: $10.3 trillion in estimated AI infrastructure investment through 2032. That amounts to 3.6% of GDP a year, dwarfing the investment booms that built America's railroads , highways, electric grid and telecom networks. Why it matters: The AI boom has become far too big and too costly for even the largest tech companies to finance alone. This has resulted in trillions of dollars in demand for outside capital — and the potential risks that come along with that, according to new research being presented Friday at the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity. Financing the buildout will require tapping bond markets, banks and private credit on a massive scale, adding to the flood of debt competing for investors' money at a time when borrowing costs are already surging. So far, those higher costs appear to be doing little to curb the industry's appetite to build. The knock-on effect: The more capital the buildout absorbs, the greater the potential pressure on borrowing costs elsewhere in the economy. In effect, any other entity that needs capital — from the U.S. government financing its $2 trillion per year deficit to an individual seeking a home mortgage or car loan — is in competition for funds with these hyperscalers. What they're saying: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia Business School professor behind the new paper on how the AI infrastructure boom is being financed, says the industry's appetite for investment remains remarkably resilient to higher rates. "They are so gung-ho to build these things" that even recent rate hikes and historically high long-term yields won't "deter too much of that development," Van Nieuwerburgh told reporters recently. Morgan Stanley estimates that Big Tech will need roughly $2.9 trillion to expand its computing capacity through 2028 — with more than half coming from outside investors, according to the paper. Case in point: Facebook parent Meta chose to finance most of its $30 billion Hyperion data center through outside investors, even though doing so meant paying substantially more to borrow. The project's debt carries an interest rate at least 1 percentage point higher than Meta likely would have paid on its own debt, adding more than $5 billion in costs over the life of the deal, the paper estimates. Threat level: The surge of outside money — much of it from private credit — allows the AI boom to keep scaling. But it spreads possible risks across the financial system, often through financing structures that are harder for investors and regulators to track. The infrastructure would need to generate $3.7 trillion in annual revenue in the next six years to earn a 10% return — roughly 9% of GDP. "The risks have been spreading throughout the financial system," Van Nieuwerburgh said, as the industry taps pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, private credit and other sources of outside capital. "With that expansion comes more complexity, more opacity, and it's becoming difficult to track where the risks are being distributed," he said. "These risks are coming to a pension fund near you, so to speak." What to watch: Van Nieuwerburgh says the influx of outside capital risks allowing the buildout to race ahead of actual demand. "Sooner or later, we're going to have oversupply, just like we do in every real estate cycle, and then the prices will collapse," he said. "I don't see why this time is different." The bottom line: The AI investment boom is now a major force in the broader economy, boosting growth while putting new pressure on capital markets and the financial system. " This AI buildout is by far the largest ... it's 50% larger than the second-largest, which was the railroad buildout," Van Nieuwerburgh said.

More tree planting, wetland restoration and drainage work could take place in parts of Northamptonshire to "safeguard nature for generations to come".
West Northamptonshire Council has approved its first Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) which was required by the Environment Act 2021 and is the responsibility of all authorities.
It said the area was one of England's "most nature-depleted areas" and its wildlife sites "are often small, in poor condition, and isolated from one another".
Working with a range of partners the council hopes to improve landscapes that are "under unprecedented pressure" with some species in decline.
A spokesperson for the council said: "A healthy natural environment is essential for tackling climate change and wider environmental challenges.
"The diversity of habitats and species provide essentials such as clean and plentiful water, food, clean air, productive soil, flood protection, shading and cooling, as well as benefits like space for recreation, exercise and wellbeing."
Nigel Stansfield, Reform UK's cabinet member for environment, recycling and waste, said: "Our aim is to safeguard nature for generations to come, and create cleaner, greener spaces that meet the needs of local communities and offer them an opportunity to connect with nature."
He said it was vital to have a workable strategy that sets out "how we intend to safeguard nature for generations to come."
Stansfield added he hoped the strategy would get organisations, landowners and local people to take action "to ensure our natural environment becomes more robust and resilient to provide the benefits we often take for granted".

A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 has formally said her allegation was untrue.
The unnamed woman filed a lawsuit in 2024 claiming she had been drugged and raped by Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, and Sean "Diddy" Combs at a party after the MTV Video Music Awards in 2000.
The stars denied the allegation and she dropped the lawsuit last year. Carter then sued her and her lawyers.
In a statement filed in that case on Thursday, she wrote: "Shawn 'Jay-Z' Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr. Carter. Mr. Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever."
The woman, known in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, also said: "My claims that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me while a third celebrity, [name redacted] watched are false. There is no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter.
"I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone."
Jay-Z and family's 'trauma'
Carter had vehemently denied the accusations, saying they were a "blackmail attempt" and describing them as "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations".
When the accuser dropped her case in February 2025, the rapper, who is married to singer BeyoncÃ©, said: "The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed."
The woman, from Alabama, has now been removed from Carter's lawsuit.
She said she had not received any money from the rap superstar or anyone acting on his behalf, and had not been paid to make her latest declaration.
The rapper is still suing the woman's former lawyers, led by Tony Buzbee.
In a statement to Rolling Stone, external, which first reported Jane Doe's new declaration, Buzbee said he had not seen it.
He said: "We have multiple lawyers (at least four) who dealt with Ms Doe long before she met me. She gave the exact same story to each. If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that's new information."
When Carter filed his lawsuit against the woman and her lawyers in February 2025, Buzbee claimed at the time that Carter's investigators had "repeatedly harassed, threatened and harangued this poor woman for weeks, trying to intimidate her and make her recant her story".
In her new declaration, the woman said: "I never received any threat from Mr Carter or anyone acting on his behalf."
'No due diligence'
Setting out the events that led to her allegation, the woman said she saw an advert on Facebook in September or October 2024 looking for people who might have sexual assault claims against Combs. "The ad triggered memories of being raped when I was 13 years old," she said.
She was contacted by a law firm but was not provided with a draft of the lawsuit containing her allegations and did not authorise it before it was filed in October 2024, she said.
She also said Buzbee and other lawyers acting on her behalf filed it "without conducting any independent investigation, background inquiry, or due diligence, and without obtaining any corroboration of the allegations".
She said: "The October Complaint alleges that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me when I was a minor while an unnamed celebrity watched. As discussed above, these allegations were false."
Buzbee also represents numerous other people who have made allegations against Combs.
Combs denied Jane Doe's claims, which his lawyer described at the time as one of a number of civil cases "pushed forward by an attorney more focused on media headlines than legal merit".
In July 2025, Combs was convicted by a criminal court on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends, and is currently serving a four-year prison sentence.
The BBC has contacted Mr Combs for comment.

Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray after fighting broke out this week between regional forces and the national army.
Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the much smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray.
"Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme.
The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.
Burbridge said there had been a scarcity of cash in Tigray for the past eight months, with people unable to access ATMs so the lack of internet services would be "devastating for everybody".
Many people rely on banking and mobile money applications for transactions, with the majority using Ethio Telecom and Safaricom's networks to access these services.
Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting fears of a return to a full scale civil war and reports of panic buying.
During the two-year conflict which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world.
Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions.
It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - with estimates that some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Sunday, the party in control of Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government.
On Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police.
There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara.
Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.
Additional reporting by Peter Mwai, BBC Verify

One of the three attendees who was shot at Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has passed away from complications stemming from his injuries, according to the Pennsylvania attorney general.
Jim Copenhaver, 76, was struck twice when a gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop. Another attendee, Corey Comperatore, was killed in the shooting and Trump's ear was grazed by a bullet.
Copenhaver died on Wednesday at a hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, according to a statement from the Allegheny County medical examiner shared with local media.
The gunman, 20-year-old Thomas Crooks, was killed by Secret Service after he opened fire.
In a post on his social media site Truth Social, Trump called Copenhaver a "true American patriot".
"More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice," Trump said. "Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne."
An attorney for Copenhaver's family said his dedication to the US was a "defining part of his life".
"As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered," the lawyer said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
In an interview with CBS a year after the Butler rally, Copenhaver and David Dutch, the third attendee who was shot, said they had been through infections and surgeries after being wounded.
Copenhaver was shot in the arm and the abdomen. A year later, the bullet was still lodged in his body next to his spine, he told CBS, causing him to walk with a cane.
Both Dutch and Copenhaver sued the federal government for damages in June, arguing the Secret Service failed to ensure their safety and was therefore liable for their injuries.
Republicans in the US House of Representatives also paid tribute to Copenhaver on Friday, saying in a social media post: "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance."

1091afd5ed7d.text: By — James Pollard, Associated Press James Pollard, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-live-day-4-of-the-2026-united-nations-general-assembly Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Day 4 of the 2026 United Nations General Assembly World Sep 25, 2026 9:17 AM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — New players hit the United Nations General Assembly sidelines this week as humanitarian groups searched for a counterweight to foreign aid cuts that have hampered global fights against disease, malnutrition and poverty. Watch the UN General Assembly live in the video player above. Nonprofits, foundations and corporations pack Manhattan ballrooms and closed-door meetings each September to direct some sliver of the world's attention — and funding — to their missions. Timed annually to the U.N. General Assembly's high-level meetings, the scramble is even more urgent after recent sharp declines in funding sent by some of the richest countries to poorer ones. Across the many conferences, forums and roundtables, the week exposed the gulf between the biggest aid organizations, who have the money and connections to weather this period of public aid retrenchment, and others grappling with their role in the changing landscape for humanitarian funding. Please check your inbox to confirm. Big movers still made big pledges. The Gates Foundation touted its $1 billion commitment to AI-powered tools for farmers, educators and health workers. Bill Clinton called on Clinton Global Initiative attendees to "step into the void created by retreating governments." There, former USAID administrator Samantha Power highlighted the ways her coalition to end childhood lead poisoning adapted when U.S. President Donald Trump's administration dismantled her former agency, USAID. "Philanthropies took risks. Governments took ownership. Multilateral institutions invested and the coalition kept moving," Power, a Harvard professor, said Wednesday at CGI. "That is the story of optimism I want to leave you with today." Other mid-sized actors described a mixed mood. Major foundations are still in "soul-searching mode," according to Global Fund for Children co-CEO John Hecklinger. His fund serves as an intermediary between well-endowed foundations and more grassroots nonprofits. Funders, he finds, understandably can't fill every gap but are also hesitant to maintain the previous status quo. "There's not this forced, strategic approach. The vision is disjointed," said Ann Lee, the co-founder and CEO of Community Organized Relief Effort. "It's very, very sort of ad hoc." Nonprofits turn to new donor countries Still, the U.N. sidelines brought out new nonprofits and funders eager for impact. Eleanor Crook Foundation CEO William Moore spent the week garnering support for his fledgling nonprofit to eradicate child deaths from acute malnutrition. Operation End Starvation launched this summer with a $100 million, two-year commitment from the U.S. State Department. But Moore anticipates needing 17 times more every year to purchase enough therapeutic foods such as peanut butter paste and get them into starving children's mouths. On Wednesday, OES announced a $5 million grant from the Gates Foundation. The goal is to eventually become for malnutrition what vaccines alliance Gavi is for immunizations or what The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria is for the deadliest infections. His pitch: OES will pay for overhead and match one-third of government money through philanthropy if countries cover the costs of the foods and delivery. Moore noted one lunch he had scheduled with Nigeria's health minister — part of a sector-wide shift to partner with the high-burden countries where aid organizations work. "They've said, 'We're ready for this. We're ready to take on this additional responsibility. We want to own the systems that are needed to improve the livelihoods of our people,'" Moore said. "We're really excited as philanthropy also to be of service to that." Moore's nonprofit is among a growing number turning to Arab Gulf nations. Moore said Operation End Starvation is having good conversations with official state donor entities and the philanthropies affiliated with their royal families. The region's leaders have recognized a need "to fund and to bridge the gap" created by aid cuts, according to Hammam bin Nasser bin Juraied, executive director of the Arab Gulf Programme for Development. An 'openness to collaboration' Other aid groups are working more closely with local partners in hopes of reducing overhead costs and increasing their impact. Education Cannot Wait Director Maysa Jalbout, whose nonprofit lost funding from the Trump administration, said they've committed to delivering at least half their funds through local organizations. She's trying to raise $600 million to provide education for 10 million crisis-affected children by 2030. She's actually continued to see support from Germany, the United Kingdom and Switzerland. She found herself speaking more than usual this week with philanthropies and the private sector about their "collective responsibility" to meet the increased demand for aid. That includes new partners to provide meals, water and electricity in schools. "There is this level of, at least on our part, openness to collaboration that comes out of need that maybe we haven't seen before," Jalbout said. Other leaders saw a greater presence from family offices — the private advisers who manage the affluent's wealth. Agnes Dasewicz, chief investment and program officer at the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet, said she encountered many family office advisers at a breakfast organized by an informal network of women in climate. Zambia is close to resolving a months-long dispute with the US over a proposed health agreement, the African nationâs foreign minister told Semafor. Mulambo Haimbe said Washington had agreed to remove contentious data-sharing provisions. The US State Department has not publicly confirmed the change.
The US has struck health agreements with African nations that involve sharing data with Washington about pathogens that could spark epidemics in their countries as a condition of getting the funding.
Haimbe said the two sides had also agreed to drop a disputed linkage between the health agreement and a separate critical-minerals deal, another point of contention that Zambia had raised publicly earlier this year.
âI believe that it has now been agreed that those provisions be replaced completely,â Haimbe said of the data terms. âThe linking, the coupling of the critical minerals agreement with the health assistance â¦ has also been set aside.â
Haimbe said the revised agreement was now at a stage where the two sides could sign it. The comments come after Haimbe met US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Chris Kulukundis in New York this week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. A statement from Zambia said the two countries had reaffirmed their strategic partnership and agreed to deepen cooperation in health, investment and critical minerals, but did not mention the disputed provisions or confirm that they had been removed.
The proposed agreement would provide US health assistance to Zambia over five years for a proposed grant valued around at $1.5 billion, with the US contributing just over $1 billion.
Know More
The dispute became public earlier this year as Washington sought to negotiate new health agreements with African governments that tied US assistance to commitments on health systems, data and other areas.
Zambia objected to provisions covering the use of health data and also resisted Washingtonâs effort to link the health agreement to cooperation on critical minerals. Haimbe said in May that the two agreements should be treated separately.
The disagreement came as Zambia was seeking to attract more investment into its copper and other critical-minerals industries while maintaining longstanding economic ties with China and developing closer commercial relations with the US.
Haimbe told Semafor that Zambia wants to work with both countries without giving either preferential treatment. âMe being in Beijing does not mean that Iâm against Washington and vice versa,â he said.

Alexisâs view
One of the most eye-catching features of this UN General Assembly has been the drive to secure deals â particularly for critical minerals â playing out on the margins of the gathering.Â
From the African perspective, the subtext boils down to one word: resilience. These deals offer partnerships, a ballast in a fractured world. And, increasingly, the aim is to partner with other countries closer to home.
Mineral-rich African nations are converging around a push to pivot from simply exporting raw materials to a greater emphasis on local processing to add value and jobs that can generate long-term growth. The underlying motivation for African policymakers is to untether their economies from commodity cycles and, by extension, the upheavals that come with them.
There are dangers, of course. UN Secretary-General AntÃ³nio Guterres warned of potential exploitation around the scramble for minerals. âNo more plundering,â he said at an event in New York.
But this emphasis on building resilience goes far beyond the issue of mineral resources. It was on show this week at Semaforâs The Next 3 Billion event, permeating discussions on a range of subjects. In public health, the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention stressed the need for the continent to manufacture its own vaccines, and to do so in regional groupings. Similarly, Africa Finance Corporationâs head emphasized the role African financial markets and pension funds can play in boosting economic growth.
Nowhere is this approach clearer than in energy. That thinking is driving talk of a refining hub in East Africa. And, again, the idea is premised on working together. One key success of Aliko Dangoteâs mega-refinery in Nigeria is that it showed the importance of developing autonomy. Africaâs largest crude producer, so long undermined by its lack of refining capacity, doesnât need to rely on the rest of the world for fuel anymore.
Kenyaâs trade minister told Semafor that for his country, the lesson is that resilience requires more than securing supplies, but also building the capacity to process them closer to home and doing so at a scale that serves regional markets. That is the logic behind the proposed $16 billion Dangote refinery in Lamu, which breaks ground next week. âAfrica is now standing up to its role,â he said.

ced8539bd7d4.text: House Republicans are on track to lose their majority just a little over one month out from the midterm elections, according to a nonpartisan election forecaster. Why it matters: Cook Political Report shifted 15 House races toward Democrats on Friday, the latest sign that the political environment is deteriorating for Republicans. Democrats only nee a net gain of three seats to take the majority. Cook now projects Democrats are most likely to gain between five and 15 seats, which would give them a 220-230 seat majority next year. The big picture: Republicans have spent much of the cycle arguing that redistricting and a sizable financial advantage would give them more breathing room. But new Democratic maps in California and Utah are largely offsetting Republicans' redistricting gains elsewhere, according to Cook. Republicans still hold a financial edge over Democrats. The National Republican Congressional Committee entered the final stretch with $13 million more in cash on hand than the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee — a record advantage for this point in the cycle. State of play: Democrats are favored in 208 races, compared with 205 for Republicans after Friday's ratings changes. There are now 17 Republican-held seats rated as Toss Ups, compared with just five Democratic-held seats. Republicans would need to win a majority of the Toss Up races to keep control of the House, according to Cook. Zoom out: Some of the most competitive House races are overwhelmingly in districts President Trump won in 2024. Trump is underwater in many of those districts, driven in large part by dissatisfaction with his handling of the economy , according to Cook. The median Toss Up district voted for Trump by 7 percentage points in 2024. What they're saying: "Nobody outside the D.C. bubble cares what a bunch of pundits slap on a race rating," NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella told Axios in a statement. "House races are won in the districts, and Republicans have the stronger ground game, air superiority across the battleground, and historic financial firepower while Democrats are still begging for cash just to prop up their socialist bailout fund." Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from the NRCC.

Cyber-criminals who hacked the FBI say they have extremely sensitive medical data for thousands of its special agents.
BBC News has seen samples of the stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations, which contain information such as blood and urine test results, and doctors' notes mentioning conditions such as a "shellfish and banana allergy".
The records include agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical concerns including 'blood in the urine' and 'high cholesterol'.
Experts say the hack - which the FBI is investigating - could leave agents vulnerable to scams, blackmail and targeted attacks, as well as help criminals impersonate law enforcement officers.
"The list maps thousands of agents against their medical and fitness records," said Etay Maor, vice-president of threat intelligence at Cato Networks.
"Passwords can be reset if stolen, but medical records cannot, so once this data is out, it stays compromised for good. That permanence, applied across an entire workforce, is what makes this leak so serious."
The FBI has not responded to requests for comment. However, on Wednesday it acknowledged the breach and said it was "aggressively investigating" how it happened.
The cyber-criminal group ShinyHunters claims it breached FBI systems on Monday, and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.
The group also shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.
Unusually, the hackers are not demanding money. Instead, they are seeking a retraction of an FBI advisory published in May, which they claim "offended" them.
The samples shared with journalists appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses.
The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.
Professor Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, has described the hack - if confirmed - "as serious as it gets when it comes to data breaches."
'Phishing, impersonation, identity fraud'
The news agency Reuters reports that some of the data includes information on agents, external involved in investigations relating to Russia, China and drug cartels.
Reporting by 404 Media suggests details of a previously little-known FBI hacking unit may also have been exposed, external.
It was initially thought the breach affected the FBI's 38,000 current employees, but the hackers now claim the number could be far higher.
The group says it underestimated the scale of the data theft and now claims to hold sensitive information on around 60,000 current and former FBI staff.
Jamie Akhtar, chief executive and co-founder of CyberSmart, said the hackers' claims should be treated with caution but that the breach appeared to be extremely concerning.
"Such data could be used for highly convincing phishing, impersonation, identity fraud, blackmail or even operations targeting law-enforcement personnel, making the potential implications particularly serious," he said.
The hackers, who communicate with reporters in English via the messaging service, Telegram, say they will publish the full dataset in five days unless the FBI meets their demands.
ShinyHunters is an international hacking collective that has been active since 2019 and has been linked to a number of high-profile cyber-attacks, including incidents affecting Rockstar Games and the education platform Canvas.
The group claims it exploited a vulnerability in an Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI, gaining access to multiple platforms including FBIJobs, FBI BEAST, which handles background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which stores medical records, and FBI BICS, which contains investigative information.
In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was still trying to determine whether the hackers had breached its systems directly or compromised a third-party provider.
"We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk," the statement said.

"Just as our ancestors reached across the ocean centuries ago to trade, to learn, and to build a better world, our two countries do really the same thing, and we're very proud of it," he said. READ MORE: As China and U.S. compete for AI dominance, both have shared concerns over safety Xi's day will begin at the White House, where Trump and first lady Melania Trump will host the Chinese leader and his wife, Peng Liyuan, for tea. Their visit falls during China's Mid-Autumn Festival, a national holiday when families traditionally gather to celebrate the end of harvest, sharing mooncakes, round pastries filled with a sweet paste, over tea. The Trumps feted their guests Thursday night with a black-tie state dinner attended by technology industry titans. Earlier in the day, Trump gave Xi a personal tour of his White House flourishes, including a gallery wall of presidents and a new 100-foot-long (30-meter-long) granite helicopter landing pad — and pointed out his ballroom, still under construction. Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan toured the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art. dc1e9e5a8ba2.text: By — Gene Johnson, Associated Press Gene Johnson, Associated Press By — Julie Carr Smyth, Associated Press Julie Carr Smyth, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/man-who-was-shot-during-2024-trump-campaign-rally-in-butler-pennsylvania-has-died Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Man who was shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has died Nation Sep 25, 2026 9:42 AM EDT James Copenhaver, one of three campaign rally attendees shot in 2024 during an assassination attempt on then-candidate Donald Trump, has died in Pittsburgh, his lawyer said Thursday. He was 76. Copenhaver was in the bleachers during the event in Butler, Pennsylvania, when a 20-year-old gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop, grazing Trump's right ear with one bullet. Copenhaver was struck in the arm and in the abdomen, wounds that left him with lingering injuries and walking with a cane. READ MORE: 5 things to know about the Trump rally shooting Two other attendees were also shot — David Dutch, who survived, and Corey Comperatore, who shielded his family from gunfire and was killed. Copenhaver died Wednesday at Allegheny Health Network's West Penn Hospital in Pittsburgh, according to a statement from the Allegheny County medical examiner cited in local media accounts. Copenhaver's lawyer, Joseph Feldman, said in a statement issued on behalf of the family that he died surrounded by loved ones. The statement did not specify if his death was directly related to the injuries he suffered at the rally. READ MORE: Butler still struggles with aftermath of assassination attempt ahead of Trump's return Copenhaver and his wife, Marianne Copenhaver, sued the federal government in June, alleging that the Secret Service and Department of Homeland Security had "utterly failed" to provide appropriate security at the rally. Copenhaver's injuries required multiple surgeries, including a transection of his colon, and he had lingering kidney and other damage, including a loss of feeling in his leg. The lawsuit described the wounds as "debilitating, grievous, permanent and life altering." The family's statement Thursday called Copenhaver above all else a devoted husband, father and grandfather who instilled the values of hard work, integrity and the service to others in his children. "James's dedication to this great country was a defining part of his life," it said. "As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered. James was a true American patriot who believed deeply in the freedoms and ideals upon which this nation was founded, and he embodied the very best traits of our great nation." In a statement posted to social media, Trump on Thursday called Copenhaver "a true American Patriot." "Jim showed tremendous bravery, courageously continuing to FIGHT, FIGHT, FIGHT, and maintaining a positive spirit despite unimaginable hardships," Trump wrote. Johnson reported from Seattle and Smyth from Columbus, Ohio. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a â¬120m (Â£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges.
In December 2025, the European Commission said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account.
But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control.
Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies.
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed an application, external with the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss âthe case.
It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court".
The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law".
It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy.
In a press briefing on Friday, external, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court.
He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act.
In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators had accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data.
Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability".
"Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms.
"The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X.
"The days of censoring Americans online are over."
His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely".
The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark.
The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU.
However, the EU is also conducting several other investigations into the platform, including one into its integrated AI assistant Grok over concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people.

A global boom in biofuels intended to ease expensive gasoline and diesel imports caused by the Middle East war could require an additional area the size of Germany to be converted for fuel production, new analysis by think-tank Chatham House found. As fuel prices soar, major economies including Brazil, India, Indonesia, and the US are advancing policies to expand biofuel mandates in petroleum products. Global biofuel production is expected to rise by around 70% between 2025 and 2030. French President Emmanuel Macron recently asked the European Commission to allow more biofuels in diesel to help keep prices under control.
Chatham House found that if growing demand was not carefully managed, it was likely to lead to more deforestation and push up prices of key crops and products, such as corn and vegetable oil, which would worsen food security. These long-term pressures on land would be difficult â perhaps even impossible â to reverse, the report said. âPolicymakers must therefore treat biofuels as a targeted transitional measure to help bridge the current oil crisis, rather than a permanent solution to the problem of energy security,â the reportâs authors concluded.

Oil prices fell slightly on news that Tehran made a new proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which Iranâs foreign minister said could unblock the key trading route within a week and restart talks to end the war. The proposal builds on an earlier agreement to extend a ceasefire, which collapsed in July. US and Iranian negotiators are discussing a phased deal to reopen the strait and lift Washingtonâs economic blockade, Reuters reported.

Timâs view
We should probably talk less about data centers. That might sound like blasphemy, and also hypocritical, given how often I do exactly that. To be clear, the challenges have barely begun: What weâre seeing being built today is only a small fraction of the data center capacity in the pipeline. âIf thereâs a single narrative in the market that is most starkly divorced from the fundamentals weâre seeing on the ground, itâs that the demand for AI infrastructure and the energy that supports it is in some way fragile,â Connor Teskey, CEO of Brookfield Asset Management, told me this week.
But if thereâs one thing I took away from New York Climate Week, itâs that the raging debate around AI infrastructure is just the tip of the iceberg of a much larger economy-wide struggle to cope with surging power demand. Between now and 2030, according to S&P Global, only 18% of new global power demand will come from data centers. The rest â air conditioning, onshore manufacturing, electrified buildings and vehicles â will also require an unprecedented and challenging power infrastructure buildout that barely got a mention in the dozens of conversations I had this week.
We can already take a few lessons from the data center experience that will apply to the broader power rush, starting with that itâs a crucible for innovation. âLarge loads have been a catalyst to so much new innovation because weâve never had the opportunity to think about adding net new clean power at a big scale,â Veery Maxwell, founding partner of clean tech investment firm Galvanize, told me. But itâs clear that without more rapid policy reform and technology advances, the imperative of fast growth will lead to the adoption of solutions that are both unsustainable for the climate and economically inefficient, such as installing more behind-the-meter gas turbines. Power project developers and their customers â Big Tech or otherwise â also need to be much more transparent and accountable to the communities they build in to avoid backlashes and blockages that only make the problem harder and more expensive to solve.
Even as policymakers and hyperscalers chip away at the narrow data center challenge, our current moment of AI infrastructure anxiety only proves how much we need to brace for many more difficult conversations ahead.
Thank you so much to everyone who took time to meet me this week. Special shoutout to those of you who joined our happy hour last night, always my favorite evening of Climate Week, which this year brought together people working on critical mineral mining, commercial-scale solar, trade research, energy bonds, low-carbon fuels, Taiwanese drones, environmental lawsuits, and the âGrateful Dead of carbon creditsâ (although donât ask me to explain what that last one means). Special thanks to our excellent contributor ChloÃ© Farand, who always makes my life much easier. Weâre back to our regular programming next week.

The News
Namibiaâs president has a message for foreign investors eyeing the countryâs critical minerals: build processing plants at home, or look elsewhere.
âWhen you are coming to Namibia, you donât want to be a briefcase business,â Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah told Semafor at an Invest Africa event on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week. âYou have to put up a processing plant in our country.â
Namibia is a mining-based economy, she said, whose minerals have for too long been exported raw and shipped back as finished goods. The country is a major uranium producer with deposits of lithium, rare earths, copper and graphite. In exchange for processing at home, she offered investors a long-term partnership and a stable place to do business, pointing to 36 years of peace since independence. She also wants foreign firms to team up with local entrepreneurs, âso that you become part and parcel of us.â
Her pitch reflects a hardening line across the continent. With demand for critical minerals surging and Washington and Beijing competing for supply, African governments are betting they have the leverage to demand more than royalties. About a dozen countries, including Guinea, Malawi and Zimbabwe, have restricted exports of unprocessed minerals to force local refining, borrowing from Indonesiaâs nickel playbook. The goal is to capture more of the value chain, and the jobs that come with it, rather than remain suppliers of raw inputs for other countriesâ industries.
Know More
Nandi-Ndaitwah is also going further than many peers on ownership. Asked whether local partnership would be mandatory for foreign investors, she told Semafor: âIn fact, we are putting it in the law.â
That promise has a long history. Namibiaâs empowerment framework won cabinet approval in 2015 and was meant to become law by 2018. It stalled over a clause forcing businesses owned by previously advantaged Namibians to cede 25% to previously disadvantaged citizens, which was dropped in 2018. Business groups also warned it would scare off foreign investment. As recently as last October, officials described the bill as at an âadvanced stage.â
Mining is moving faster. Namibia has required 15% local ownership for new mining licenses since 2021. Officials floated a 51% threshold last year, drawing pushback from the Chamber of Mines, which warned against importing other countriesâ models.
Nandi-Ndaitwah dismissed comparisons with South Africaâs empowerment rules, saying it depends on the approach. She cited tourism conservancies she oversaw as environment minister. There, investors started with 60% to 70% stakes that stepped down to roughly 51-49 with local communities.
Step Back
Behind the hard line is a jobs emergency. âOver 40% of our people are unemployed. And we are sitting on a time bomb,â Nandi-Ndaitwah told Semafor. âEven when you have your mine there, itâs not safe.â
Nandi-Ndaitwah won the presidency in 2024 on a pledge to spend 85 billion Namibian dollars (about $5 billion) creating 500,000 jobs by 2029, a steep target for a country of 3 million people with a GDP of about $14 billion.
She framed the stakes in continental terms: without opportunity at home, young Africans will keep leaving. âIf they have to leave, it is by choice,â she said. âBut as it stands now, they are pushed out by the conditions in the continent.â Offshore oil discoveries could bankroll her jobs promise, or deepen the sense that Namibiaâs wealth flows elsewhere.

Exquisitely preserved feathers, the first ever found in fossilized dinosaur poop, are providing a peek into how some ancient birds lived — and possibly went extinct.
Dense bristles suggest some of the feathers could repel water, possibly as well as those of modern pelicans, researchers report September 10 in Current Biology. And their central shafts are filled with air pockets, a trait that in modern birds keeps plumage lightweight yet stiff enough for flight. “That’s something we’re seeing for the first time in the Age of the Dinosaurs,” says vertebrate paleontologist Jingmai O’Connor of the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago.
The find also offers a clue that might explain why, among birds, there were winners and losers in the mass extinction that ended the dinosaurs’ reign about 66 million years ago. The ancestors of modern birds survived the asteroid-triggered event while many other types of birds, including the group these feathers came from, died out.
One of O’Connor’s colleagues unearthed the fossilized dung, or coprolite, in 2016 in Montana’s Hell Creek Formation. If it weren’t for a “lucky break” on the coprolite’s surface that put one feather on full display, her team might never have known it had feathers inside, O’Connor says.
The scientists used micro-CT scans to 3-D map the coprolite’s inner contents. Leg bones and fish scales suggest the bird was aquatic — a member of a group called hesperonithiforms — and that it had eaten shortly before its demise. And while some of the feathers resembled those of modern birds, others were more primitive and stringy, which could have made it difficult for the bird to maintain body heat.
Poor insulation might explain why hesperonithiforms and their close kin didn’t survive the deep chill that followed the asteroid impact, O’Connor says. But researchers need more feathers from various bird species during that time period to test the hypothesis. And fossilized feathers are incredibly rare.
Now that it’s clear poop can be an excellent guardian of plumage, O’Connor says, “people should start looking.”

101c4284b74c.text: ICE has received more than $75 billion to expand operations since President Trump returned to office — and wasted millions on scaled-back and mismanaged projects, a new GAO report found. Why it matters: In rushing to execute Trump's mass deportation agenda, the agency failed to properly develop a strategic plan, according to the Government Accountability Office report. Driving the news: The report found that ICE invested billions in six new initiatives without conducting necessary analyses. The report concluded that "[i]n the absence of a comprehensive strategic plan to guide detention expansion, ICE has wasted funds on unsuccessful detention initiatives and lacks important information about the long-term affordability of its investments." For example, the agency purchased more than $2.5 billion in detention facilities and warehouses but didn't calculate how much the properties would cost to maintain after the first three years, when its current federal funding will expire without additional congressional authorization. Catch up quick: ICE received an unprecedented amount of money to bolster operations, including $45 billion through the One Big Beautiful Bill in 2025 and more than $31 billion from the Secure America Act in June 2026. That additional funding helped increase ICE's daily detained population by 71% between January 2025 and July 2026. By the numbers: ICE rushed to purchase 11 warehouses to be converted into immigration facilities, but in June 2026, ICE officials told GAO that they were going to sell seven of them. The reported cost of all 11 warehouses was roughly $1.07 billion. The sell-off caused ICE to lose about $7.7 million in nonrecoverable purchasing costs, such as zoning assessments. ICE continues to pay utilities and security costs at these locations, costing an additional $12.8 million, per August estimates. The agency also spent $7.1 million on unneeded meals at Fort Bliss because the vendor contract didn't allow for fluctuations in occupancy levels. At Guantanamo Bay, the Defense Department spent $2.85 million assembling tents that were never used after Homeland Security determined they "did not meet detention standards." Zoom out: In some cases, the agency bypassed its normal contracting procedures, without negotiating costs. At the since-shuttered, so-called Alligator Alcatraz in Florida, the bed rate was $249 per day, approximately 171% higher than ICE's median rate of $92. What we're watching: GAO recommended ICE develop a comprehensive strategic plan, and the Department of Homeland Security agreed. But ICE projected that the plan won't be completed until Aug. 31, 2027, prompting GAO to conclude that given the "potential for continued waste of taxpayer dollars, more timely completion may be warranted." The Africa Finance Corporation advised Senegalâs government to resist growth-limiting conditions as Dakar negotiates its new $2.2 billion International Monetary Fund program, the multilateral lenderâs CEO revealed.
Speaking at Semaforâs The Next 3 Billion summit in New York, Samaila Zubairu said the AFC engaged directly with Senegalâs new administration after the discovery of undisclosed loans under the prior government sent public debt past 130% of GDP. Zubairu said Dakar should insist on revenue expanding investments â such as infrastructure and formalizing mineral value chains â rather than relying solely on fiscal belt-tightening. âGrowth is the only way out of tight fiscal positions,â he said, adding that African economies must be allowed to grow their economies to overcome debt problems. âWe canât pay back if we donât have revenue,â said Zubairu.
The AFCâs intervention in Dakar highlights an escalating effort by African regional lenders to counter traditional Western-led bailout conditions. The IMF classifies at least a third of African countries as being in debt distress, or at least at high risk of it. A number of other nations â such as Ethiopia, Ghana, and Zambia â have in recent years agreed to IMF deals that mandated budget cuts and sparked public debate and protests.

Nigeriaâs largest interest rate cut in two decades raised the possibility of an easing cycle next year, analysts said. The central bank said its 3.5 percentage point cut this week was a reset aimed at making monetary policy more effective.
The move should help debt-laden firms to refinance existing borrowing or access new capital more easily, Lagos-based investment bank CardinalStone said in a note. The move could also reduce the Nigerian governmentâs debt service costs, Nigerian economist Bismarck Rewane said.
Nigeria has faced high inflation in the three years since the removal of fuel subsidies raised costs for households and businesses. A sequence of rate hikes to tackle inflation is now giving way to cuts, and increased oil and gas export earnings that have boosted the naira should give room for further reductions, said David Omojomolo of Capital Economics.

Nigeria and the US signed an agreement to increase Washingtonâs investment into the West African countryâs minerals sector. The investment framework is the latest step in Abujaâs push to compete for investment dollars flowing into Africaâs minerals sector.
Governments across the continent are prioritizing local value addition instead of raw minerals exports and are focused on improving processing capacity. Nigeria, which values its minerals sector at about $700 billion, launched a grant program this year that will fund up to 70% of exploration costs by mining license-holders to identify untapped reserves of more than 44 minerals â including lithium, nickel, cobalt and rare earths â across 500 locations. Global demand for many of the minerals has soared in recent years due to their use in the energy transition or digital infrastructure that underpins AI.
